loop:0.t: The R L Loop. Learning by doing: try something, see what happens, adjust.

loop:1.t: Meet Pip. This is Pip, a mouse in a small maze. In the top corner sits a piece of cheese. Close by sleeps a cat. Two rocks block the middle. Pip has never been here. Nobody gives it a map or tells it what to do. Whatever it learns, it must find out by trying things. That is reinforcement learning.

loop:2.t: Two sides: agent and environment. Every R L problem splits the world in two. The agent is the one that makes choices: here, Pip. The environment is everything else: the walls, the rocks, the cheese, the cat, and the rules for what happens next. Pip controls only its own choices. It cannot move a rock or wake the cat.

loop:3.t: State: where things stand. The state describes the situation now. Since the cheese, cat and rocks never move, it is just Pip’s cell. Cells are numbered 1 to 20; Pip starts in 16. What the agent senses is its observation. Pip always knows its cell, so here they match. A camera robot sees only part of a room; then they differ, and it must act on what it observes.

loop:4.t: Actions: four moves. In every state Pip picks an action: up, right, down or left. That is the whole menu. The environment decides what an action does. A move goes one cell over, but if a wall or a rock is in the way, Pip bumps into it and stays where it is. From cell 16, down and left both bump.

loop:5.t: Reward: one number per step. After every action the environment hands Pip a reward, a single number. Stepping onto the cheese pays plus 1, onto the cat minus 1, and every other step 0, bumps included. Cheese or cat ends the walk. The task’s designer chose these numbers. Pip cannot change them and does not know them in advance. Built into Pip is only this: more reward is better.

loop:6.t: One turn of the loop. Put it together. The agent looks at the state and picks an action. The environment applies its rules and answers with two things: the next state and a reward. Then the same thing happens again from the new state. That cycle is the R L loop. Every method in this course runs on it.

loop:7.t: Counting time. Time counts t equals 0, 1, 2, and on. At time t, Pip is in state S t and picks action A t. The answer comes one tick later, so R tplus 1 is the reward for A t. A walk reads S0, A0, R1, S1, A1, R2, and on. The third move, A2, pays R3; a 14-move walk ends at t equals 14.

loop:8.t: Pip’s first move. Pip knows nothing yet, so it picks each action at random, as if rolling a four-sided die. It has no memory either, so it may repeat a bump. Its first roll, at t equals 0: right. The environment moves Pip from cell 16 to cell 17 and pays 0. In symbols: S0 equals 16, A0 equals right, R1 equals 0, S1 equals 17.

loop:9.t: A bump. Pip’s third move, at t equals 2: it is in cell 18 and rolls down. There is a wall below. The environment’s rule says Pip stays put, so S3 equals 18 again, and R3 equals 0. Pip’s wishes don’t matter here: the environment decides what an action does. A wasted move still uses up a time step.

loop:10.t: Round and round. The loop keeps turning: state, action, reward, next state. Pip bumps the wall again, steps back and forth, and walks into a rock. Every one of these moves pays 0. After 13 moves, Pip has collected no reward at all. Each log line shows t, the cell, the action, where Pip lands and the reward.

loop:11.t: The walk ends. On its 14th move, at t equals 13, Pip steps up onto the cheese: R14 equals plus 1. Cheese and cat are terminal states: when Pip reaches one, the walk stops, here at t equals 14. One walk from the start to a terminal state is called an episode. Afterwards Pip is put back in cell 16, and a fresh episode begins.

loop:12.t: Episode after episode. Let random Pip walk episode after episode. On this chart each bar is one episode: further right means walked later. Its height is how many steps it took. Teal ended at the cheese, rose at the cat. The first ten: 14 steps to the cheese, 13 to the cat, 67 to the cat, and so on. Only 3 of these 10 reach the cheese.

loop:13.t: What blind wandering gets. After 100 episodes only 26 reached the cheese. One clear reason: the cat can be entered from four open cells, the cheese from only two, and the cat sits on the way to the cheese. Episodes average 63 steps; about 4 moves in 10 are bumps. A small arrow marks bars too tall to draw; those episodes still ended at the cheese or cat.

loop:14.t: No answer key. Notice what Pip is never told. Nobody says “up was the right move in cell 10”. It only gets rewards, and in episode 1, 13 steps paid 0 before one paid plus 1. Which of those steps earned the cheese? Pip must work that out itself. This is the big difference from supervised learning, where every example comes with the correct answer.

loop:15.t: The goal. What is Pip trying to do? Collect the most reward in total over an episode, not just on the next step. Every move but the last pays 0, so the next reward alone says almost nothing. A rule for choosing actions is a policy. Rolling the die is one, the random policy; it averages minus 0.48 per episode. Later reels find much better ones.

loop:16.t: Your turn: be the agent. Now you are the agent. Tap an arrow to pick an action. The environment answers with the next state and the reward, and the log records each turn. Try bumping into a rock, then reach the cheese. When the episode ends, tap anywhere to start a new one.

loop:17.t: The same loop, everywhere. Bigger problems use the same loop. DeepMind’s Atari player D Q N, in 2015, saw screen pixels, chose joystick moves, and was rewarded by score changes. AlphaGo, in 2016, was rewarded only at a game’s end: win or lose. Chat assistants are tuned with R L from human feedback, R L H F: often the whole reply is one action, scored once by a model of which answers people prefer.

loop:18.t: Recap. The agent picks actions; the environment answers each one with a reward and the next state. That loop repeats until a terminal state ends the episode. Nobody tells the agent the right move. Its goal is the most reward in total. Adding rewards up sounds simple, but the next reel finds a catch.

returns:0.t: Rewards  and  Returns. Why the agent cares about the total, not just the next snack.

returns:1.t: One number per step. Back in Pip’s maze, with the same rules: cheese plus 1, cat minus 1, every other step 0. In the last reel Pip walked at random, and its first episode took 14 steps. Here are its rewards, one per step: thirteen zeros, then plus 1. How good was that episode as a whole?

returns:2.t: Add them up: the return. Add up all the rewards from a moment until the episode ends. That sum is called the return. For episode 1, counted from the start: thirteen zeros plus one, so the return is 1. The return is the score for a whole stretch of the walk, not for one step.

returns:3.t: Writing it down. The return from time t, G t, adds every reward after t: R tplus 1 plus R tplus 2 and so on, up to R T. T, the end time, is the episode’s number of moves. It starts at tplus 1 because action A t’s reward arrives one tick later. After the end nothing is left: G T equals 0. Episode 1: T equals 14, G0 equals 1.

returns:4.t: Why the total counts. Why not judge a move by its own reward? From cell 16, going up, going right and bumping the wall all pay 0. The next reward cannot tell them apart. What differs comes later, and the return covers the whole rest of the episode. One walk’s return credits all its moves, good or bad alike; averaging many walks sorts them out, as later reels show.

returns:5.t: Same return, very different walks. Now compare three random episodes that all ended at the cheese: episode 10 took 10 steps, episode 1 took 14, and episode 5 took 147. Each one’s return is exactly 1. With these rewards, the return ignores how long Pip wandered. A detour of a hundred steps costs nothing, so Pip has no reason to hurry.

returns:6.t: A step cost. A common fix is a step cost: the designer changes the rules so every step that does not land on the cheese or cat pays minus 0.1, bumps included. Cheese plus 1 and cat minus 1 stay, and both still end the walk. Every number from here on uses this new rule. Why 0.1? Just a small choice; we will see that the size matters.

returns:7.t: Shorter walks win now. Recount with the step cost. A cheese walk of n steps has n minus 1 ordinary steps, so its return is 1 minus 0.1 times (n minus 1). A cat walk scores minus 1 minus 0.1 times (n minus 1). The shortest walk, 7 steps, scores 0.4. Episode 10 scores 0.1, episode 1 minus 0.3, and episode 5 minus 13.6. The total now prefers short walks.

returns:8.t: A picture of all 100. All 100 random episodes. Across: steps. Height: return, with the step cost. Most returns are negative, so zero sits near the top; 8 long episodes fall off the right edge. Teal ended at the cheese, rose at the cat. Each dot sits on one of two lines, the cat line 2 below. Every extra step costs 0.1, so on each line shorter is better.

returns:9.t: A return from every step. Returns can start at any time. On the shortest walk, from cell 10, the last before the cheese, only the plus 1 is left: G6 equals 1. One step earlier: minus 0.1 plus 1 equals 0.9. Each return is the next reward plus the return after it. Backward: 1, 0.9, 0.8, down to 0.4 at the start. Later reels average such returns into a value.

returns:10.t: The return is a gamble. From the same start, random Pip’s returns vary wildly: the best of 100 scored 0.3, the worst minus 30.2. The return depends on every random move, so it is a random number; here it averages minus 6.7. Averaged over many episodes from a cell, under one way of choosing moves, it is what a later reel calls a value. Choose moves differently and that changes.

returns:11.t: Careful: the cost changes the goal. Size matters. With a cost of 1.5 per step, the shortest cheese walk scores 1 minus 1.5 times 6 equals minus 8, but running into the cat, 5 steps, scores minus 1 minus 1.5 times 4 equals minus 7. Now rushing to the cat has the highest return, so an agent maximising it would do that. It chases the return you wrote down, not the one you meant.

returns:12.t: Reward what you want. This happens with real agents. In 2016, OpenAI trained an agent on the boat racing game CoastRunners, where points come from hitting targets along the course. The agent found a lagoon where three targets kept reappearing. It kept circling there, crashing and catching fire, never finishing the race, and still scored more than finishing would. The reward said points, not winning.

returns:13.t: Tasks that never end. Pip’s walks always end. Many tasks don’t: a thermostat or a trading program just keeps going. These are continuing tasks; their sum has no last term. Earning plus 1 every step, such an agent’s return would be 1, 2, 3, growing forever. Two very different agents could both have an infinite return, and we could not compare them. The next reel fixes this.

returns:14.t: Your turn. Drag the step cost and watch three walks: the shortest way to the cheese, the 14-step episode 1, and the quickest way into the cat. Bars show each walk’s return. At 0 the two cheese walks tie. Small costs reward hurrying. Just above 0.2 the quick cat walk overtakes episode 1, and above 1 it beats even the shortest cheese walk.

returns:15.t: The big bet. R L rests on one idea, the reward hypothesis: any goal can be written as getting the largest expected return, the total reward averaged over the agent’s own random choices and the environment’s. Richard Sutton, a founder of the field, framed it. It is a working assumption, not a theorem, and still debated. In practice it has carried R L far, given carefully designed rewards.

returns:16.t: Recap. A reward scores one step. The return adds up all the rewards from a step until the episode ends, and that total is what an agent tries to make large. How you set the rewards decides what “good” means: a step cost makes short walks win, and too big a cost can make the cat win.

discount:0.t: The Discount Factor gamma. A reward tomorrow is worth a bit less than a reward today.

discount:1.t: Two loose ends. The last reel left two problems. With plain rewards, a 10-step and a 147-step walk to the cheese both return 1; a step cost fixed that, but too big a cost made the cat the best plan. And a never-ending task’s sum can grow forever. Discounting helps with both. Its knob must be chosen too, but it can never make the cat look good.

discount:2.t: Sooner is better. Would you take 100 rupees today or 100 rupees in a year? Most people take it today. You can use it now, and who knows what happens in a year. So a reward far in the future should count for a little less than the same reward now. R L builds this in with one number.

discount:3.t: The discount factor gamma. This is the discount factor gamma (gamma), from 0 to 1. The next reward counts fully. Each step of delay multiplies by gamma: one step, gamma; two steps, gamma times gamma, written gamma squared; k steps, gamma to the power k. The bars show gamma equals 0.9: 1, 0.9, 0.81, 0.73. gamma equals 1 means no discount; gamma equals 0 means only the first reward counts.

discount:4.t: The discounted return. Now redefine the return. The first reward counts fully, the next is multiplied by gamma, the one after by gamma squared, and so on. G t equals R tplus 1 plus gamma R tplus 2 plus gamma squared R tplus 3 plus ... With gamma equals 1 this is the plain sum from the last reel. With gamma below 1, every reward still counts, just less the later it comes.

discount:5.t: Back in the maze. Drop the step cost: cheese plus 1, cat minus 1, other steps 0 again, and take gamma equals 0.9. On the shortest walk, the plus 1 is the seventh reward, six steps after the first. So it counts 0.9 to the sixth: 0.9 times 0.9 times 0.9 times 0.9 times 0.9 times 0.9 equals 0.53. The discounted return of the shortest walk is 0.53.

discount:6.t: Long walks lose, cats stay bad. Same three random episodes. Episode 10, 10 steps: 0.9 to the ninth, 0.39. Episode 1, 14 steps: 0.25. Episode 5, 147 steps: about 0.0000002. Shorter walks win, with no step cost. A discounted cheese is always above 0, a discounted cat below 0, so the cat is never the best plan. Wandering forever earns 0: better than the cat, worse than any cheese.

discount:7.t: Counting backward again. Again count from every step of the shortest walk. From the last cell before the cheese, the return is 1. One step earlier, the plus 1 is one step later: 0.9. Then 0.81, 0.73, down to 0.53 at the start. The rule: G t equals R tplus 1 plus gamma times G tplus 1. A later reel builds on it; it is the seed of the Bellman equation.

discount:8.t: Reason 1: the future may not come. Why multiply by gamma? One honest reason: suppose each step has a 1 in 10 chance of cutting the walk short. The lights go out, or Pip is called home, and nothing more is earned, good or bad. We sent Pip along the shortest walk 10,000 times like that. It reached the cheese 5,302 times: 53.0 percent, close to 0.9 to the sixth, 0.53.

discount:9.t: gamma as a survival chance. gamma equals 0.9 acts like a 9 in 10 chance per step that the world goes on; a reward six steps away survives six chances: 0.9 to the sixth. Averaged over cut-offs, the fragile world’s plain return equals the discounted return exactly. That is reason one: the far future is less certain. It is a reading of gamma; in practice the designer picks it.

discount:10.t: Reason 2: sums stay finite. The never-ending task paying plus 1 per step has a sum that grows forever. Discounted with gamma equals 0.9, 1 plus 0.9 plus 0.81 plus ... reaches 6.5 after 10 steps, 8.8 after 20, 9.9 after 50. It never passes 10: by the geometric series, the sum of gamma to the k is 1 divided by (1 minus gamma). Now every agent’s return is finite and comparable.

discount:11.t: How far ahead does it look?. That same 1 divided by (1 minus gamma) is a rule of thumb for how far ahead an agent effectively looks. With gamma equals 0.9 it is 10 steps; with gamma equals 0.99, 100. Why? A fragile world ending with chance 1 in 10 per step lasts 10 steps on average. Not a hard cut-off: a reward that far away still counts about 0.35.

discount:12.t: A crumb or the cheese?. gamma can change which plan is best. A crumb worth plus 0.3 sits in cell 6, two steps up; eating it also ends the walk. The cheese, plus 1, is seven steps away. Crumb plan: 0.3 times gamma. Cheese plan: gamma to the sixth. gamma equals 0.5: crumb wins, 0.15 to 0.016. gamma equals 0.9: cheese wins, 0.53 to 0.27. They swap at gamma about 0.79.

discount:13.t: Your turn. Drag gamma. Pip does not know the maze, but we do, so for each setting we compute the best plan, with discounting, and Pip walks it. Later reels show how Pip learns this. Bars: each plan’s worth from the start. Below about 0.79 the crumb wins: the cheese is too far away to matter. Above it, Pip is patient enough for the cheese.

discount:14.t: The price of patience. Why not always use gamma near 1? Then the far future’s luck counts more too. Random Pip’s 100 discounted returns, at three gamma values: At gamma equals 0.5 they squash to almost 0: steady, but barely telling cheese from cat. At 0.99 they spread nearly from minus 1 to plus 1, so judging the start from a few walks depends on which walks you saw.

discount:15.t: Where you meet gamma. Discounting is old: economists discount future money the same way, through interest rates. In R L, the designer picks gamma as part of the problem setup. DeepMind’s Atari player D Q N used gamma equals 0.99. Games that always end, like Go, can use gamma equals 1. People? Studies suggest we care far more about today versus tomorrow than day 100 versus day 101, unlike a constant gamma.

discount:16.t: Recap. The discount factor gamma makes a reward k steps after the first count gamma to the k. Later rewards count less because the future is uncertain and sooner is better, and the sum stays finite even in never-ending tasks. Small gamma is impatient, gamma near 1 is patient but its returns vary more. The agent looks roughly 1 divided by (1 minus gamma) steps ahead.

mdp:0.t: Markov Decision Process. The board game that almost every R L problem is written as.

mdp:1.t: Writing the world down. Pip the mouse is back in its maze. Every step, Pip notes which cell it is in, its state, picks a move, its action, and gets a reward. This reel writes the maze’s rules down so precisely that a computer could run them. That rulebook is called a Markov Decision Process, or M D P.

mdp:2.t: Ingredient one: states. First, list every situation Pip can be in. Here a state is simply Pip’s cell, numbered as in the first reel, 1 to 20. Cells 7 and 13 are rocks, so there are 18 states. Two are special: landing on the cheese or the cat ends the walk. These are terminal states. That leaves 16 cells where Pip still has to choose a move.

mdp:3.t: Ingredient two: actions. Next, list the moves. Pip has the same four actions in every cell: up, right, down and left. One convention matters: if a move points into the outer wall or a rock, Pip bumps and stays put. That still counts as a step.

mdp:4.t: Ingredient three: rewards. Then the rewards. A reward is paid for the step that lands on a cell: plus 1 for the cheese, minus 1 for the cat, and the walk ends there. Every other step pays 0, bumps included. In general a reward may depend on the cell, the move and the landing cell, written R(s, a, s prime). Here only the landing cell matters.

mdp:5.t: A wet floor. Now a twist: someone mopped the floor. When Pip tries a move, it goes that way 8 times in 10. The other 2 times it slides sideways, relative to the direction it tried: 1 in 10 to its left, 1 in 10 to its right. It never slides backwards. So the same action can lead to different cells. The world has become random.

mdp:6.t: Try it at the start. Pip stands at the start and tries right, again and again. Right leads on to the next cell. A slide up lands one cell higher. A slide down hits the outer wall, so Pip stays put. The bars count where each try ended, one bar per outcome. In the first 10 tries: 9 moved right and 1 slid up.

mdp:7.t: A thousand tries. Keep going to 1000 tries. The bars settle: 795 moved right, 102 slid up and 103 stayed put. That is 0.795, 0.102 and 0.103 of the tries, close to the 0.8, 0.1 and 0.1 built into the floor. Each single try is a surprise, but the chances behind them are fixed. The dashed lines mark 800 and 100.

mdp:8.t: Transition probabilities. These chances are written P(s prime given s, a), read “P of s prime given s and a”: the probability that Pip lands in cell s prime, the next state, after taking action a in state s. If Pip bumps and stays put, s prime is s. For each cell and move, the landing chances add up to 1. Sixteen cells times four moves: 64 such lists.

mdp:9.t: The whole rulebook. The pieces together: states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards, and the discount gamma (gamma), here 0.9. Like rewards, the designer picks gamma: it says what we want, not how the floor behaves. That list is an M D P. Pip does not read this rulebook; it learns by trying, like those 1000 tries. Computing the best plan from the rulebook, as the discount reel did, is called planning.

mdp:10.t: Why “Markov”?. Here is the key assumption. The chances of what happens next depend only on the current state and action, not on the path that led there. This is the Markov property. Pip can reach this cell straight from the start, or after a detour along the bottom row. Either way, trying right gives the same 0.8, 0.1 and 0.1.

mdp:11.t: Checking it in data. Over 2000 random walks, whenever Pip tries right here, we log where it came from and where it lands, skipping bumps in place. From below: 0.799, 0.093, 0.108. From the right or above: nearly the same. This is the test when the rules are hidden: rows further apart than luck allows mean the cell is not enough. Built Markov, our maze passes.

mdp:12.t: When the cell is not enough. New rule: the cat wakes after Pip’s 10th step, and pounces if Pip is beside it. Next to the cat, step 4 is safe, step 12 is not. The cell alone no longer predicts what comes next: not Markov. Adding “is the cat awake?” fails: a sleeping cat might wake next step. The state must hold the clock: the cell plus steps taken so far.

mdp:13.t: Cells, not paths. Why does Markov matter so much? Because of it, anything Pip works out about what to do or what to expect can be stored per cell, for just 16 cells. If the past mattered, Pip would need an entry for every path instead. Counting paths from the start, a bump counting as a step: 3 after one step, 37 after three, 202,435 after ten.

mdp:14.t: Every visit counts. In those 2000 random walks, Pip stood on this cell 16,047 times. 13,887 of those arrivals came by a path it had never walked before. Filed by path, almost every page of Pip’s notebook would hold one lonely visit. Filed by cell, all 16,047 share one page. Markov alone allows that pooling: what happens next does not depend on how Pip got here.

mdp:15.t: Your turn. Pip memorises a shortest route as a fixed list: up three, then right four. The slip chance, the total chance of sliding sideways, was 0.2 so far. Drag it: Pip runs the list 1000 times. Bars count endings: cheese, cat, or nowhere. At 0.2 only 229 reach the cheese: a list cannot react to slips. A rule for every cell can: a policy, coming next.

mdp:16.t: Where MDPs are used. The name honours Andrey Markov, who studied chains of random events in the early 1900s. In the 1950s Richard Bellman used MDPs for planning under uncertainty. Robot navigation, stock and inventory planning and board games are often MDPs. When one snapshot is not Markov, people widen the state: DeepMind’s Atari player fed in the last four screen images, so a ball’s motion showed.

mdp:17.t: Recap. An M D P writes a world down as states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards and gamma. The same action can lead to different cells, but the chances are fixed. The Markov property says the next step depends only on the current state and action. That is what lets everything Pip gathers be filed per cell instead of per path.

policy:0.t: Policies. The agent’s rulebook: in this situation, do that.

policy:1.t: The list that broke. In the last reel, Pip memorised the shortest route as a list of seven moves. On the wet floor, only 229 of 1000 runs reached the cheese. Here is why. On move 2, Pip slid right into a new cell. The list still said “up” and then “right”, which here point into rocks. In this run, Pip bumped five times, and the list ran out.

policy:2.t: A rule for every cell. Instead Pip writes a rule card: one move for every cell, a policy, written pi (pi). pi of s is the move it picks in state s. Why is the cell enough? The maze is Markov: the cell tells all about what can happen next. This card, policy A, follows shortest routes; at the start, where up and right tie, it picks up.

policy:3.t: Slip, then recover. Watch policy A on the wet floor. On move 2, Pip slides right instead of going up. No problem: the new cell has its own arrow, pointing back to the route. Pip reaches the cheese in 9 steps instead of 7. A policy keeps working after surprises, because it never assumes where Pip will be. It only asks: where am I now?

policy:4.t: How many rule cards?. How many policies are there? Each of the 16 cells can hold any of 4 arrows: 4 multiplied by itself sixteen times, about 4.3 billion. Most are silly: arrows into walls or round in circles. Scoring one card fairly takes thousands of walks, so trying them all is hopeless. Finding a good one without trying everything is what the rest of R L is about.

policy:5.t: Two candidates. A second card, policy B, copies A with one arrow changed: in cell 8, just left of the cat, B points down, into a rock. Pip only lands in cell 8 by slipping down from the top row, so most of the time B looks just as good. Is it really worse? Not knowing the maze’s rules, Pip must find out by walking.

policy:6.t: Scoring a walk. Score each walk by its return: the rewards, each discounted by gamma (gamma) equals 0.9 per step of delay. The only reward is the last: 0.9 to the power of steps minus one, plus for cheese, minus for cat. Seven steps: 0.9 to the sixth, 0.53. Walks still going at 100 steps stop and score 0, having earned nothing; A and B never get there.

policy:7.t: Walk 1: a tie. Pip walks once with each card. To be fair, both walks use the same dice: the same slips at the same moments, so any difference comes from the arrows, not luck. Walk 1: twice Pip slides into the outer wall and stays put, but both walks follow the same arrows to the cheese in 9 steps. Return 0.43 each. It tells nothing about the difference.

policy:8.t: Walk 2: the trap. On the top row, Pip slips down into the changed cell. A points up: Pip climbs back to the cheese in 10 steps: 0.39. B points into the rock. Pip bumps, then slips into the cat: minus 0.48. Not just bad luck: from cell 8, B can only bump or slip into a rock or the cat, so once there it always ends on the cat.

policy:9.t: Five thousand walks. Up: the average return of all walks so far. Across: number of walks. The lines jump early, then flatten. After 5000: A 0.331, B 0.288, each give or take about 0.005 of luck, so the gap is real. B ends on the cat 1,030 times, A 641. Judge a policy by its average return. Measured from every cell, that average is its value: next reel.

policy:10.t: Rolling dice on purpose. So far each cell held one fixed move: a deterministic policy. A stochastic policy holds chances instead, written pi(a given s), read “pi of a given s”: the chance of action a in state s. The first reel’s random Pip was one: a quarter per move. Careful: two kinds of chance now. The wet floor is the world’s chance; these dice are Pip’s choice.

policy:11.t: Why roll dice?. Two reasons. A learner must explore: slips reach new cells, but always following its arrow, Pip never tries other moves. Against an opponent, predictability is punished: in rock, paper, scissors, play each a third of the time. A fixed maze has no opponent. Each cell has a best move, so putting all the chance on it cannot hurt: the best policy needs no dice.

policy:12.t: Dial in randomness. Drag epsilon (epsilon): on each move, with chance epsilon, Pip ignores its arrow and picks a random move. Otherwise it follows policy A. At 0, plain policy A: 0.331. At 0.2, the 0.85 and 0.05 card from two steps back: 0.233. At 1, Pip ignores its card: minus 0.031, close to 0 rather than clearly negative, because discounting shrinks the late endings of long random walks.

policy:13.t: Your turn: write a card. Tap a cell to turn its arrow a quarter clockwise. After each change Pip walks your card 5000 times from the start, same dice. A scores 0.331. Can you beat it? Barely. Exactly, from the rulebook, the best card is worth 0.3345, A 0.3339; it differs from A in one cell and scores 0.332 on these walks. Or break A: which cells matter?

policy:14.t: Where policies live. A thermostat runs a tiny deterministic policy: too cold, heat on; warm enough, heat off. A robot’s controller maps sensor readings to motor commands. AlphaGo, which beat Lee Sedol at Go in 2016, used a policy network: given a board, it output a probability for every legal move, a stochastic policy learned first from millions of human moves, then improved by playing against itself.

policy:15.t: Recap. A policy pi is a rule from state to action: an arrow in every cell, so it keeps working after any slip. It can be deterministic, or stochastic with pi(a given s). To compare policies, run each many times and average the returns. One walk is luck. That average, from every cell, is next: the value of a policy.

values:0.t: Value Functions. How good is it to be here? How good is this move?

values:1.t: Back in the maze. Stepping onto the cheese pays plus 1, onto the cat minus 1, and either ends the walk; other steps pay 0. The return adds the rewards, each step later multiplied by one more gamma (gamma), here 0.9. The floor is dry again: every move goes where Pip intends. All randomness now is Pip’s own habit, so numbers differ from the policy reel’s on purpose.

values:2.t: Pip’s policy. Pip uses policy A from the policy reel, the rule card with an arrow in every cell, with the epsilon (epsilon) dial at 0.2: one move in five is a random direction. So the arrow wins 85 times in 100, each other move 5 times. Bumping into a wall or rock leaves Pip in place, and still counts as a step.

values:3.t: One walk. How good is it to start in the bottom-left corner with this policy? Let’s try. Walk 1: Pip follows the arrows up and along the top and reaches the cheese in 7 steps. The first step’s reward counts fully, and each later one is multiplied by one more 0.9. The plus 1 came on step 7, so the return is 0.9 multiplied 6 times: 0.53.

values:4.t: Same start, different walks. Walk 2: Pip gets distracted twice, once stepping back down, once bumping the top wall. Cheese on step 10, return 0.39. Walk 3: beside the cheese, a random move points down, onto the cat. Return minus 0.48 after 8 steps. Walk 4’s only random move, at the start, picks up, the arrow’s own direction, so nothing changes: 0.53. Same cell, same policy, different returns.

values:5.t: Keeping score. Let’s put the returns on a chart. Across is the walk number, up is the return, from minus 1 to plus 1. Each dot is one walk: gold means the walk reached the cheese, rose means the cat. The dark line is the average of all returns so far. After four walks: (0.53 plus 0.39 minus 0.48 plus 0.53) divided by 4 equals 0.24.

values:6.t: Many walks. Pip keeps walking. Early on the average jumps around: after 10 walks it is 0.28, after 100 walks 0.44. Each new walk moves the average less and less. After 1000 walks it has settled at 0.40, give or take about 0.015 of leftover wobble. That settled number is what we were after.

values:7.t: The value of a cell. The average return of many walks that start in a cell and follow the policy is that cell’s value. In probability terms it is the expected discounted return: the number the average closes in on as walks pile up. We write it V of s, said “V of s”, where s is the state, here a cell. So V(start) is about 0.40.

values:8.t: A whole notebook. Now do the same from every cell: 1000 walks each, and write the average in the cell’s corner. That is Pip’s notebook of values for this policy. Stronger gold shading means a higher value. The cheese and cat cells get no walks. Standing on them, the walk is already over, so their value is 0 and they stay blank.

values:9.t: Reading the notebook. Beside the cheese the value is 0.87, not 1. The arrow points at the cheese, but one move in five is random, and one in twenty goes down, onto the cat. Two cells three steps from the cheese: on the top row 0.68, beside the cat only 0.60. From there, a random move to the right lands on the cat.

values:10.t: A different policy. Meet the Wanderer: a policy with no arrows at all. Every single move is random. Same maze, same rewards, same way of computing returns. The Wanderer’s first walk from the start wanders back and forth and does find the cheese, but only on step 35. By then the plus 1 has shrunk to a return of 0.03.

values:11.t: The Wanderer’s notebook. 1000 Wanderer walks from every cell give a new notebook. Every value is negative: the start is worth minus 0.03, the cell left of the cat minus 0.53. Why? A random walker usually meets the cat first: from the start, 77 walks in 100 end there, about three in four. The cat has four entry cells, the cheese two. Long walks shrink any reward to almost nothing.

values:12.t: Values belong to a policy. Same cell, two numbers: the start is worth 0.40 under the arrows, minus 0.03 under the Wanderer. A value means something only for a given policy, so we may write V with a small pi (pi). The arrows win in every cell, so they are the better policy wherever Pip starts. If each won somewhere, neither would be better everywhere; it would depend on the start.

values:13.t: How good is a move?. The notebook says how good a cell is. To choose a move, Pip wants to know how good each move is. The action value, written Q of s, a, said “Q of s and a”, is the average return when Pip takes move a first, then follows the policy as usual. It is measured the same way: many walks, each forced to start with that move.

values:14.t: The four moves beside the cheese. Right pays plus 1 at once: Q equals 1. Down is the cat: minus 1. Left gives 0.69; up bumps the wall, wasting a step: 0.80. The best move has the biggest Q. Weighted by the policy’s chances, pi(a given s), 0.85 for the arrow, 0.05 per other move: 0.85 times 1 plus 0.05 times (0.80 minus 1 plus 0.69) equals 0.87, the notebook value.

values:15.t: Why values are worth having. V answers “how good is it here?”: compare cells, and policies cell by cell. Q answers “how good is this move?”: the biggest Q is the best next move if Pip follows the policy afterwards. If a move’s Q beats the habit’s value, switching to it only helps: every visit to that cell gains, and gains add up. Much of R L builds on this.

values:16.t: The catch. Measuring by walking is slow. This notebook took 16,000 walks and 76,481 steps. The Wanderer’s took 601,861 steps. And every number is still a little noisy. Yet neighbouring numbers are clearly linked: 0.87 beside the cheese, 0.76 one step back, a little less than 0.9 times as much. The next reel turns that link into a shortcut, the Bellman equation.

values:17.t: Your turn. Drag the slider to change how often Pip moves at random; the notebook is remeasured with 1000 walks per cell. With no randomness every walk from a cell is identical, so one walk gives the value. At “always”, Pip is the Wanderer. Tap a cell to send Pip on one walk from there and compare its return with the notebook.

values:18.t: Where values show up. AlphaGo, in 2016, had a value network: shown a Go position, it estimated the game’s expected result for the player to move, plus 1 for a win, minus 1 for a loss. Chess programs score positions in a similar spirit. Many modern learners, including those used to fine-tune chatbots, train a value estimate called a critic to judge how well things are going.

values:19.t: Recap. A cell’s value is the expected discounted return when Pip starts there and follows its policy: the average over many walks. Change the policy and the values change. Q scores a move: take it first, then follow the policy. Pick the move with the biggest Q.

bellman:0.t: The Bellman Equation. Value of here equals reward now plus discounted value of next.

bellman:1.t: A shortcut?. Here is Pip’s notebook from the last reel: for each cell, the average return of 1000 walks that start there and follow policy A with one move in five random, on the dry floor. Measuring it took 76,481 steps of walking. Neighbouring numbers look related. If the value of a cell could be worked out from its neighbours, Pip could skip most of that walking.

bellman:2.t: Split a walk in two. One walk from the start: cheese on step 7, return 0.53. Cut after the first step, the rest is its own walk from the cell above, with return 0.9 multiplied 5 times: 0.59. Seen from the start, everything after step 1 counts 0.9 times less. Return equals first reward plus 0.9 times return of the rest equals 0 plus 0.9 times 0.59 equals 0.53.

bellman:3.t: Average both sides. The split holds for every walk, so on average too. The rest is a fresh walk from the landing cell: Pip’s rule ignores the past, the Markov property. Check: 876 walks went up first, about 850 expected. Their rests averaged 0.45, near that cell’s value, 0.46. So value here equals average of [ reward plus 0.9 times value where Pip lands ]: the Bellman equation.

bellman:4.t: What exactly is averaged?. Two kinds of chance. Pip’s own: which move, pi(a given s): 0.85 for the arrow, 0.05 each other. The floor’s: where it lands, P(s prime given s, a). Today’s dry floor sends each move to one known cell. On the mdp reel’s wet floor, a move goes ahead 8 times in 10, each side once in 10, and the rule averages over that too.

bellman:5.t: Where can Pip land?. Take the cell beside the cheese. The arrow says right: 85 times in 100, 80 by habit and 5 by chance. Each other move: 5 times in 100. Right: the cheese, plus 1, and the walk ends, so the next value is 0. Down: the cat, minus 1, also 0 after. Up bumps the wall: Pip stays, reward 0. Left: one cell back, reward 0.

bellman:6.t: Check it with real numbers. Each move scores its reward plus 0.9 times the notebook value where it lands: on a dry floor, exactly its Q. Up stays here, worth 0.87; left lands on 0.76. The last reel’s forced walks measured these Qs as 0.80 and 0.69, with a little noise. Weighted by how often each move happens: 0.87. The notebook says 0.87: to two decimals, the rule holds.

bellman:7.t: Another cell. The start: up, 85 times in 100, lands on 0.46; right on 0.45. Down and left bump, so Pip stays on 0.40. All rewards are 0, so the rule is just 0.9 times the average landing value. The rule gives 0.41, the walks gave 0.40. Close, not equal: even 1000 walks leave a little noise. True values obey it exactly; soon we compute them.

bellman:8.t: A recipe with no walking. Turn the rule around to compute values. Start with a blank notebook, every number 0. Apply the rule to every cell, using the current numbers for the landing cells, and write the results into a fresh notebook. One pass over all cells is a sweep. Repeat until the numbers stop changing; we will see why they do. Pip never takes a step.

bellman:9.t: Sweep 1. From all zeros, only cells next to the cheese or the cat change. Beside the cheese: 0.85 times 1 for the cheese, 0.05 times minus 1 for the cat, the rest are 0: 0.80. The cell below the cheese gets the same, 0.80. The two other cells beside the cat get minus 0.05: a 5 in 100 chance of stepping onto it. Everything else stays 0.

bellman:10.t: The news spreads. Each sweep, good news moves one cell further from the cheese. After 3 sweeps each number counts exactly the discounted rewards expected in Pip’s first 3 steps; after 7, in its first 7. So the start stays near 0 until sweep 7: the cheese is 7 steps away. Then it jumps, then creeps up as longer walks add their smaller rewards.

bellman:11.t: Until nothing changes. The start cell’s number after each sweep: across, sweep number; up, value. The dashed line is where it settles. By sweep 13 every number has its final two decimals; by sweep 16 none moves by more than 0.001. Why settle? The rule multiplies every landing value by 0.9, so each sweep leaves at most 0.9 times the old biggest error, here even less.

bellman:12.t: Walks versus sweeps. Left: 1000 walks per cell. Right: 16 sweeps. They agree within 0.014, and the sweeps have no noise. From here on, the notebook shows swept values. The walks took 76,481 steps. The sweeps did 16 passes over 16 cells, 4 moves each: 1,024 small sums, each about as cheap as one step. A wet floor, with three landings per move, would triple the sums.

bellman:13.t: The catch. Sweeps need the maze’s rules: for every move in every cell, where Pip can land, how likely, and what it pays. That is a model: here the world’s rulebook, not a neural network. The walks needed none of it. Often no model is given. Later reels keep the Bellman rule but swap known probabilities for real experience, a step at a time: T D learning.

bellman:14.t: The best Pip could do. The best any policy could do: pick the best move in every cell, and keep picking the best afterwards. Value here equals the biggest, over moves, of reward plus 0.9 times value where that move lands. That is the Bellman optimality equation. Its solution, V star, is the best policy’s value: no policy beats it in any cell. Swept, it settles after 7 sweeps.

bellman:15.t: Reading the best map. Each cell’s best move has the biggest Q: reward plus 0.9 times V star where it lands. These arrows lead straight to the cheese; on ties, as between the rocks, either is best. The best policy needs no random moves: the start is worth 0.53, against 0.40 for Pip’s habit. On a wet floor, scores would first average over landings, then the max picks.

bellman:16.t: Your turn. Drag the slider to run more sweeps of Pip’s policy, starting from all zeros, and watch the news spread from the cheese and the cat. Tap any cell to see the rule at work there: its four moves, how likely each is, and the numbers from the sweep before.

bellman:17.t: Where it shows up. In the 1950s Richard Bellman called this dynamic programming: link each state to those one step later. Planners with a model sweep it. Without one, T D learning nudges values toward reward plus gamma times the next state’s value. Q-learning and the 2015 Atari player D Q N aim at reward plus gamma times the biggest Q in the next cell: the best next move’s value.

bellman:18.t: Recap. A walk’s return is its first reward plus gamma times the return of the rest. Averaging gives the Bellman equation: value here equals expected next reward plus gamma times expected value of where you land. Sweep it over all cells until nothing changes to get values without walking, given the model. Put a max over moves inside for the best possible values.

explore:0.t: Exploration versus Exploitation. Order your favourite dish, or try something new?

explore:1.t: Tonight’s dinner. Meet Pip, a mouse with a favourite café: The Usual. The food there is always good. Last week a New Place opened down the road. It might be wonderful. It might be awful. Pip can only eat in one place tonight. Which one?

explore:2.t: Two ways to choose. Going back to The Usual is exploiting: using what you already know works. Trying the New Place is exploring: taking a choice you know less about, to learn something. Exploring might cost Pip a good dinner tonight. It might also find a better café for every night after.

explore:3.t: It depends on what’s ahead. If Pip leaves town tomorrow, tonight is the last dinner. A great discovery would have no later dinners to improve, so The Usual is the safe bet. If Pip just moved here, a great find pays off for hundreds of dinners. Exploring is an investment: you pay now, and the reward comes later, from better choices.

explore:4.t: The cheese arcade. To study this, Pip visits an arcade with four cheese machines, A, B, C and D. Each lever pull drops a crumb, worth 1, or nothing, worth 0. Each machine has its own hidden chance of dropping a crumb. Pip gets 1000 pulls tonight and wants as many crumbs as possible. Unlike the maze, nothing moves: after every pull the same four machines wait.

explore:5.t: A peek at the secret. We will peek inside the machines, so we can judge Pip’s choices. Pip cannot see this. A drops a crumb 30 percent of the time, B 55 percent, C 70 percent, and D only 15 percent. So C is the best machine. Pip has to find that out by pulling.

explore:6.t: Pip the exploiter. First Pip tries each machine once. A drops a crumb. B, C and D drop nothing. Then Pip follows a simple rule: always pull the machine that has paid best so far. That is A, with 1 crumb in 1 pull. This rule is called greedy.

explore:7.t: Stuck. After 1000 pulls, Pip pulled A 997 times and collected 308 crumbs. It never went back to C. Why? B, C and D still show 0 crumbs from their single try, and A’s average never drops to 0. One unlucky pull of C, the best machine, decided the whole evening.

explore:8.t: Pip the explorer. Same visit, same luck: each machine drops its crumbs in the same order as before, so C’s first pull misses again. This time Pip always explores: every pull goes to a random machine. Pip learns a lot: its averages end close to the secret chances. But it collects only 398 crumbs, because three pulls in four go to machines worse than C.

explore:9.t: Each pull has a hidden cost. To compare the two, imagine someone who knew the secrets. They would pull C every time and expect 70 crumbs per 100 pulls. Every pull of another machine gives up some of that. A pull of B gives up 0.70 minus 0.55, which is 0.15 of a crumb. A gives up 0.40, D gives up 0.55, and C gives up nothing.

explore:10.t: Regret. Add up those costs over the evening and you get Pip’s regret: the price of not knowing. The exploiter’s regret is 399.5. The explorer’s is 279.3. Regret counts chances, not luck: a pull of A costs 0.40 whether or not this pull happened to drop a crumb. So regret measures the choices, not the dice.

explore:11.t: One visit is not enough. That was one visit. With different luck, the exploiter might have found C. So let’s run 2000 visits of 1000 pulls each and average. Here is the chart. Left to right: pulls during the evening. Upward: total regret so far, averaged over all visits. Lower is better. A line that goes flat has stopped losing.

explore:12.t: Explore always, or never?. Gold, always explore: straight, steep, ending at 275. Red, always exploit: only 78. A twist: in the visit we watched, the exploiter lost more. That was bad luck; on average it does far better. But red never flattens. In 1299 of 2000 visits greedy settled on C, its most-pulled machine. In the other 701 it stuck to B, A or D and kept losing.

explore:13.t: A little of both. A mixed Pip: one pull in ten goes to a random machine, any of the four, the rest to the best so far. Its teal line ends at 42, lower than both. Random pulls rescue an unlucky start: C gets more tries, and its true quality shows. Yet it pays for random pulls forever. How much to explore, and smarter ways, come next.

explore:14.t: Your turn. Tap a machine to pull its lever. You get 20 pulls. Pull the ones you believe in, but don’t forget the ones you haven’t tested enough. After your last pull, the secret chances and your regret appear. Tap again to start over.

explore:15.t: Where you meet this. A music app plays songs you love, but also slips in new ones to learn your taste. A website shows its usual page to most visitors and a new design to some, to see which works better. Some medical trials also adapt as results come in, sending more patients to the treatment that is doing better. Each is the arcade in disguise.

explore:16.t: Recap. Exploit what you know, or explore to learn more: every choice under uncertainty faces this. Never exploring can lock you onto a worse option after one unlucky try. Always exploring wastes most of your pulls. Regret measures the price of not knowing. The next reels show smarter ways to keep it small.

bandits:0.t: Multi-Armed Bandits. R L with one room and a row of slot machines.

bandits:1.t: One-armed bandits. Old slot machines had a single lever, an arm, and they slowly took your money. People called them one-armed bandits. Pip’s cheese arcade has four machines, so it is a multi-armed bandit: a row of options, each paying out by its own hidden rule. It is the simplest puzzle in reinforcement learning, and one of the most useful.

bandits:2.t: The pieces. Each machine is an arm. Each turn Pip pulls one arm: its action. The reward is a crumb, worth 1, or nothing, worth 0. Each arm has its own reward distribution, the hidden rule for what it pays: here, a crumb with some fixed chance. So an arm’s true average reward per pull equals that chance. Pip never sees it.

bandits:3.t: No map to plan over. In the maze, every move changed where Pip stood, and the next choice depended on it. In the arcade nothing changes: after any pull, the same machines wait, same chances. There is no situation, or state, to track. One 1000-pull visit plays the part of an episode; its return is simply the total crumbs, undiscounted. Every turn the only question is which arm to pull.

bandits:4.t: Estimate by averaging. Pip can’t see B’s chance, but it can estimate it. Pip pulls B five times: crumb, nothing, crumb, nothing, crumb. Its estimate of B is the average reward so far: 3 crumbs in 5 pulls, so 0.6. The true chance is 0.55. Close, but five pulls can’t pin it down exactly.

bandits:5.t: Update as you go. No list of rewards is needed. Each pull updates that machine’s one number: new estimate equals old plus (reward minus old) divided by n, where n counts that machine’s pulls so far. B’s five pulls again: each line is exactly the average so far. Why? The new average is (old times (n minus 1) plus reward) divided by n, which rearranges to the same rule.

bandits:6.t: Why divide by n?. The bracket, reward minus old estimate, is the surprise: how far the pull landed from expected. Dividing by n sets the step. The first pull moves the estimate all the way, the tenth a tenth of the way: every pull counts equally, right for machines that never change. T D learning keeps the shape but fixes the step, since what it averages shifts as Pip learns.

bandits:7.t: The greedy player. A full 1000-pull visit, visit 94 of our numbered, seeded visits. Pip plays greedy: it pulls each machine once, then always the arm with the highest estimate, ties broken at random. Under the machines: crumbs out of pulls so far. Bars: Pip’s estimates; yellow box: current favourite. After four pulls, B and C each show 1 crumb in 1 pull: a tie.

bandits:8.t: A lucky start for B, an unlucky one for C. Pull 5, B by coin flip: nothing, 0.5. Pull 6, C: nothing, 0.5. Another tie; pull 7, C: nothing again, 0.33. B now leads; pull 8: a crumb, 0.67. B’s average never dips below C’s 0.33 again, so C is never pulled again. Two misses in a row hit a 70 percent machine about one time in eleven.

bandits:9.t: Frozen. After 1000 pulls, B got 995 pulls and its estimate settled at 0.54, near its true 0.55. C’s is still 0.33, from three pulls long ago, though its true chance is 0.70. The chart follows both estimates through the visit: solid lines are Pip’s estimates, dashed lines the true chances. B’s line wanders and settles. C’s line never moves again.

bandits:10.t: Why greedy can’t recover. An estimate changes only when its arm is pulled. If it is too high, greedy keeps pulling that arm, and extra pulls bring it down: self-correcting. If too low, greedy stops pulling the arm, so the mistake is never corrected. Here A, C and D are stuck below their true chances. Greedy fixes over-optimism, never pessimism. Over 2000 visits it froze like this in 701.

bandits:11.t: Your turn. A simple fix: try every machine several times before going greedy. Drag to choose how many tries. Too few, and an unlucky start still freezes a good machine out. Too many, and Pip wastes pulls on A and D. The best number depends on the visit length and on how close the machines are, which Pip doesn’t know in advance.

bandits:12.t: Where bandits live. The first paper on this problem, by William Thompson in 1933, asked how to choose between two medical treatments. Herbert Robbins framed the general problem in 1952. Today bandit methods choose which headline, ad or page design to show each visitor. Each click is a reward, and each option is an arm.

bandits:13.t: Recap. A multi-armed bandit: several arms, each with an unknown reward distribution, and no states. Pull one arm per turn, collect as much as you can. Estimate each arm by its average, updated as you go. Pure greedy can freeze out a good arm after an unlucky start, because low estimates never get re-checked. The next reels show smarter ways to explore.

epsgreedy:0.t: epsilon-Greedy. Mostly do the best thing, occasionally roll the dice.

epsgreedy:1.t: Greedy needs a nudge. Four arcade machines each drop a crumb with a hidden chance, shown here but not to Pip. Greedy Pip tries each once, then always pulls the best average so far. Visit 266, a new one, starts as badly: A paid first, the others didn’t, so greedy pulled A 997 times in 1000. Its regret, expected crumbs lost against always pulling C, is 399.5.

epsgreedy:2.t: Spin before you pull. The fix is almost silly. Before each pull, Pip spins a little wheel. A small slice says random: pull any machine, chosen at random. The rest says best so far: pull the greedy choice. The size of the random slice is called epsilon, the Greek letter epsilon. This rule is epsilon-greedy.

epsgreedy:3.t: What epsilon equals 0.1 means. With epsilon equals 0.1, nine pulls in ten go to the favourite and one in ten is random. A random pull lands on the favourite too, one time in four. So the favourite gets 92.5 percent of pulls, each other machine 2.5 percent. Every machine keeps getting a few pulls, however bad it looks. This is the policy reel’s epsilon-random rule.

epsgreedy:4.t: Visit 266 again. Same visit, same crumbs in every machine, but now Pip spins first. The first four pulls try each machine once, as before: A pays, B, C and D don’t. Then the wheel mostly says best so far, and best so far is A. The top corner shows each spin.

epsgreedy:5.t: Random pulls. Pull 15: the wheel says random, and the random pick happens to be A itself. Pull 19: random again, B, nothing. Pull 25: random, B, a crumb. Between them, the greedy pulls keep going to A. Its average sits near 0.3. C and D still show 0 from their single tries.

epsgreedy:6.t: Pull 32. Pull 32: random, and this time it picks C. A crumb! C now shows 1 crumb in 2 pulls, an average of 0.5. That beats A’s 0.28. So from now on, best so far means C. C pays 6 of its next 8 pulls, and its average climbs. One lucky spin undid one unlucky first try.

epsgreedy:7.t: After 1000 pulls. C got 901 of the 1000 pulls, and its average settled at 0.71, close to the true 0.70. Regret for the visit: 33.9, against 399.5 for greedy. Every estimate keeps getting fresh pulls, so a wrong first impression can always be corrected. That is the whole point of epsilon.

epsgreedy:8.t: 2000 visits. The chart: total regret so far over 1000 pulls, averaged across 2000 visits. Lower is better. Greedy, red, ends at 77.6; epsilon-greedy with epsilon equals 0.1, teal, at 42.1. Of the 701 visits where greedy stuck on a worse machine, epsilon-greedy ended on C in 598; in the other 103 it still trailed on B. It lost only 5 of the visits greedy got right.

epsgreedy:9.t: The price: exploring forever. Look at the teal line near the end: it never goes flat. Even once Pip is sure C is best, one pull in ten is still random, and three in four of those hit worse machines. Over the last 500 pulls, it still rises about 0.032 per pull. Greedy’s lucky visits pay nothing once C is found, but its unlucky ones pay forever.

epsgreedy:10.t: Exploring blindly. Random pulls ignore all Pip has learned. In visit 266 the wheel said random 94 times. D, the worst, got 16, A 25, and B, the close runner-up, 31. The wheel splits them evenly on average, about 23 each; the spread is luck. Smarter explorers, U C B and Thompson sampling in the next reels, check where Pip is unsure or a machine might be best.

epsgreedy:11.t: Your turn. Drag epsilon to change the size of the random slice. Each line is one epsilon, labelled at its end, averaged over 2000 visits. At 0 Pip is plain greedy and sometimes freezes. Too much epsilon wastes pull after pull on bad machines. In this arcade the lowest line is epsilon equals 0.05, at 36.6, a little better than 0.1.

epsgreedy:12.t: Explore less as you learn. Early on, exploring is cheap and useful; later it mostly wastes pulls. So let epsilon shrink. Here epsilon equals 10 divided by pulls so far, capped at 1: random for roughly ten pulls, 1 in 10 after 100, about 1 in 100 by the end. Average regret: 26.6, below 42.1 for fixed epsilon equals 0.1, and near the bandits reel’s best try-first number.

epsgreedy:13.t: But not too fast. Shrink epsilon too fast and Pip is greedy again. With epsilon equals 1 divided by pulls so far, it is a quarter after the first four tries, and a visit averages only 5.6 random pulls. Average regret: 48.3; C got over half the pulls in only 75 percent of visits. So epsilon needs tuning, and closer machines or longer visits would favour other settings.

epsgreedy:14.t: Where you’ll see it. epsilon-greedy is everywhere because it is one line of code. Pip already used it in the T D learning reel: one move in five was random, so epsilon was 0.2. DeepMind’s Atari player D Q N, published in 2015, started with epsilon equals 1, fully random, lowered it to 0.1 over its first million frames of play, and kept it there, so it never stopped trying new moves.

epsgreedy:15.t: Recap. epsilon-greedy: with chance epsilon pull a random arm, otherwise the arm with the best average. Every arm keeps being re-checked, so an unlucky start can be undone. It is simple and often good enough. But it explores blindly, spending as many random pulls on hopeless arms as on promising ones, and epsilon has to be tuned. Shrinking epsilon over time helps.

ucb:0.t: Upper Confidence Bound. Be optimistic about what you haven’t tried much.

ucb:1.t: Back at the arcade. Pip is back at the cheese arcade: four machines, A to D. Each pull drops one crumb or nothing, and each machine has its own hidden chance of a crumb. Pip keeps an estimate for each machine: crumbs divided by pulls. Greedy can get stuck. epsilon-greedy unsticks it with random pulls. This reel shows a smarter way to explore.

ucb:2.t: Random pulls are blind. With epsilon equals 0.1, every tenth pull goes to a random machine, even one Pip knows is bad. Over 1000 pulls, averaged over 2000 visits, D gets 27 pulls, almost all dice rolls. The dice never stop: Pip pays for them on pull 10 and pull 10,000 alike. Yet in the first 1000 pulls, U C B checks D just as often; the difference comes after.

ucb:3.t: Two kinds of “looks bad”. Picture two machines. One gave nothing in its only pull. The other gave 6 crumbs in 40 pulls. Both look poor. But one pull says almost nothing: that machine might still be great. Forty pulls say a lot. A smart explorer should spend its tries where it is unsure, not spread them evenly.

ucb:4.t: How much does an average wobble?. Take machine B, true chance 55 percent, over 30 visits. Each dot is the average of B’s first 3 pulls in one visit. With 3 pulls only four averages are possible, and the dots use all of them, 0 to 1. Averages of the first 30 pulls: 0.37 to 0.8. More pulls, less wobble; roughly, 4 times the pulls halves it.

ucb:5.t: The benefit of the doubt. U C B gives each machine a hopeful score: its estimate plus a bonus. The bonus is big when Pip has pulled the machine only a few times and small when it knows the machine well. Then Pip pulls the machine with the highest score. A machine can win because it is good, or because Pip barely knows it. This is optimism in the face of uncertainty.

ucb:6.t: Upper Confidence Bound. Think of the bonus as stretching each estimate up to the top of the range the true chance could plausibly reach. Few pulls, wide range, tall cap. That top is an upper confidence bound, hence the name U C B. If a machine is truly worse than C, pulling it shrinks its cap until its top drops below C’s. After that, Pip checks it only rarely.

ucb:7.t: The bonus, in words. U C B’s bonus: c times square root of (2 times log t divided by n). c is a scale, 1 in the classic UCB1; n, this machine’s pulls: 4 times the pulls, half the bonus, like the wobble. t: total pulls. Its natural log, log t, grows forever, slowly: 4.6 at 100, 6.9 at 1000. An ignored machine’s bonus thus creeps up: always another look, but rarely.

ucb:8.t: Pull 5: the first scores. We follow one visit, number 24. As before, Pip first pulls each machine once. A, C and D give nothing; B gives a crumb. Now t equals 4 and every n equals 1, so every bonus is the same: 1.67. Scores: A 1.67, B 2.67, C 1.67, D 1.67. B wins. A score above 1 is fine: it is a hopeful score, not a chance.

ucb:9.t: C gets a second look. Pulls 5 to 8 go to B twice, then A, then D. On pull 9, C, still pulled only once, has the biggest bonus. Scores: A 1.94, B 1.84, C 2.04, D 1.44. Pip pulls C... nothing again: 0 of 2. Plain greedy, in this same visit 24 with the same dice, never went back to C; it pulled B 997 times in 1000.

ucb:10.t: Patience pays. C now has 0 crumbs from 2 pulls. But every pull of another machine raises t, so C’s bonus slowly grows. On pull 20 its score is on top again (1.72). This time the crumbs come. By pull 40, C has 10 of 14. The gold caps shrink as machines are pulled, and C’s bar rises toward its true 70 percent.

ucb:11.t: Where the checks go. After 1000 pulls here: A 58, B 242, C 671, D 29. All four tops sit near one height, 0.83. U C B pulls the highest top, which levels the tops. D’s estimate is far below C’s, so it keeps a tall cap: few pulls. B is close to C, so its cap must be thin: many pulls. Promising machines get checked more, hopeless ones less.

ucb:12.t: Keeping score. Is U C B better than epsilon-greedy? Recall regret: every pull of C adds 0, B adds 0.15, A 0.40 and D 0.55, the crumbs given up compared with always pulling C. The chart: left to right, pulls; upward, total regret so far, averaged over 2000 visits. First, epsilon-greedy with epsilon equals 0.1, the teal line: 42 after 1000 pulls.

ucb:13.t: A surprise. Now UCB1, in gold. After 1000 pulls its regret is 61: worse than epsilon-greedy! Big early bonuses make it check B a lot: 169 pulls on average, against 104 for epsilon-greedy. Both lines still climb. But epsilon-greedy never stops paying: one pull in ten is a dice roll, forever. U C B’s checks get rarer as its caps shrink, so its climb keeps slowing.

ucb:14.t: The long game. So play longer: 10,000 pulls, averaged over 500 visits. UCB1 overtakes epsilon-greedy at about pull 2,800 and finishes far lower: 141 against 294. From pull 5000 to 10,000, epsilon-greedy’s regret grows by 138, UCB1’s by only 26. The card shows why: after pull 1000, epsilon-greedy pulls the hopeless D about 225 more times, UCB1 only about 23.

ucb:15.t: A fair comparison. From earlier reels: shrinking epsilon equals 10 divided by t ended 1000 pulls at 27; trying each machine 10 times first, 25. Both beat UCB1’s 61. Even at 10,000 pulls, shrinking epsilon wins: 80 to 141. What does U C B buy? No schedule to pick; those 10s suit only this arcade. A guarantee, proven for any arcade. A tuned bonus, c equals 0.25, beats them all.

ucb:16.t: Your turn. Drag c, the bonus scale, to replay 2000 visits. At c equals 0, no bonus: plain greedy, settling on the wrong machine in 701 of 2000 visits. Too big, and Pip re-checks machines it already knows. Here c equals 0.25 does best, ending at 14, but that is tuned to this arcade; with c equals 0.1, C gets under half the pulls in 533 visits.

ucb:17.t: The fine print. UCB1’s guarantee: for rewards from 0 to 1, regret grows at most logarithmically, so each doubling of the pulls adds about the same. Here: 25 from 2500 to 5000 pulls, 26 from 5000 to 10,000. The proof needs the bonus at least this big. It assumes the chances never change. If a much-pulled C got worse, its thin cap would make Pip slow to notice.

ucb:18.t: Where it is used. Optimism goes back to Lai and Robbins, 1985; UCB1 and its guarantee to Auer, Cesa-Bianchi and Fischer, 2002. A game program tries moves in its head before playing; each candidate is like an arm. In 2006 Kocsis and Szepesvári used the U C B score at every such choice: UCT. It powered strong Go programs; AlphaGo’s search used a related rule to pick moves to explore.

ucb:19.t: Recap. U C B scores each machine as its estimate plus a bonus for uncertainty, and pulls the top score. The bonus shrinks as a machine is pulled and creeps up while it is ignored. So U C B spends its checks on machines that could still turn out best, and its regret keeps flattening while epsilon-greedy’s grows at a steady rate.

thompson:0.t: Thompson Sampling. Act on a random guess drawn from your beliefs.

thompson:1.t: Pip’s hunch. Back at the cheese arcade: machines A to D, each dropping a crumb or nothing, each with a hidden chance. Pip could keep one estimate per machine. But “1 crumb from 1 pull” and “50 crumbs from 100 pulls” are very different evidence, even though the first estimate looks better. This reel tracks that difference with a belief, and lets the belief do the exploring.

thompson:2.t: A curve of hunches. Here is how Pip pictures one machine, B, before pulling it. Left to right: every chance of a crumb the machine could have, from 0 to 1. Height: how plausible Pip finds that chance. Pip knows nothing yet, so every chance is equally plausible: a flat line. The tallest point always marks the most plausible chance.

thompson:3.t: One crumb. B’s first pull drops a crumb. Which chances fit that? Chance 0.9 would drop a crumb 9 times in 10, chance 0.1 only once. So after one crumb, 0.9 is nine times as plausible as 0.1, and chance 0 is ruled out. Height at each chance equals how likely that chance makes what Pip saw. The flat line tilts into a ramp.

thompson:4.t: Then nothing. The second pull drops nothing. Now a chance of 1 is ruled out too: such a machine never fails. Multiply the old heights by how likely each chance makes “nothing”, and the ramp bends into a hill around 0.5. Then rescale, so the tallest point is full height again. This way of updating a belief with evidence is called Bayes’ rule.

thompson:5.t: More pulls, narrower hill. Keep pulling B. After 10 pulls with 5 crumbs, the hill narrows around 0.5. After 100 with 54 crumbs, a thin spike near 0.54, near B’s true 0.55. These curves are the Beta distribution. With w crumbs and l nothings, Pip’s belief is Beta(1 plus w, 1 plus l). Its peak is the estimate, crumbs divided by pulls; its width, how unsure Pip is.

thompson:6.t: The rule: one draw each. Thompson sampling uses the curves like this. Every turn, Pip draws one random chance from each machine’s curve: draws land more often where the curve is tall. Then it pulls the machine whose draw came out highest, and updates that one curve. At the start all four curves are flat, so the four draws are just random numbers.

thompson:7.t: The first pulls. We follow one visit. Pull 1: A’s draw, 0.86, is highest. A drops nothing, so its curve tilts toward low chances. Pull 2: A’s draw is just 0.09, and C wins with 0.30. Nothing again. Each pull shows the draws, one dot per machine; the highest decides. B’s draws happen not to win at first, so it stays untried for a while.

thompson:8.t: B gets lucky. B drops crumbs on 8 of its first 9 pulls. Its hill moves high, so its draws usually win, and Pip pulls B again and again. C, meanwhile, has 0 crumbs from 2 pulls. Its curve leans low but is still wide: by its curve, the chance that C is better than 0.5 is still 1 in 8. That width keeps C in the game.

thompson:9.t: C’s comeback. On pull 22, C’s wide curve throws a lucky draw, 0.66, just above B’s 0.65. C drops a crumb. More chances follow: by pull 60, C has 5 crumbs from 7 pulls, and its hill has caught up with B’s. Nobody told Pip to explore. The width of C’s curve did it.

thompson:10.t: Picked as often as it might be best. At pull 40, how often does each machine win? Over 4000 draws, B wins 83 percent, C 8 percent, D 8 percent, A 1 percent. The secret: Thompson sampling pulls each machine as often as Pip believes it could be the best. A machine’s share shrinks only as Pip grows sure it is worse; D, 1 crumb in 3, is still uncertain: 8 percent.

thompson:11.t: Narrowing down. Fast-forward to pull 1000 in this visit. C’s curve has become a spike near 0.70, from 872 pulls. A and D were pulled only 6 and 7 times, so their curves stay wide. That is fine: Pip never needs to know exactly how bad D is, only that it is very unlikely to beat C.

thompson:12.t: Keeping score. Compare by regret: each pull gives up 0.70 minus the chance of the machine pulled. Chart: total regret over 1000 pulls, averaged over 2000 visits, lower better. epsilon-greedy with epsilon equals 0.1 ends at 42, UCB1 at 61, Thompson sampling, purple, at 18. It also beats shrinking epsilon, 27. Only U C B with a bonus tuned to this arcade, c equals 0.25, edges it: 14.

thompson:13.t: Your turn. Pull the machines yourself: tap a machine to pull it once, and watch its curve change. Or tap the button to let Thompson sampling choose: you will see its four draws first. Try pulling one machine many times, and see how thin its curve gets.

thompson:14.t: The fine print. It needs a starting belief; here it was flat, every chance equally plausible. A strong wrong start can slow it. Beta curves fit crumb-or-nothing rewards; other rewards need other belief shapes, often only approximate. Its randomness helps when many choices come before results return: a diceless rule like U C B would send every waiting visitor to the same machine; Thompson’s draws spread them out.

thompson:15.t: Where it is used. William Thompson proposed it in 1933, to choose between two medical treatments, then it was largely forgotten. Around 2010 it returned: Microsoft engineers used a version for Bing ad placement, and in 2011 Chapelle and Li at Yahoo found it excellent for ads and news recommendations. Proofs in 2012 showed its regret, like UCB1’s, grows only logarithmically. Today it is common in website tests.

thompson:16.t: Recap. Keep a belief curve for each machine: how plausible each chance is, given the crumbs so far. Every turn, draw one chance from each curve and pull the highest. Wide curves sometimes draw high, so unsure machines get explored; narrow low curves almost never win, so bad machines get dropped. No epsilon schedule or bonus to tune, only a starting belief.

valueiter:0.t: Value Iteration. Know the rules? Spread value outward from the goal, step by step.

valueiter:1.t: Planning at a desk. Stepping onto the cheese pays plus 1, onto the cat minus 1, and either ends the walk. Other steps pay 0, bumps into walls or rocks leave Pip in place, and gamma (gamma) is 0.9. This time we hold the rulebook, its model: for every cell and move, where Pip lands and what the step pays. With it we plan at a desk while Pip waits.

valueiter:2.t: The best-move rule. The Bellman reel swept the rule for Pip’s distracted habit until it settled, then swapped the average over moves for the best move. That gives the best possible values, V star (V star): value here equals the best over moves of reward plus 0.9 times value where it lands. Sweeping it over every cell, from all zeros, is value iteration. Watch the best arrows appear.

valueiter:3.t: One cell, four scores. Take the cell beside the cheese in sweep 1, with every number still 0. Right: the cheese, plus 1, and the walk ends, so nothing is added. Up bumps the wall: 0 plus 0.9 times 0. Down is the cat: minus 1. Left: 0 plus 0.9 times 0. The best score, 1, becomes the cell’s new number, and its arrow points right, at the winning move.

valueiter:4.t: Sweep 1. Do that for all 16 cells, each using pre-sweep numbers. Only the two cells beside the cheese reach 1. Next to the cat the best score is 0: just don’t step on it. Where three or four moves tie, there is no arrow yet, only a question mark. After one sweep most cells are like that: every move still scores 0.

valueiter:5.t: The news spreads. Each sweep, the good news moves one cell further: 0.90 two steps from the cheese, 0.81 three steps away, and so on. A cell gets its arrow as soon as one move beats the others. At sweep 7 the news reaches the start: 0.53. Where two routes are equally short, two moves tie for best and both arrows stay, as at the start.

valueiter:6.t: When to stop. Sweep 8 changes nothing: these are V star. Dry, a number is final once it appears: three steps from the cheese, 0.9 times 0.9 equals 0.81, and no longer route beats that. The arrows, the best-scoring move in each cell, form the best policy. Its walk to the cheese takes 7 steps. Work: 8 times 16 cells times 4 moves equals 512 scores.

valueiter:7.t: A wet floor. Someone mops the floor, as in the M D P reel. A tried move goes that way 8 times in 10, sliding to each side 1 in 10, never backwards. Sliding into a wall or rock means staying put. Rewards and gamma are unchanged, so any change in numbers comes from slipping alone. The rulebook now lists every landing of each move, with its chance.

valueiter:8.t: A move’s score is an average. A move’s score, its Q, averages its landings: chance times (reward plus 0.9 times value there). The cell takes the best Q: Pip picks the move, not the landing. Beside the cheese, sweep 1: right hits the cheese 8 times in 10, the cat 1 in 10: 0.8 minus 0.1 equals 0.7. Up, into the wall: 0.1, from a lucky slide onto the cheese.

valueiter:9.t: Sweeping the wet floor. Numbers grow from the cheese again but don’t stop after 7 sweeps. The start is 0 until sweep 7, then 0.12, 0.20, 0.26, 0.30, still creeping at sweep 14. After 7 sweeps each number is the best expected from walks cut off at 7 steps; each sweep allows one more. Slides make walks long, so extra steps keep adding less and less, because of gamma.

valueiter:10.t: When to stop, now. Each sweep’s biggest change in any cell: across, sweep number; up, the change, each line ten times smaller. Grey dots: unneeded sweeps. Stop below 0.001: sweep 16. Each later change is at most 0.9 times the one before, so together they add at most 0.001 times (0.9 plus 0.81 plus ...) equals 9 times 0.001. Against 400 sweeps, the real gap is under 0.001.

valueiter:11.t: The arrows settle first. The arrows stop changing at sweep 10; the numbers creep on until sweep 16. The start points right in sweeps 7 to 9, then flips to up for good. The best move often shows before its exact value does. Mid-sweep you cannot tell the arrows are final, so the stopping rule watches the numbers. The next reel, policy iteration, works on arrows directly.

valueiter:12.t: Dry arrows, wet arrows. Left, the best arrows on the dry floor; right, the wet floor. The clearest change is right below the cat: dry, the best move was right; wet, it is down, away from the cat. Where the dry floor had two equally short routes, slipping makes one better by a hair, so ties disappear. At the start, up beats right only in the third decimal.

valueiter:13.t: Why go down?. Below the cat, going right risks a slide up, onto the cat, 1 time in 10. Going down risks nothing: its slides either bump into the rock and stay, or land one cell to the right. The detour costs two extra steps, yet the averages favour it: 0.45 for down against 0.41 for right.

valueiter:14.t: Does it matter?. Send Pip from below the cat 1000 times. With the dry floor’s arrow, right, 207 end on the cat; only this cell differs. With the new arrow, down, only 114, though walks get longer. Why not zero? Both cells beside the cheese touch the cat, so the last step always risks sliding onto it. The policy can’t remove that risk, only stop adding more.

valueiter:15.t: Your turn. Drag the slip chance, the total sideways chance, so far 0.2. Value iteration reruns from zeros. More slipping means longer walks, so numbers creep for more sweeps, and arrows bend away from the cat. At 0.3 the start takes the bottom route; at 0.4 the cells beside the cheese push into the wall, awaiting a lucky slide. Tap a cell to start Pip there.

valueiter:16.t: The catch. Value iteration needs the whole rulebook, and every sweep visits every cell, move and landing. Here that is 16 cells. Go has so many legal positions that writing their number takes 171 digits: no table could hold them. And often nobody hands you a rulebook at all. Later reels learn values from experience instead, and replace the table with a network.

valueiter:17.t: Where it shows up. Richard Bellman introduced this step-by-step computation in the 1950s as dynamic programming. Value iteration is still a standard solver when the rules are known and small enough to list: inventory planning, maintenance schedules, robot routes on a known map. Q-learning aims at a similar target, reward plus gamma times the best Q of the next cell, but estimates it from experience.

valueiter:18.t: Recap. Given the rulebook, value iteration sweeps one rule over every cell, from zeros: value here equals the best Q, the top move’s average of reward plus gamma times landing value. It closes in on V star. Stop when the biggest change is tiny; the best arrows are the best policy. On a slippery floor it bends away from danger, because the averages count the slides.

policyiter:0.t: Policy Iteration. Judge your plan, fix it, repeat, until nothing changes.

policyiter:1.t: Another way to plan. Wet floor: a tried move goes that way 8 times in 10, sliding to each side 1 in 10. Bumps leave Pip in place. Stepping onto the cheese pays plus 1, onto the cat minus 1, both end the walk, other steps pay 0, and gamma (gamma) is 0.9. We hold the rulebook, the model, so we plan at a desk, improving a whole plan in rounds.

policyiter:2.t: A bad first plan. A plan, or policy, puts one arrow in every cell, and Pip always tries that move. Any randomness now comes from the floor alone. Start with a plan that is clearly bad: every arrow points up. From the start, Pip walks up to the top corner and then pushes against the wall, moving on only when it happens to slide.

policyiter:3.t: Round 1: evaluate. First, measure this plan: compute its notebook as in the Bellman reel, now averaging over landings. Each cell: the average of reward plus 0.9 times value there, using only the plan’s move. Sweep from zeros until nothing moves more than 0.001: 24 sweeps, more than value iteration needed, because its walks are long and news travels slowly. The start is worth only 0.01.

policyiter:4.t: Reading the bad notebook. Below the cheese the plan is already right: up, to the cheese, worth 0.77. Beside the cheese it pushes into the wall; only a slide reaches the cheese: 0.40. Below the cat, up walks straight into it: minus 0.83, and bottom-row cells lower left drift in too. Left of the cat: 0.00, as a slide onto the cat loses about what moving up gains.
