policyiter:5.t: Round 1: improve. Fix the plan: score each move in every cell by this notebook, averaging reward plus 0.9 times value over landings. That is its Q: the move once, then the plan. Point each arrow at the best Q, keeping old arrows on ties, so no flip-flops. Beside the cheese, up: 0.40; right: 0.8 times 1 minus 0.1 plus 0.1 times 0.9 times 0.40 equals 0.74. Switch.

policyiter:6.t: Ten arrows change. Done in every cell, 10 of 16 arrows change. The top row now runs right; below the cat, the arrow turns away. Some look odd. Left of the cat it now pushes into the rock: up gains little, risks sliding onto the cat; the rock is safe. Two bottom-row cells point left. They win only by the bad plan’s notebook; next round rejudges them.

policyiter:7.t: Round 2. Evaluate the new plan, starting its sweeps from the last notebook: 23 sweeps (from zeros it would take 24). The start jumps from 0.01 to 0.32. Improve again with the new numbers: only 3 arrows change. Left of the cat it points up again, below the cat it now goes down, around the cat, and one bottom-row cell turns right.

policyiter:8.t: Rounds 3 and 4. Round 3: 10 sweeps, start 0.32, and just 1 arrow changes, in the bottom row. Round 4: 4 sweeps, start 0.33, and no arrow changes at all. When improving changes nothing, we stop. This is exactly the plan that value iteration, the previous reel, found on the same floor, including the detour below the cat.

policyiter:9.t: Round by round. Here are the four rounds in a table. Each row is one round’s plan: how many sweeps its evaluation took, what that plan makes the start worth, and how many arrows its improvement changed. Round 1’s fix shows up in row 2: the start jumps from 0.01 to 0.32. After that, rounds only fine-tune: 10, 3, 1, 0 arrows changed.

policyiter:10.t: Why it never gets worse. Beside the cheese, the old plan, up, is worth 0.40. Right once, then the old plan: its Q, 0.74, which is why right was picked. Wherever Pip lands, the new arrow passed that test too, so using it twice is no worse, then three times, and on. The new plan, always: 0.77. Across the maze, 15, 7, 4 numbers rose per round; none fell.

policyiter:11.t: Why it stops at the best. Switches need a strictly higher Q, so each changing round strictly gains; no plan returns, and with 4,294,967,296 plans the rounds must end. At the end each arrow has its cell’s best Q. Beside the cheese: right 0.77, up 0.71, left 0.44, down minus 0.64. Any other move, used once then ours, is no better, nor twice, and so on: no plan beats ours.

policyiter:12.t: Rounds versus sweeps. Policy iteration needed 4 rounds; value iteration needed 16 sweeps. But each round hides a whole evaluation: 61 sweeps in total. Those sweeps are cheaper, one move per cell instead of four. Counting move scores: 1,232 here against 1,024 for value iteration, about the same. Value iteration is the extreme case: its max picks the best arrow and does one evaluation sweep at once.

policyiter:13.t: Your turn. Pick a different first plan and watch the rounds. Starting all right takes 3 rounds; all down or all left take 7 each, because they reach the cheese only by sliding: their early notebooks are mostly zeros, so news spreads slowly. Every start ends at the same plan. Tap a cell to see its four Q values in the round on screen.

policyiter:14.t: The big template. Evaluate a plan, then improve it using that: this loop is everywhere in R L. Loosened, it is generalised policy iteration: evaluate with a few sweeps, improve only some cells, or shift the plan a little, then repeat. Later reels, like actor-critic, learn without a rulebook: a critic estimates values from experience, and an actor nudges the plan toward moves the critic rates higher.

policyiter:15.t: Where it shows up. Ronald Howard described policy iteration in 1960, in his book on dynamic programming and Markov processes. It remains a standard way to solve planning problems whose rules are known, like stock and maintenance decisions. Its biggest legacy is the loop itself: judge the current behaviour, then nudge it toward what the judgement says is better.

policyiter:16.t: Recap. Policy iteration starts from any plan and repeats two halves: evaluate the plan’s notebook, then point each arrow at its best-scoring move. Each round is at least as good as the last, in every cell. When no arrow changes, the plan is the best one. Few rounds, but each holds a full evaluation.

mc:0.t: Monte Carlo Learning. Play to the end, then learn from what really happened.

mc:1.t: Back in the maze. The floor is dry again: every move goes where Pip intends. Stepping onto the cheese pays plus 1, onto the cat minus 1, and either ends the walk; other steps pay 0. A bump leaves Pip in place but counts as a step. gamma (gamma) is 0.9. Pip follows its habit from the values reel: the arrow, except one move in five goes a random direction.

mc:2.t: No rulebook. No one told Pip where moves lead or what they pay, so it can’t work values out on paper. It can only walk. The values reel started 1000 walks in every cell: already Monte Carlo, the wasteful kind. Real Pip always starts in the corner. Monte Carlo learning learns from the complete walks it actually takes, named after the famous casino.

mc:3.t: One walk, seven returns. Walk 1, as in the values reel: cheese in 7 steps. When it ends, Pip writes a return into every cell it passed, not just the start. A cell’s return counts rewards from the step leaving it to the walk’s end. Beside the cheese that is 1. Each cell further back waited one step longer, one more times 0.9, down to 0.53 at the start.

mc:4.t: A notebook of averages. For every cell the notebook keeps two things: how many returns it has, n, and their average. A new return nudges the average: new equals old plus (return minus old) divided by n. The hundredth return moves it only a hundredth of the way. Some versions nudge by a fixed fraction instead, so old walks fade: useful when the habit keeps changing.

mc:5.t: Walk 2: twice in one cell. On walk 2 Pip steps back down once and bumps the top wall once, passing three cells twice. Which return counts? Here, only each walk’s first visit. Counting every visit also works: after 1000 walks the two notebooks differ by at most 0.04. The start averages (0.53 plus 0.39) divided by 2 equals 0.46. Beside the cheese: (1 plus 0.9) divided by 2 equals 0.95.

mc:6.t: Walk 3: same path, opposite lesson. Walk 3 starts along the same path. Halfway, Pip can’t write anything: whether these cells lead to cheese or cat is still unknown. Then, right beside the cheese, a random move points down, onto the cat. Every return on the path is negative. The start’s average drops to 0.15, beside the cheese to 0.30. A single walk can swing the notebook a lot.

mc:7.t: Many walks. Pip keeps walking from the start. After 10 walks the start reads 0.28, after 100 walks 0.44, after 1000 walks 0.40: exactly the values reel’s number, because these are the same 1000 walks. But now every cell on the route got its own returns from those walks too, at least 964 each, with no extra walking.

mc:8.t: Where Pip rarely goes. Compare the values reel, which started 1000 walks in every cell. Along Pip’s usual route the notebooks agree within 0.01. Off the route, cells got only 33 to 59 returns, mostly from the same few walks, and are off by about 0.1: below the cheese, 0.73 against 0.87; below the cat, only 3 returns, minus 0.33 against 0.59. Monte Carlo only learns where Pip goes.

mc:9.t: How much one return varies. Here are all 1000 returns from the start. Across is the return of one walk, from minus 1 to plus 1. Each bar counts how many walks gave that return: gold walks reached the cheese, rose ones the cat. They spread from minus 0.53 to 0.53, because every random move until the end of the walk changes the return. Only the average of many walks settles, near 0.40.

mc:10.t: Your turn. Drag the slider to choose how many of Pip’s walks the notebook has seen. Tap any cell to see every return it has collected, as dots on a line from minus 1 to plus 1, with its average. Try the start, then a cell in the bottom right. With few walks, see how far one return can pull an average.

mc:11.t: From judging to improving. Someone else gave the arrows; the notebook only judged them. To improve, cell values aren’t enough: without a rulebook, Pip can’t tell where moves lead. So Pip averages per move: Q(cell, move), said “Q of cell and move”, the average return after that move there, first visit per walk. Choosing by Q changes the habit: policy iteration’s evaluate-then-improve loop, done after every walk.

mc:12.t: A habit built from averages. Pip drops the arrows; every Q starts at 0. In each cell it takes the biggest-Q move, ties broken at random. One move in five is random anyway, so bad-looking moves still get tried. Walk 1 wanders for 51 steps and ends on the cat. Every move it used now averages negative, so next time an untried move, still at 0, looks better.

mc:13.t: The catch: wait for the end. Walk 4 takes 493 steps. In the top-left corner, “up” has the least bad average, minus 0.006: the walks that tried it were so long the cat’s minus 1 had shrunk to almost nothing. So Pip bumps that wall 151 times. Averages can’t change until the walk ends; a walk that never ended would teach nothing. T D learning, in a coming reel, updates after every step.

mc:14.t: How Pip got out. After walk 4, up and down in the corner both averaged just below 0, the best there, so long walks went on. The way out: a walk reaching the cheese gives every move it used a positive return. On walk 8 Pip left the corner rightward and reached the cheese. “Right” got the corner’s only positive average, 0.02, so Pip now turns right there.

mc:15.t: 200 walks later. Bars: steps per walk, up to 100, faint line at 10; teal cheese, rose cat. After about 19 walks most take 7 to 10. The biggest-Q arrows take the shortest route, 7 steps. Over 40 reruns, 35 found it; 5 kept a 9-step detour, since the shorter way, tried mostly by random moves, still looked worse. With 1000 walks, 4 of the 5 find 7.

mc:16.t: Where you’ve seen this. The name dates from the 1940s, when Stanislaw Ulam and John von Neumann used random sampling for physics calculations at Los Alamos. A classic R L example is blackjack: the value of holding 18 is estimated by playing many hands to the end and averaging the results. AlphaGo, in 2016, also judged Go positions partly by playing fast games to the end and averaging who won.

mc:17.t: Recap. Monte Carlo learning needs no rulebook. After each complete walk, every cell passed gets its return, and its average moves toward it. The returns are real outcomes, but they vary a lot, and cells Pip rarely visits stay rough. Averages per move, Q, let Pip improve its own habit. The price: nothing is learned until the walk ends.

td:0.t: Temporal-Difference Learning. Learn a guess from a slightly better guess, every single step.

td:1.t:
Welcome back to Pip's maze.Same cheese, same cat, and a dry floor, so every move goes where Pip points.
The faint arrows are Pip's habit.The numbers are what that habit is worth, worked out by the sweeps.Point eight seven beside the cheese.Point four at the start.Pip must now learn them the hard way.

td:2.t:
The sweeps had a cheat sheet.
Monte Carlo didn't need that, but it had to wait until each walk was over.
Now Pip gets neither shortcut.Every guess starts at zero.And it has to learn while it walks.

td:3.t:
Picture driving home from the office.You expect the trip to take half an hour.
Ten minutes in, you're still on track.Then, a traffic jam.You don't wait until you're home to feel late. You update right there, to forty minutes.
Time so far, plus a fresh guess for the rest.That's the whole trick behind T D learning.

td:4.t:
Look at the start cell.The arrows show every move Pip might make, and how likely each one is.Mostly up.
The Bellman rule averages over all of them. That needs the rulebook.
Now watch Pip take one real step.T D uses just that: the reward, plus point nine times its guess where it landed.

td:5.t:
Here comes Pip's first walk.Watch the highlighted cell.After every step, Pip updates the cell it just left.
But nothing has happened yet.No reward, and every guess is still zero.So the target is zero, and nothing changes.
Six steps in a row, and the notebook stays blank.

td:6.t:
Watch the last step.Pip moves from the cell beside the cheese, onto it.Plus one!
The walk is over, so there's nothing to add. The target is just one.Pip's old guess was zero.
That gap, between what happened and what Pip expected, is the T D error. Think of it as surprise. Here, the surprise is a full one.

td:7.t:
Watch the cell beside the cheese. Pip doesn't jump to one.
It moves just a fifth of the way, to point two.That fraction is alpha, the learning rate.The match with one move in five is a coincidence.
Why so cautious? The next walk might end on the cat.Small steps let the good and bad walks average out.

td:8.t:
Walk two, sped up.Watch Pip step beside the cheese.
That cell already reads point two.So the cell Pip just left gets a little credit too.A guess learned from a guess. That's bootstrapping, the heart of T D.
Then a bump into the wall, and a small dip.Then the cheese lifts the guess to point three six.

td:9.t:
At each cheese, split the plus one in two.Yellow is what Pip expected.Orange is the surprise.
Watch the orange shrink.Then, on walk three, a random move sends Pip into the cat.A big negative surprise, and the guess drops.
So the next cheese surprises Pip all over again.

td:10.t:
Now Pip walks two hundred times.Look at the start cell around walk fifty. It already reads point three five, and the truth is point four.
Gold is the guess beside the cheese.Dashed is the true value, point eight seven.
The gold line hovers, dipping at every rose tick, every cat.

td:11.t:
Here are the two notebooks side by side.T D on the left.The exact sweeps on the right.
Beside the cheese, T D reads point nine eight.Why so high?The last cat scare was fifteen walks ago, and every good walk since nudged it up.
A fixed alpha never lets the guesses settle. They keep wobbling around the truth.

td:12.t:
Now Monte Carlo, on the left, trained on these very same walks.
Monte Carlo ends closer almost everywhere.Along Pip's usual route, it's within a hundredth of the truth.In rarely visited cells, T D is far off.
Why? These walks are short, so waiting for the end costs almost nothing. T D shines when walks are long, or never end.

td:13.t:
Look right of the start.The small numbers are visits.T D updated this cell nine times, more than Monte Carlo's eight returns.
But each update leaned on the next cell's guess, and that was still almost zero.The cheese's news never reached this far.
Give it the true values, and the same nine updates land on point four.

td:14.t:
Same walks, smaller step.Alpha is now point oh five.Watch the blue line grow over the pale gold one.
Blue is much calmer.But it's slow.At walk one hundred, the start reads only point oh eight.
Monte Carlo's one over n step is slower still. It shrinks so fast that the early zeros linger.

td:15.t:
Your turn. Drag the alpha slider, and the same two hundred walks replay with that learning rate.
Gold is beside the cheese.Teal is the start.Watch how far the lines jump around their dashed targets, and how long teal takes to climb.
Big alpha is quick but jumpy. Small alpha is calm, but slow.

td:16.t:
These dots are Pip's surprise at the cheese, across all two hundred walks. They sink, then jump after each cat.
Surprise also moves earlier.
Wolfram Schultz saw monkey dopamine neurons do the same. They fired for surprise juice, then for the light that announced it.

td:17.t:
So T D filled in the notebook from experience alone.But notice, the habit itself never changed.
Say Pip stands here and wants a better move.Where does each arrow lead? Watch the question marks.Without the rulebook, Pip can't tell.
The fix is a number for each move. That's Q-learning, coming next.

td:18.t:
So that's T D learning.
The target is one real step: the reward, plus gamma times the guess where Pip landed.Alpha sets how far to move.Big alpha learns fast and wobbles. Small alpha is steady, but slow.

qlearning:0.t: Q-Learning. Learn the value of every move, even while acting randomly.

qlearning:1.t: Where T D left off. In the T D reel, Pip followed a fixed habit: the arrows, with one move in five random. T D learning worked out, from experience, how good each cell is under that habit. Here is that notebook, with the true values of the habit, which T D’s guesses head toward. Now Pip wants to do better than its habit. Can the notebook tell it which move is best?

qlearning:2.t: A notebook is not enough. From the bottom row’s middle, the cell to its right is worth 0.59, to its left 0.45. Right looks better, if Pip knows “right” leads there. Pip doesn’t know the rules: only after a move does it see the reward and where it landed. It could learn the rules too, a later topic. Q-learning skips them and learns a value for each move directly.

qlearning:3.t: A number for each move. Pip now keeps four numbers per cell, one per move, drawn as triangles, each pointing its way. Gold is positive, rose negative. Each is an action value, Q of s, a. In the values reel it meant: make move a, then follow the habit. Here: make move a, then act as well as possible: the best policy’s Q, Q star, said “Q star”. All start at 0.

qlearning:4.t: Choosing needs no map. To move, Pip looks only at its own cell and takes the move with the biggest number, ties broken at random. Bumping a wall is a move too, with its own number. One move in five is still random, any direction, so every move gets tried. This habit is epsilon-greedy, with epsilon (epsilon) equals 0.2: greedy means taking the biggest number.

qlearning:5.t: The update, in words. After each move, Pip updates that move’s number. The target: that move’s reward, plus 0.9 times the biggest of the four numbers where it landed. Then it nudges the old number a fifth of the way toward the target. That fifth is alpha (alpha), the learning rate, as in T D learning. On the cheese or cat, the walk ends and nothing is added.

qlearning:6.t: In symbols. With s the cell Pip left, a its move, r the reward, and s prime, said “s prime”, where it landed: Q of s, a becomes Q of s, a plus alpha times (r plus gamma times max Q(s prime,  times ) minus Q of s, a). “max Q(s prime,  times )” is the biggest of the four numbers in s prime. gamma (gamma) equals 0.9 and alpha equals 0.2, the same knobs as in T D learning.

qlearning:7.t: Walk 1. All numbers are 0, so every choice is a tie, a coin toss. For 23 steps every update says “0 stays 0”. On step 24, from the cell below the cheese, one of the one-in-five random moves points up, onto the cheese: reward plus 1, walk over. Target 1, so that one number, “up” in that cell, goes from 0 to 0.2. Nothing else changes.

qlearning:8.t: The news travels back. Walk 2 ends stepping right onto the cheese, so “right” there becomes 0.2. Walk 3: Pip steps right into that cell, whose biggest number is 0.2. Target equals 0 plus 0.9 times 0.2 equals 0.18, and “right” in the cell it left becomes 0 plus 0.2 times 0.18 equals 0.036. As in T D, a guess learned from the next guess, but stored on a move.

qlearning:9.t: The max ignores what comes next. Walk 7. Pip steps right into the cell beside the cheese and updates at once, before choosing its next move. The biggest number there is 0.672, for “right”: target 0.9 times 0.672 equals 0.605, and the old 0.236 becomes 0.31. The target asks: what if Pip makes the best move from here? Whatever Pip actually does next plays no part.

qlearning:10.t: Bad news stays with the bad move. Then Pip’s next move is a random one: down, onto the cat. Reward minus 1, walk over. Only that cell’s “down” number changes, from 0 to minus 0.2. “Right” keeps its 0.672. With one number per cell, as in the T D reel, this minus 1 would have pulled down the whole cell’s value. Four numbers keep a bad move apart from a good one.

qlearning:11.t: Walk by walk. Two of the four numbers beside the cheese. Across: walk number, 1 to 20; up: the number after that walk. Gold is “right”, onto the cheese; rose is “down”, onto the cat. “Right” climbs: 0.2, 0.36, 0.49 ... 0.96 after 20 walks. Cat scares only push “down” lower. “Right” never drops: it lands on the cheese, so its target is always exactly 1.

qlearning:12.t: 300 walks later. Repeat for 300 walks. Bars show each walk’s steps; teal cheese, rose cat. Early walks wander: 24, 20, 28, 31 steps. Last-100 average: 8.9. Arrows show Pip’s best guess at the best move; small numbers count visits. Rarely visited cells off the route can be wrong: the bottom row’s two left arrows are not best moves. A ? means all four numbers are still equal.

qlearning:13.t: The best route’s numbers. Along the arrows, each cell’s biggest number: 1 beside the cheese, then 0.9, 0.81, down to 0.53 at the start. These are the values of always taking the shortest route: the Bellman reel’s V star, learned from walks alone. Under the old habit that cell is worth 0.87. Q-learning learned 1, despite Pip’s random moves: the max makes every target assume the best next move.

qlearning:14.t: Why they sit still. In the T D reel, a fixed alpha of 0.2 kept the guesses wobbling. Here they settle exactly. Why? The floor is dry, and the max ignores Pip’s random next move. Once the next cell’s numbers settle, every target for a move is the same number, walk after walk: nothing left to wobble. T D’s targets kept changing because random moves changed where Pip went next.

qlearning:15.t: But Pip still stumbles. Those numbers describe a Pip that never moves at random. The real Pip still does, one time in five. Each dot: one of its last 100 walks, at its return; gold cheese, rose cat. 6 met the cat; the average is 0.39, not 0.53. Q-learning learns the best way to act, not how Pip acts while learning. The next reel learns the real walker’s numbers.

qlearning:16.t: Your turn. Drag epsilon, how often Pip moves at random, to rerun all 300 walks. At every setting the start’s number reaches 0.53. More randomness means more cells visited: at 1, all 16 arrows are best moves, at 0.2 only 11. But a more random Pip earns less along the way. Tap a cell to drop Pip there and follow the arrows.

qlearning:17.t: Where it came from. Chris Watkins introduced Q-learning in his 1989 PhD thesis. In 1992 he and Peter Dayan proved the table reaches the best values, if every move everywhere keeps being tried and steps shrink suitably. Our run broke both, yet found the route; its rarely tried cells stayed wrong. In 2015 DeepMind’s D Q N swapped the table for a network reading Atari screens: one Q per joystick move.

qlearning:18.t: Recap. Without a map, keep a number for every move: Q of s, a. Pick the biggest, explore now and then. After each move, nudge its number toward the reward plus gamma times the best number where you landed. Because of that max, the numbers head for the best way to act, even while Pip acts at random.

sarsa:0.t: SARSA. Learn the value of what you’ll actually do next.

sarsa:1.t: A new room. Pip has a new room: six cells wide, four tall, no rocks. It starts bottom left, the cheese sits bottom right, and between them, along the bottom row, four cats sleep. The old rules hold: dry floor; stepping onto the cheese pays plus 1, onto a cat minus 1, either ending the walk; gamma (gamma) is 0.9; bumps leave Pip in place.

sarsa:2.t: Two ways across. The short way runs along the cats: up one, five steps right, down onto the cheese. Seven steps: 0.9 multiplied six times, 0.53. One row higher takes nine steps: 0.43. Without random moves, the short way wins. But Pip moves at random one time in five: on the row above the cats, one move in twenty points down at a cat.

sarsa:3.t: What Q-learning learns. First, Q-learning, exactly as in the last reel: 500 walks, one move in five random. Its arrows take the short way, right along the cats. That fits what Q-learning measures. Every target assumes the best next move, so its numbers describe a Pip that never moves at random. In the top rows, which Pip rarely visits, the arrows are rough guesses.

sarsa:4.t: SARSA’s one change. SARSA changes one thing. When Pip lands, it first picks its next move, with the same habit: the biggest number, or one time in five a random move. Then it updates using the number of that move, the one it will really make, not the biggest one. Then it makes it. Its name lists what one update uses: State, Action, Reward, next State, next Action.

sarsa:5.t: In symbols. With a prime, said “a prime”, the next move Pip has already picked in s prime: Q of s, a becomes Q of s, a plus alpha times (r plus gamma times Q(s prime, a prime) minus Q of s, a). The only difference from Q-learning is inside the target: Q(s prime, a prime) instead of max Q(s prime,  times ). If the walk is over, there is no next move and nothing is added.

sarsa:6.t: One SARSA update. Walk 26 of SARSA’s own run. Pip steps right onto the cell above a cat, and picks its next move: a random one, down, whose number is minus 0.2. So the target is 0 plus 0.9 times minus 0.2 equals minus 0.18, and the old 0.42 drops to 0.3. Q-learning would have used the best number there, 0.73: target 0.66, new 0.47.

sarsa:7.t: Then it really goes down. SARSA commits to the move it picked: Pip steps down onto the cat. Reward minus 1, walk over, so that number becomes minus 0.36. Picking a move in advance is what makes SARSA honest about Pip. Its targets contain the random moves Pip really makes, so cells where a random move is dangerous get lower numbers.

sarsa:8.t: The edge gets a bad name. After 500 walks, compare one cell on the row above the cats, second from the left. Q-learning says “right” is worth 0.66: the perfect value of the short way. SARSA says only 0.15, because walking on along the cats, a random move will sometimes take Pip into a cat. For SARSA, “up”, away from the cats, is the best move here: 0.36.

sarsa:9.t: Two routes. From the start, follow each learner’s arrows. Q-learning hugs the cats. SARSA climbs two rows, keeping an empty row between itself and the cats. In this run, with Pip still random one move in five, Q-learning’s arrows are worth 0.15 from the start, SARSA’s 0.25. These exact values come from sweeps over the room’s rules, as in the Bellman reel; Pip never sees them.

sarsa:10.t: Is this one run a fluke?. To check, run both learners 100 times with different random seeds, 500 walks each. The chart shows what Pip actually earned while learning: each dot is the average return of 25 walks, averaged over the 100 runs. Across is the walk number; up is the return. Orange is Q-learning, teal is SARSA.

sarsa:11.t: SARSA earns more while learning. Over all walks, SARSA earned 0.18 per walk, Q-learning 0.15. SARSA’s route is longer, but only 12 in 100 of its walks met a cat, against 22 for Q-learning. Early on both wander, earning about the same. Then SARSA’s numbers settle away from the cats, while Q-learning’s route keeps costing cats. Q-learning chose the cat-side route in 61 of 100 runs, SARSA in none.

sarsa:12.t: So who is right?. Both, about different Pips. Without random moves, Q-learning’s route would be worth 0.53, SARSA’s only 0.43. While Pip still explores, SARSA’s is worth more. Q-learning learns the best way to act, whatever Pip does meanwhile. SARSA learns the best way given its own habit, random moves included. Rule of thumb: if learning mistakes cost something real, use SARSA; if only the final route matters, Q-learning.

sarsa:13.t: Your turn. Drag epsilon. Each setting reruns both 100 times and draws each one’s most common route. The more random Pip is, the more SARSA avoids the cats. At 0.2 the other SARSA runs take the top row or a mix; in 91 of 100 its arrows never touch a cell above a cat. At 0 the rules coincide; with little randomness SARSA earns a bit less.

sarsa:14.t: Where it came from. Gavin Rummery and Mahesan Niranjan described the method in 1994 as “modified connectionist Q-learning”; Richard Sutton suggested the name SARSA. A room like this one is the cliff walking example from Sutton and Barto’s textbook. The lesson carries over: when mistakes made while learning are costly, as for a real robot near stairs, learning about the behaviour you actually have can be the safer choice.

sarsa:15.t: Recap. SARSA picks its next move first, then updates toward the reward plus gamma times that move’s number. So its numbers include Pip’s own random moves. Near danger it learns a safer route and earns more while exploring. Q-learning, with its max, learns the best route for a Pip that never moves at random.

onoff:0.t: On-Policy versus Off-Policy. Learn only from your own behaviour, or from anyone’s?

onoff:1.t: Two jobs. In the last two reels Pip learned four numbers per cell while moving epsilon-greedy: mostly the biggest, one time in five random. Such a learner has two rules. The behaviour policy picks the moves that make the experience. The target policy is the rule whose values the numbers describe; careful, not the update target. A policy is just a rule for picking moves.

onoff:2.t: SARSA: one rule. SARSA’s update target uses the next move that its epsilon-greedy habit really picks, random moves included. So its numbers describe epsilon-greedy: the very rule that is acting. Run in this maze, its biggest number at the start is 0.34, close to what its Pip really earned, 0.37. When the two rules are the same, the learning is on-policy: you learn about exactly what you do.

onoff:3.t: Q-learning: two rules. Q-learning also acts epsilon-greedy, but its update target uses the biggest number: it assumes the best next move every time. Its numbers describe the greedy rule, a Pip that never moves at random. That is why they said 0.53 at the start while Pip really earned 0.39. Learning about one policy while following another is off-policy learning.

onoff:4.t: Why Q-learning can do it. Q of s, a asks: what happens after move a in cell s? The maze answers with a reward and a landing cell, the same whoever chose the move. Then the max fills in the best way to carry on. So nothing in Q-learning’s update target depends on who acted. SARSA’s needs the walker’s next move, so it describes that walker.

onoff:5.t: Someone else’s diary. Remember the Wanderer, the mouse whose every move is random? Pip finds a diary of 100 of its walks from the start: every cell, move, reward and landing, 7,148 steps in all. Only 27 of those walks reached the cheese; 73 ended on the cat. The quickest took 17 steps. Can Pip learn the best route from this, without taking a single step itself?

onoff:6.t: Replaying the diary. Pip replays the diary step by step, applying Q-learning’s update as if it had made each move, 10 times over. The start’s biggest number: 0.45 after one reading, 0.53 after two, 0.53 after 10. Fast: one reading is 7,148 updates across every cell. Both shortest routes, left side or bottom, get the perfect numbers, 0.53 up to 1, though the Wanderer walked neither.

onoff:7.t: SARSA, same diary. Replayed with SARSA, the same diary gives the Wanderer’s own values, since its update target uses the Wanderer’s next move. At the start, all four are close to minus 0.03. Why near 0, when 73 walks in 100 met the cat? The walks average 71 steps, and 0.9 multiplied 70 times is 0.0006: late endings barely count. Correct, but useless for Pip.

onoff:8.t: Why off-policy matters. Learning one rule while following another opens doors. Pip can reuse old experience, replaying it many times instead of walking again. It can learn from other walkers: a random one, a human, an older self. It can explore wildly yet learn the best way to act. The random diary even fixed the bottom-row arrows Pip’s own walks got wrong: 16 of 16 are best moves.

onoff:9.t: Risk: only what the data shows. Another diary, from a careful mouse that follows the habit’s arrows and never moves at random: 100 walks, all the same 7 steps. Q-learning learns that route perfectly, and nothing else. In 9 of 16 cells the four numbers never moved. Drop Pip in one of those cells and it has no clue. Off-policy data can only teach about moves someone actually tried.

onoff:10.t: Risk: a rule that never acted. Off-policy numbers describe a rule that never acted. In the cat room they described a greedy Pip, but the epsilon-greedy walker met more cats than SARSA’s. At scale a network replaces the table, so changing one guess shifts others. Guesses chasing guesses can run away; off-policy data has no walk of that rule to correct them. This is Sutton and Barto’s deadly triad; more later.

onoff:11.t: Your turn. Pick whose experience Q-learning learns from: Pip’s own epsilon-greedy walks, the Wanderer’s random diary, or the careful mouse’s diary. The diaries are replayed ten times. Tap a cell to drop Pip there and follow the arrows. Where the data never went, Pip has no clue.

onoff:12.t: Where you meet them. Off-policy: Q-learning, and D Q N, which in 2015 replayed past Atari moves from memory in random order. sack, a 2018 robot-control method, does the same. Learning purely from logged data is offline R L. On-policy: SARSA, and P P O, from 2017, used to fine-tune chatbots. P P O learns a policy directly, no Q table. It gathers fresh experience with its current policy, learns briefly, then discards it.

onoff:13.t: Recap. The behaviour policy acts; the target policy is what the numbers describe. Same rule: on-policy, like SARSA. Different rules: off-policy, like Q-learning. Off-policy learners can reuse old experience and learn from others, but only about moves the data contains, and they are harder to keep stable.

traces:0.t: Eligibility Traces  and  T D(lambda). Give credit to recent steps, fading into the past.

traces:1.t: Two ways to pass the news. Pip follows its habit, one move in five random, learning each cell’s value. Cheese plus 1 and cat minus 1 come on stepping onto them, ending the walk. gamma (gamma) is 0.9. T D learning updates every step from the next cell’s guess; Monte Carlo waits for the real return. The best of both? The trick also works for Q-values, in SARSA and Q-learning.

traces:2.t: After walk 1. Walk 1: the familiar 7-step trip to the cheese. With T D only the cell beside the cheese learns: 0 plus 0.2 times 1 equals 0.2. Other steps had nothing to pass on. Fixed-fraction Monte Carlo moves every cell the same fifth of the way to its return: 0.2 beside the cheese, down to 0.11 at the start. One walk reached the whole path.

traces:3.t: Who deserves the credit?. Which earlier moves earned the cheese? This is the credit assignment problem. T D passes credit back about one cell per walk: here its guess for the start first moves on walk 7, and after 10 walks is only 0.0004. Monte Carlo credits every cell at once, but only after the walk, and one unlucky ending shakes the whole path. Is there a middle ground?

traces:4.t: Looking n steps ahead. T D’s target looks one step ahead; Monte Carlo looks to the end. In between is the n-step target: the next n real rewards, discounted by 0.9 per step as in a return, then 0.9 multiplied n times times the guess where Pip is n steps later. If the walk ends sooner, stop there. One step is T D, the whole walk Monte Carlo.

traces:5.t: A fading memory. Smoother than waiting n steps: give each cell a mark, its eligibility trace, and set a dial lambda (lambda) from 0 to 1. Each step, every mark first shrinks, times 0.9 times lambda; then the cell Pip just left gets mark 1. With lambda equals 0.8, after step 1 the start has 1; after step 2, 0.72, the cell above it 1.

traces:6.t: One surprise, many cells. Each step Pip computes the T D error as usual: reward plus 0.9 times next guess minus old guess. Then every cell moves by alpha times T D error times its mark. On walk 1 every T D error is 0 until the cheese: 1. That single surprise updates the whole recent path: 0.2 beside the cheese, then 0.144, 0.104, and on, down to 0.028 at the start.

traces:7.t: The dial lambda. At lambda equals 0 marks vanish after one step: plain T D. At lambda equals 1 marks shrink by 0.9 per step, like discounting, so on walk 1 each cell gets the plus 1 as its return would: exactly Monte Carlo. Later, guesses shift mid-walk, so only close. Between, it acts like an average of all n-step targets, longer ones weighted less. This is T D(lambda).

traces:8.t: A fair race. Pip’s habit never changes, so every lambda can learn from the very same walks. Each is scored by its error: its average gap from the true values on the 7 cells of Pip’s usual route. True values: the values reel’s notebook, 0.87 beside the cheese, 0.40 at the start. To avoid a lucky draw, we average the race over 200 sets of walks.

traces:9.t: The first 50 walks. Across: walks 1 to 50. Up: the error, averaged over all the sets of walks. Lower is better. After 10 walks, T D’s error is still 0.40; with lambda equals 0.8 it is 0.17, with lambda equals 1 only 0.09. Spreading each surprise over the recent path makes early learning much faster. But watch the rose line creep back up.

traces:10.t: Fast early, noisy later. Bars: error after 20 and 200 walks, one scale. At 20 walks lambda equals 0.9, in the middle, wins. After 200, plain T D wins: 0.06 against 0.10 for lambda equals 1. Why? Large lambda leans on the real rest of the walk, so one cat ending jolts many cells, as in Monte Carlo. Small lambda leans on neighbours’ guesses, which already average many walks.

traces:11.t: Is one alpha fair?. Every lambda used alpha equals 0.2, but large lambda spreads surprises widely and may want smaller steps. Now each gets its best alpha, 0.05 to 0.5. After 20 walks lambda equals 0.9 wins, 0.07. After 200, smaller steps help all, and lambda equals 0.5 edges ahead: 0.037, against 0.045 for T D and 0.046 for lambda equals 1. T D’s late win was partly the shared alpha.

traces:12.t: Your turn. Drag lambda. The maze shows this run’s notebook after 10 walks, and the bars show the averaged error after 20 and 200 walks for your setting. At 0, watch the news stay near the cheese; at 1, it reaches the start at once. Which lambda would you pick for 20 walks? For 200?

traces:13.t: The cost. Traces cost: each step updates every marked cell, not one. With lambda equals 0.8, a mark stays above 0.01 for 15 steps, so on a long walk Pip updates up to 15 cells per step instead of 1. Smaller marks can be dropped. Here, a revisited cell’s mark resets to 1, not adding up. And lambda is one more dial to tune, with alpha.

traces:14.t: Where you’ve seen this. Richard Sutton introduced T D(lambda) in 1988. Gerald Tesauro’s T D-Gammon (1992) used it to learn backgammon by playing itself, coming close to the best human players. The same lambda lives on in G A E (generalised advantage estimation, 2015). It judges how much better a move turned out than the cell’s value, blending short and long lookaheads with lambda; the popular P P O method commonly uses it.

traces:15.t: Recap. An eligibility trace is a fading mark on recently left cells. Each T D error updates every marked cell, in proportion to its mark, so one surprise reaches the whole recent path. lambda sets how slowly marks fade: 0 is T D, 1 is Monte Carlo-like. Large lambda learns fast early but is noisier; in between is often a good compromise.

funcapprox:0.t: Function Approximation. Too many states for a table? Learn a function that generalises.

funcapprox:1.t: Out of the maze. Pip has left the maze for an open meadow: no cells, no walls inside. Its position is just two numbers, x from left to right and y from bottom to top, each between 0 and 1. The rules stay: plus 1 on the step landing inside the cheese circle, minus 1 inside the cat’s circle, either ending the walk. gamma (gamma) is still 0.9.

funcapprox:2.t: Moves on bumpy grass. Pip still has four moves: up, right, down, left. A move carries it 0.15 that way, plus a small random wobble from the uneven grass. Three moves right from the start (0.10, 0.10) landed at (0.25, 0.11), then (0.39, 0.09), then (0.53, 0.08). The fence round the meadow stops Pip at the edge.

funcapprox:3.t: Pip’s habit. As in the values reel, Pip follows a fixed habit. Below 0.7 high, it goes up. Higher, it steps toward the cheese along whichever gap is bigger, sideways or up and down. One move in five goes a random direction instead. Here is walk 1: 10 moves; move 4 was random. We want this habit’s values: from each spot, the expected discounted return.

funcapprox:4.t: A notebook for every spot?. Each maze cell’s number was visited again and again. Here positions are real numbers and the wobble random, so every landing spot is new. Pip took 10,000 walks, from walk 2 on with random starts. It stood on 66,674 spots and, except when squeezed into a fence corner, never on exactly the same spot twice. A notebook page per spot would never be reread.

funcapprox:5.t: Chop it into squares?. We could cut the meadow into squares and keep one number per square. With 16 by 16 squares that is 256 numbers, and each learns only from its own visits. Worse, two neighbouring squares are almost the same place, yet what one learns teaches the other nothing. Finer squares mean more numbers and fewer visits each; coarser ones blur everything together.

funcapprox:6.t: Nearby spots, similar values. The habit’s true values, colour by colour: gold good, rose bad, stronger for bigger. We worked them out with 100 test walks from the middle of each square, something Pip cannot do; it must learn them. Note the dark band below the cat: from there the habit climbs straight into it, minus 0.69 at (0.60, 0.30). Mostly, though, nearby spots have similar values.

funcapprox:7.t: Four measurements. So instead of naming the spot, Pip describes it with a few measurements, called features: its x, its y, its distance to the cheese and its distance to the cat. At the start these are 0.10, 0.10, 1.06 and 0.71. Spots that are close have similar measurements, so a rule built on them treats them alike. That is generalisation.

funcapprox:8.t: A recipe with five knobs. The simplest rule: multiply each measurement by its own number, add them up, plus a fixed amount b. Those five numbers are weights, the knobs Pip can turn. Such a rule is a linear recipe. All five knobs start at 0, so the recipe guesses 0 everywhere. One recipe guesses for every spot on the meadow, even spots never visited.

funcapprox:9.t: Nudging the knobs. T D target: reward plus 0.9 times the landing guess, or just the reward at the end. Walk 1’s last step, from (0.81, 0.75) into the cheese: target 1, guess 0, error 1. Each knob moves by step size times error times its measurement, with 1 for b. At step size 0.05, b becomes 0.050. That is a gradient step on (target minus guess) squared, target held fixed: bigger measurements sway the guess more, so move more.

funcapprox:10.t: One nudge moved every spot. That single nudge changed the guess everywhere. The spot Pip left now guesses 0.115. The start, far away, now guesses 0.073, and the spot below the cat 0.093, though nothing happened there. This sharing is the whole point, and its danger: every lesson about one spot spills onto all the others.

funcapprox:11.t: Training the recipe. Train on all 10,000 walks; random starts cover the whole meadow. Pip nudges after every move, and the step size shrinks from 0.05 to 0.003, so late walks only fine-tune. Chart: the average gap between guess and true value over the 240 grass squares. It drops from 0.47 to 0.21, mostly in the first few hundred walks, then wobbles as walks tug the shared knobs.

funcapprox:12.t: What a straight recipe can’t draw. Left: the true values. Right: the trained recipe. It gets the big picture, good near the cheese, poor far away, but misses the band below the cat: at (0.60, 0.30) the truth is minus 0.69, the recipe 0.06. Why? The recipe only adds up measurements. A dip only where Pip is near the cat’s x and below it needs measurements combined, and adding can’t do “and”.

funcapprox:13.t: A tiny neural network. Hand-making a measurement for that band needs the answer already. Instead, a tiny neural network: the four measurements, scaled to minus 1 to 1, feed 8 hidden units, each summing them with its own weights and squashing the result into minus 1 to 1. The output sums those with more weights: the guess. Lines: weights; gold positive, rose negative, thicker bigger. 49 knobs, starting small and random. From the start’s measurements it guesses 0.19.

funcapprox:14.t: Same nudge, through the network. Each knob moves by step size times error times how much turning that knob would change this guess. For the recipe that was the measurement. In a network it is computed layer by layer, output first: backpropagation. At walk 1’s end it guessed 0.175 beside the cheese: error 1 minus 0.175 equals 0.825. One nudge at step size 0.1 lifts it to 0.366.

funcapprox:15.t: The network learns the shadow. The same 10,000 walks, now nudging the network, step size 0.1 shrinking to 0.005. Blue is its average gap, gold the recipe’s. The network ends at 0.14 against 0.21. The band below the cat appears: at (0.60, 0.30) the network says minus 0.35, the truth minus 0.69. But it is too wide: at (0.41, 0.34), truly worth 0.23, it says minus 0.16.

funcapprox:16.t: The catch: shared knobs. Walk 56 was one move into the cheese: one nudge, raising that spot by 0.064. The far-off start moved too, by plus 0.014. T D targets use the same knobs, so nudges move them too. Shared knobs, guesses from guesses and different-policy data can blow learning up together: Sutton and Barto’s deadly triad. Here the third was missing: Pip learned about its own habit, and stayed calm.

funcapprox:17.t: Your turn. Tap a spot on the meadow to teach Pip “this spot is worth 1”: 5 nudges there, step size 0.05, from the trained model. Watch which other spots change with it. Slide to switch between linear recipe and network. The recipe moves near and far spots about equally. The network moves nearby spots more, but far ones too: never only the spot you tapped.

funcapprox:18.t: Where you’ve seen this. In 1992 Gerald Tesauro’s T D-Gammon learned backgammon with exactly this mix: a neural network for the values of board positions, trained with T D targets from games against itself. Later versions played close to the best human players. Today almost every large R L system uses a network instead of a table. The next reel, D Q N, does it for Q-values and learns Atari games from the screen.

funcapprox:19.t: Recap. When states are too many, or never repeat, a table cannot work. Function approximation describes a state with features and learns a function with a few knobs that gives a guess for any state. Learning nudges the knobs toward T D targets, a gradient step. Because the knobs are shared, every lesson generalises to similar states, and sometimes spills where it should not.

dqn:0.t: Deep Q-Network (D Q N). Q-learning plus a neural network: superhuman Atari from pixels.

dqn:1.t: From values to choices. In the last reel a tiny network learned the values of Pip’s meadow habit. But a fixed habit’s values don’t say how to do better. The maze had Q-learning: a number Q per spot and move, “how good is this move here, if I play well afterwards”. On the meadow, where spots never repeat, a Q table is as impossible as a value table.

dqn:2.t: Q-learning, remembered. After each move, Q-learning nudges that move’s number toward a target: the reward plus 0.9 times the largest Q at the landing spot, or just the reward if the walk ended. Taking the largest means: assume Pip plays its best from there. And Pip acts epsilon-greedy, said epsilon-greedy: one move in five at random, to keep exploring; otherwise the largest-Q move.

dqn:3.t: One output per move. The fix, as in the last reel: a network. This one has four outputs, one Q-value per move: up, right, down, left. Feed in Pip’s four measurements, and one pass gives all four. That is a Deep Q-Network, or D Q N. Its 76 knobs start random. At the start spot it says: up minus 0.28, right 0.61, down 0.04, left 0.10. Pure noise, for now.

dqn:4.t: The simple way: learn as you go. First try: after each move, one nudge on its output. Move 37 was a step left, its untrained numbers’ favourite, by a hair: 0.113 against 0.111 for right. It went from (0.86, 0.63) into the cat: target minus 1. One nudge took “left” from 0.113 to 0.101. Every knob moves only about 0.003 per nudge, so one bad moment can’t wipe out everything; the other outputs, sharing knobs, moved a little too.

dqn:5.t: It flounders. Pip learns this way for 8,000 moves, from random starts. Black dots: 30 fixed test spots, tried every 250 moves by largest Q, no random moves. The chart counts walks reaching the cheese. It hardly learns: 28 of 32 tests reach the cheese at most once. Only the very last test, after 8,000 moves, scores 27: one good test after 31 poor ones is nothing to rely on.

dqn:6.t: Problem 1: a target that runs away. Unlike a table, the target comes from the same network, at a spot only 0.15 away: nudge the guess up and the target rises too. Here the target moved a median 0.90 times as far as the guess, the same way 84 percent of the time, so a nudge closes only a sliver of the gap: 0.025 to 0.024. Frozen targets, the target network reel, mostly steady the numbers here; the next problem matters more.

dqn:7.t: Problem 2: one moment at a time. Second problem: moves arrive in order. The rose dots: 60 consecutive moves early in the next run, a few walks each hugging one patch or fence. The network bends toward each patch in turn, drifting elsewhere. Random old moves from a memory, the blue dots, would mix the whole meadow into each lesson. That is experience replay, its own reel.

dqn:8.t: D Q N’s two fixes. DeepMind’s D Q N adds two things. A replay memory keeps the last 2000 moves; each move, Pip draws 32 at random, a batch that may include the newest, and makes one nudge from their average error. A target network, a frozen copy refreshed every 100 nudges, so every 100 moves, computes targets. Each fix has its own reel; here both are on.

dqn:9.t: Now it learns. Same 8,000 moves, same dice: blue D Q N, rose the simple version. D Q N first scores 28 of 30 or better after 4,250 moves, and after 8,000 gets all 30. Effort was unequal: each D Q N nudge averages 32 moves, a simple nudge one. The replay reel’s fair race still has memory winning clearly. Over 12 seeds D Q N usually ended near 30, the simple one mostly far lower.

dqn:10.t: What the network learned. Best move per grid spot; colour is the largest Q. From the bottom left: up the side, along the top; from the right: straight up. Mostly it rounds the cat, but 10 of 40 spots right below it still point up, into it. From the start: 12 moves; over 200 wobbles, 11.9 on average. Five up and five right take about 10: good, not best. It learned this from moves and rewards alone.

dqn:11.t: Inside the network. From the start spot, the outputs read up 0.39, right 0.32, down 0.31, left 0.34. Pip picks up. The 12-move walk it takes is worth 0.9 to the power 11, about 0.31, less than its 0.39. Left, a wasted fence bump, scores above right, a good first move. It ranks the best move right here, but the numbers are only rough.

dqn:12.t: Your turn. Tap a spot on the meadow to drop Pip there. It walks by its network’s largest Q, no random moves. Teal ends at the cheese, rose at the cat, grey runs out of moves. Slide to pick how long D Q N trained. Early networks wander, bump the fence or walk into the cat; later ones take Pip round the cat to the cheese from almost anywhere.

dqn:13.t: Atari, from pixels. D Q N made its name on Atari video games. In 2013 Volodymyr Mnih and colleagues at DeepMind trained it on seven games. In 2015, in Nature, one D Q N with the same network and settings played 49 games, learning from screen pixels and score alone. Input: the last four frames, not four measurements, so motion was visible; outputs: one Q-value per joystick action.

dqn:14.t: What it did, and didn’t. D Q N reached at least three quarters of a professional human tester’s score on 29 of the 49 games, and beat earlier learning methods on most. It failed where rewards are rare, like Montezuma’s Revenge, where random moves almost never score. It needed tens of millions of frames per game, far more practice than a person. Later reels show replay, target networks and their successors.

dqn:15.t: Recap. D Q N is Q-learning with a neural network: Pip’s measurements in, one Q-value per move out, epsilon-greedy to act, and nudges toward reward plus 0.9 times the largest Q at the landing spot. Done naively, the targets run away and the lessons come one corner at a time. Replay memory and a target network made it learn, here on the meadow and on 49 Atari games.

replay:0.t: Experience Replay. Store experiences, then learn from random old memories.

replay:1.t: Pip’s network, again. The D Q N reel’s simple version floundered until two fixes came on: a replay memory and a frozen copy for targets. This reel studies the first alone, so the frozen copy stays off: targets come from the network being trained. Same network: four measurements in, one Q-value per move out. Walks start at random spots, last at most 60 moves; one move in five is random.

replay:2.t: Learning on the go. Simplest plan: learn from experience in order. Each move makes one experience, a card: where Pip stood, the move, the reward, and where it landed or that the walk ended. That is all a target needs. For fairness later, each update uses the latest 32 cards. After each move the handful slides one card, so each card serves 32 updates in a row.

replay:3.t: Near-duplicates. The latest 32 cards, on the meadow: Pip has lingered in the top-left corner, x from 0.00 to 0.17, y from 0.57 to 1.00. 15 of the 32 moves bumped the fence; when this stretch began, the network’s favourite move at all 32 spots was left, toward it. Consecutive experiences are alike, or correlated. The network gets nearly the same lesson 32 times.

replay:4.t: Old lessons get overwritten. The ringed spot below the cheese is one move from it, worth about 1; the network said 0.80. Pip never goes near, yet in 96 moves it falls to 0.29. All spots share 76 knobs, so fitting the corner shifts the cheese’s numbers, uncorrected by any card. Old lessons get overwritten. Not mainly the moving target: in run 2, frozen copy on, the same value slid from 0.96 to 0.40 in 80 moves.

replay:5.t: A shoebox of cards. The fix is experience replay. Every experience card goes into a shoebox, the replay memory, and stays there for a while. This box keeps the latest 2000 cards; when it is full, the oldest card is thrown out. So the box holds moves from many walks, all over the meadow.

replay:6.t: A random handful. Before each update, Pip draws 32 cards from the box at random: a random handful, called a minibatch (the D Q N reel’s 32 picked at random). One gradient step then fits all 32 at once, on average. This handful comes from all over the meadow. On average over the run, two cards in a random handful lie 0.60 apart; two of the latest 32 only 0.31.

replay:7.t: A fair race. Both versions train 8000 moves each, same seeds. Each update uses 32 cards and one gradient step of the same size. Only which 32 differs: the latest, or a random handful from the box. Every 500 moves, a test: from 30 fixed spots Pip follows its largest Q, no random moves. The chart counts spots from which it reaches the cheese, out of 30.

replay:8.t: The race. Four runs per version: thin lines single runs, thick their average. Teal: random handfuls; orange: the latest 32. Single runs jump a lot. After 8000 moves, replay reaches the cheese from 25.8 of 30 spots on average, the latest 32 from 7.8. Replay won 3 of the 4 runs, and its average is ahead at every test. Same work; only the cards differ.

replay:9.t: Why the shuffle helps. A random handful samples the whole meadow fairly, so each step nudges everywhere a little rather than bending toward one corner. Below the cheese, over the last 4000 moves, the replay run swings by about 0.09, the latest-32 run by 0.27. Both use each card about 32 times; replay spreads them over 2000 moves, mixed with other cards, instead of 32 updates in a row.

replay:10.t: Two maps. Run 1’s two networks at 8000 moves, mapped by largest Q: left replay, right the latest 32. Gold good, rose bad. Following the map from the start, the replay Pip reaches the cheese in 13 moves, along the bottom and up the right side; the left-side route of the D Q N reel is about as long. The other one reaches the cheese in 45 moves.

replay:11.t: Old cards, old habits. The box’s cards came from an older Pip, with older Q-values and habits. D Q N doesn’t mind: its target, as in Q-learning, asks the worth of the best move from the landing spot, whatever habit made the card. Any card gives a fair target. SARSA-like methods, learning about Pip’s current habit, would study a Pip that no longer exists, so they cannot simply reuse old cards.

replay:12.t: What about the deadly triad?. The funcapprox reel warned: a network, plus targets built from guesses, plus data from another habit can blow up. Replay has all three: old cards come from older Pips. Nothing guarantees safety, but here it stayed calm, likely because the box holds only the latest 2000 moves, so its cards come from Pips much like today’s. The next reel’s frozen copy adds more safety.

replay:13.t: Your turn. Drag the memory size (four runs each). With 32 cards even a random handful is a near-duplicate; a few hundred already work much better. Keeping all 8000 was worse here (13.8 against 25.8). Every card gives a fair target, but the box decides which spots get lessons. Likely: most cards then come from early walks, in places today’s Pip rarely visits.

replay:14.t: Where it came from. Long-Ji Lin proposed experience replay in 1992. D Q N made it famous in 2015: its memory held the latest one million moves, and each update used a random handful of 32. Without replay, D Q N’s Breakout score dropped from about 317 to about 10. One upgrade, prioritised replay (Schaul and others, 2016), draws the surprising cards, those with a big T D error, more often.

replay:15.t: Recap. Moves that follow each other are near-duplicates, and fitting the latest ones bends the shared knobs toward one corner, overwriting old lessons. Experience replay keeps the latest moves as cards in a memory and learns from random handfuls: varied, fair samples of the whole meadow, each card reused many times.

targetnet:0.t: Target Networks. Stop chasing your own tail: freeze the target for a while.

targetnet:1.t: Where replay left off. The D Q N reel spotted the problem: the target is computed by the same network being nudged, so it moves with the guess. Pip keeps the replay memory from the last reel; now we look at that chase up close. A card’s target is the reward plus 0.9 times the largest Q-value where Pip landed. Who supplies that Q-value? The very network being trained.

targetnet:2.t: One card, many steps. An experiment: take Pip’s network after 3000 moves of training, and one card. From (0.50, 0.20) Pip moved right to (0.65, 0.20), reward 0. The network values this move at minus 0.04; its target is 0 plus 0.9 times the best Q-value at the landing spot equals 0.00. Now take 200 small gradient steps on this one card and watch both.

targetnet:3.t: Chasing your own shadow. Each step pulls gold toward teal, but teal moves too. After 200 steps gold is 0.14 and the target 0.15, levelling off. No new information came in; whatever the true value, this climb came from the chase alone. Why? The nearby landing spot shares the same 76 knobs. Raising the value here raises it there, so the target runs ahead: chasing your own shadow.

targetnet:4.t: Freeze a copy. The fix: keep a second network, a frozen copy of Pip’s network, used only to compute targets. It is called the target network. Training changes the live network; the copy stays as it was. Now the target is reward plus 0.9 times the largest Q-value the copy gives at the landing spot.

targetnet:5.t: The chase stops. Same card, same 200 steps, but the target comes from the frozen copy. Teal stays at 0.00, and gold reaches it, to within 0.01, after 27 steps, then stays there. With the target held still, each update solves an ordinary fitting problem: hit a fixed number.

targetnet:6.t: Refresh every N updates. A copy frozen forever would never learn, so every N updates the live knobs are copied into it. Here N equals 50: the target holds, gold catches up, the target jumps. One card anchors nothing, so the drift remains, slower: 0.07 after 200 steps instead of 0.14. The copy slows the loop but does not remove it. In real training, other cards bring real information.

targetnet:7.t: Back to real training. Now full training: 8000 moves with replay, once with live targets and once with a copy refreshed every 100 updates. Same seeds. The chart tracks the largest Q-value at Pip’s start spot, bottom left, over 8000 moves of experience. Orange: live targets. Teal: with the copy. At move 0 the number comes from random knobs.

targetnet:8.t: Calmer numbers. Live targets jitter. Measure the jumps: the average size of the change between readings 100 moves apart, over moves 4000 to 8000, four runs each: 0.05 with live targets, 0.02 with the copy. Cheese from 30 test spots after 8000 moves: 25.8 against 28.3. So in this meadow replay did most of the work; the copy mainly steadies the numbers and adds a little.

targetnet:9.t: Your turn. Drag N, the number of updates between refreshes of the copy (four runs each; “none” means live targets). Too often, and the chase is back. Too rarely, and the targets go stale: N equals 1000 gives only 7 refreshes in the run, the calmest numbers (jumps 0.01), but only 16.0 of 30 spots reach the cheese. N equals 100 balances the two here.

targetnet:10.t: Where it’s used. D Q N (2015) used a target network refreshed every 10,000 updates. Without it, still with replay, its Breakout score fell from about 317 to about 241. Many later methods, like D D P G and sack, use soft updates instead: after every update the copy moves a tiny fraction, such as half a percent, toward the live network, so the target drifts smoothly.

targetnet:11.t: Recap. When a network computes its own targets, every update moves the target it chases: the numbers can drift and wobble. A target network, a frozen copy refreshed every N updates, holds the targets still, so each stretch of training is a fixed fitting problem. Refresh too rarely and learning slows.

doubledqn:0.t: Double D Q N. Taking a max over noisy guesses is too optimistic.

doubledqn:1.t: The max in the target. Pip now trains the full D Q N: replay memory, plus the frozen copy refreshed every 100 updates. A card’s target is the reward plus 0.9 times the largest of the copy’s four Q-values at the landing spot. That word “largest” hides a problem. To see it, leave the meadow for a moment and play with plain numbers.

doubledqn:2.t: Four moves worth nothing. Imagine a spot where all four moves are truly worth exactly 0. Pip does not know that; its guesses are 0 plus a bell-shaped random error, typically about 0.1 either way. One round of guesses: plus 0.15, minus 0.10, plus 0.07, plus 0.11. The largest guess is plus 0.15. If the target uses the largest, it says this spot is worth plus 0.15, not 0.

doubledqn:3.t: Roll again. New round, new errors. Each yellow box is that round’s largest guess. A single guess is right on average: over 1000 rounds, the guesses for “up” average 0.00. But the largest guess was above 0 in 945 of 1000 rounds, averaging plus 0.10. The max keeps picking the lucky errors. An error that always leans one way is a bias: here an overestimation bias.

doubledqn:4.t: It spreads backwards. In Q-learning and D Q N the target is reward plus 0.9 times the largest Q-value where Pip lands. Those Q-values are noisy: the network is still partly wrong, and the wobble adds chance. So the target leans high. It does not stay there. The spot one move earlier learns from that inflated number, the spot before from that one: the optimism travels back along Pip’s routes.

doubledqn:5.t: Two opinions. The fix needs two independent sets of guesses, A and B. Let A choose the move: the one with A’s largest guess. Then let B score that move, with B’s guess for it. B’s error has nothing to do with A’s, so B’s number is just 0 plus a fresh random error: no longer lucky on purpose.

doubledqn:6.t: Back to zero. Over the same 1000 rounds, the largest guess averaged plus 0.10. Choosing with A and scoring with B averaged 0.00: the bias is gone. This trick is called Double Q-learning. Hado van Hasselt proposed it in 2010 for tables of Q-values, keeping two tables and letting each pick moves for the other.

doubledqn:7.t: D Q N already has two. D Q N already has two networks, live and frozen copy. Double D Q N, by van Hasselt, Guez and Silver, 2015, uses them as A and B: at the landing spot the live one chooses the move, the copy scores it. Nothing else changes. The copy lags the live one by up to 100 updates, so their errors are only partly independent. The bias shrinks, maybe not fully.

doubledqn:8.t: One real card. At the corner (0.05, 0.05), Double D Q N run, 7050 moves in, the copy favours “up”, 0.28; the live network prefers “down”, bumping the fence. D Q N would use 0.28; Double D Q N, the copy’s “down”, 0.16. On a simple route, up the left and along the top, “up” first is worth about 0.30, “down” first 0.26. D Q N was about right; Double D Q N underestimates: it can err low too.

doubledqn:9.t: Estimates against reality. Does it matter in the meadow? At each of the 30 test spots, compare the network’s largest Q-value, its estimate, with what Pip really gets: the average discounted return of 5 walks from there following its largest Q-values. The chart shows estimate minus reality, averaged over the spots and 8 runs, so the chance in single walks mostly averages out. Above 0: too optimistic.

doubledqn:10.t: The bias shrinks. Eight runs each, averaged. Orange, D Q N: 0.23 too high after 1000 moves, 0.09 averaged over eight checks. Teal, Double D Q N: 0.11 at first, then near 0, sometimes below: 0.01 on average. The gap is mostly early: by 8000 moves both are 0.03 too high. Counting misses either way, Double D Q N is off by 0.04, D Q N by 0.09. Cheese reached: 26.6 and 25.9 of 30 spots.

doubledqn:11.t: Your turn. Back to the plain numbers. Drag the number of moves, all truly worth 0, and see a thousand rounds. More moves give the max more chances to catch a lucky error: with 2 moves the largest guess averages plus 0.06, with 16 it averages plus 0.18. Choosing with A and scoring with B stays near 0 every time.

doubledqn:12.t: Where it’s used. Van Hasselt, Guez and Silver found that D Q N’s value estimates on several Atari games were far above the scores it really earned. Double D Q N brought them down and played better on many games. The same worry shaped later methods. T D 3 (2018) keeps two critics and trusts the smaller of their two guesses. Rainbow (2017) bundles Double D Q N with other upgrades.

doubledqn:13.t: Recap. The largest of several noisy guesses is too high on average. D Q N’s target takes exactly such a max, so its numbers lean optimistic, and the optimism spreads backwards. Double D Q N lets the live network choose the move and the frozen copy score it. Their errors are only partly shared, so most lucky high guesses stop getting in for free.

pg:0.t: Policy Gradient Methods. Skip the values: directly tweak the policy to win more.

pg:1.t: Two ways to get better. In the Monte Carlo and Q-learning reels, Pip learned a number for every move, Q, then mostly picked the biggest, with a few random moves. Values first, choices second. This reel tries the other way round. Pip keeps its choices themselves, as chances, and adjusts them directly: moves that led to good outcomes become more likely. These are policy gradient methods.

pg:2.t: The door room. To see the idea clearly, start with one decision. Pip stands in a room with three doors, A, B and C. It picks one and walks through, and that ends the episode. Behind each door a crumb appears with a hidden chance, worth reward 1; otherwise the reward is 0. Pip does not know the chances. The question marks on the doors stand for them.

pg:3.t: A policy made of chances. Pip’s policy is a chance for each door, drawn as a pie. At first it is a third each: Pip has no idea which door is best, so it tries all of them. This is a stochastic policy from the policies reel, pi of a given s. Here there is only one situation, the room, so the pie is the whole policy.

pg:4.t: Turn scores into chances. Pip keeps one preference per door, any number, positive or negative. To get chances it raises e, about 2.72, to the power of each preference, then divides each by their total: softmax. All preferences 0: e to the 0 is 1 per door, total 3, so a third each. Raise C’s preference to 1: C gets 2.72, the total is 4.72, C’s chance 0.58.

pg:5.t: Why preferences?. Pip can push any preference freely; softmax still returns proper chances: all above 0, adding up to 1. No door ever gets chance 0, so Pip keeps trying every door, which helps it explore. It can approach “always C” but never reach it. Only the differences matter. Add 1 to each: 0, 0, 1 becomes 1, 1, 2, and the chances stay 0.21, 0.21, 0.58.

pg:6.t: How good is a policy?. Peek at the hidden chances: A 0.2, B 0.5, C 0.8. Pip still does not know them; we use them to score its policy. The expected return of a policy is its average reward per episode: each door’s picking chance times its crumb chance, added up. With a third each: 0.2 plus 0.5 plus 0.8, over 3, gives 0.50. Always C would give 0.8.

pg:7.t: Which way is uphill?. Which way should Pip nudge each preference to raise the expected return? The answer: the gradient, as in machine learning, but climbing, not descending. The chart keeps A and B at 0 and plots expected return against C’s preference. At 0 the slope is 0.10: raise C’s preference a little, and the return rises about 0.10 times as much. Then the dot steps uphill.

pg:8.t: Every preference at once. For softmax, each door’s gradient entry is simple: the door’s chance times how much it beats the current expected return. A: 0.33 times (0.2 minus 0.5) equals minus 0.10. B: 0, matching the average, for now. C: plus 0.10. Raising C’s preference grows C’s chance, taking a little from A and B. Gains minus losses, each times its crumb chance, leave C’s chance times (0.8 minus 0.5).

pg:9.t: Climbing, nudge by nudge. Pip adds the gradient times a step size alpha (alpha) equals 2 to the preferences, recomputes the gradient, and repeats. The gradient only describes the slope where Pip stands, so it takes many small steps. After 5 nudges the expected return is 0.67, after 20 it is 0.78, and C’s chance has grown to 0.94. The gains shrink as Pip nears the best possible 0.8.

pg:10.t: Small nudges, small changes. Why chances? First, they change smoothly. Take guesses A 0.2, B 0.51, C 0.49, always picking the biggest. Shift B and C by 0.02, to 0.49 and 0.51, and the choice flips to C. With preferences A 0, B 0.01, C minus 0.01, the same shift only moves the chances from B 0.34, C 0.33 to B 0.33, C 0.34. Learning slides gently instead of jumping.

pg:11.t: Any strength you like. Second, actions need not be a short list. Say Pip must jump a gap with any strength. A table would need an entry for every strength. A policy can instead be a bell curve over strengths, set by its centre mu (mu) and spread sigma (sigma). Same idea: nudge mu toward strengths that landed better; sigma can be learned too. Later reels show how.

pg:12.t: Random on purpose. Third, some problems need a random policy. In rock, paper, scissors, any fixed choice is beaten once spotted; the best play is a third each. This matters against adapting opponents, or when Pip cannot see everything; in the fixed maze one move per cell is enough. Picking the biggest guess, even with epsilon-greedy’s random moves, cannot learn such a mix. A policy of chances can.

pg:13.t: Back in the maze. The same idea works in the maze. Each cell gets four preferences, one per move, and its own softmax: 16 cells, 64 numbers. Each cell’s four arrows show the chances: the longer, the more likely. All preferences start at 0, so every arrow is a quarter, the random Pip from the first reel. Raise one preference, and its arrow grows.

pg:14.t: The catch. So far we used the hidden crumb chances: the gradient needed them, and Pip lacks them. In the maze it would also need the rulebook, since where moves lead decides which rewards follow. Pip must estimate the gradient from its own tries: pick a door, see the result, nudge. That is the next reel, REINFORCE. Its nudges are noisy, the theme of the reels after.

pg:15.t: Your turn. Tap a door to raise its preference by 0.5. Tap the floor to reset. Watch the chances, the expected return, and the gradient arrows telling you which way is uphill. Try raising A a few times, then C. Or tap all three doors once each: the chances do not change.

pg:16.t: Where it is used. Policy gradient methods train controllers for simulated and real robots, where actions are motor strengths. P P O, a policy gradient method from 2017, trained OpenAI Five, which beat the Dota 2 world champions in 2019. AlphaGo’s policy network was improved by policy gradient in self-play, and P P O-style training is used to fine-tune chatbots from human feedback.

pg:17.t: Recap. A policy gradient method keeps the policy itself as adjustable numbers and nudges them to raise the expected return. Softmax turns preferences into chances. The gradient says which way to nudge each preference: here, toward doors that beat the current average. Chances change smoothly, handle any action, and can stay random on purpose.

reinforce:0.t: REINFORCE. The simplest policy gradient: weight actions by the episode’s return.

reinforce:1.t: Learning from tries. In the last reel, Pip climbed toward the best door using the exact gradient. But that needed the hidden crumb chances, which Pip does not have. REINFORCE fixes this. Pip simply tries: it picks a door with its current chances, sees what happens, and nudges its preferences. No hidden chances, no rulebook, only its own experience.

reinforce:2.t: One try. All preferences start at 0, so each door has chance 0.33. Pip rolls its dice and picks door C. A crumb appears: reward 1. The idea is simple: an action followed by a good return becomes more likely. So C’s preference goes up, and the other two go down a little.

reinforce:3.t: The nudge, exactly. Each preference moves by step size alpha (alpha) times return times a factor. For the chosen door the factor is 1 minus its chance: 1 minus 0.33 equals 0.67. For every other door it is minus its chance, minus 0.33. With alpha equals 0.5 and return 1: C gets plus 0.33, A and B minus 0.17. Had the reward been 0, nothing would change at all.

reinforce:4.t: How surprising was the choice?. That factor is the gradient of the log-probability, the log of the chosen door’s chance. The nudge scales with the return and how surprising the choice was: chance 0.9 gives a factor of 0.1, chance 0.1 gives 0.9. Why? Likely doors get picked, and nudged, often; rare doors seldom, so each nudge counts more. Dividing by the chance exactly cancels how often it is picked.

reinforce:5.t: On average, uphill. One try is a rough guess. Here Pip tries 2,000 times without changing its chances, and we average reward times factor for each door. Each line is a running average; the dashed lines are the exact gradient from the last reel: minus 0.10, 0 and plus 0.10. After 2,000 tries the averages are minus 0.10, 0 and 0.10. REINFORCE’s nudges are noisy, but on average they point uphill.

reinforce:6.t: A whole walk. The maze: dry floor, plus 1 onto the cheese, minus 1 onto the cat, both end the walk, gamma (gamma) 0.9. Preferences start at 0. REINFORCE waits for the walk to end, like Monte Carlo, then gives each move the return that followed it: a move cannot change earlier rewards. Textbook REINFORCE also shrinks later moves’ nudges by 0.9 per step; like most code, we skip that.

reinforce:7.t: Walk 1. Walk 1 takes 15 moves. Pip wanders, bumps into walls 6 times, and finally steps up onto the cat: reward minus 1. Now every move gets its return: minus 1 for the last, minus 0.90 for the one before, and so on back to minus 0.23 for Pip’s first move. The labels show the return of the last move made in each cell.

reinforce:8.t: Every move pushed down. Each move’s preference changes by alpha times its return times its factor, with alpha equals 0.2. All returns were negative, so every move became less likely. Fair for the last move, up into the cat: there its chance drops from 0.25 to 0.21. But Pip’s first move, up from the start, was fine. Its chance drops too, to 0.24, only because this walk ended badly.

reinforce:9.t: The first cheese. Walk 5 is the first to reach the cheese, after 39 moves. The last move gets return 1, but Pip’s first move only 0.02: the cheese was too many steps away to matter much. So learning starts near the cheese, where returns are big, and spreads back toward the start as walks get shorter.

reinforce:10.t: 300 walks. Across: walk number. Each dot is that walk’s return from the start: gold for cheese, rose for cat. Long walks score near 0, so ticks along the bottom also mark cat walks, rose, and stopped walks, grey. The line averages the last 25 walks. Early walks are long and score near 0. Then returns climb: the last-25 average reaches 0.50, near the best possible 0.53.

reinforce:11.t: What Pip learned. After 300 walks, following the biggest arrow from the start gives a route of 7 moves to the cheese, the shortest possible. At the start, “up” now has chance 0.87. Along the way, 23 walks ended on the cat and 24 were stopped at 100 moves. Stopped walks scored 0 and changed nothing. Off the route, cells were rarely visited, so their arrows stay rough.

reinforce:12.t: Same recipe, other dice. Run REINFORCE again with different dice. The thin lines are five runs, each the average of its last 25 walks. Around walk 100 they range from 0.13 to 0.33: some runs learn early, some late. The thick line averages 100 runs. It climbs smoothly, to 0.45 over the last 25 walks. A single run is a very noisy version of it.

reinforce:13.t: Why so noisy?. Each walk’s luck colours every move. One random detour into the cat punishes the good moves before it, like walk 1; one lucky walk rewards its bumps. The bars count Pip’s 300 walks by return, from minus 0.53 to 0.53. Nudges scale with these returns, so they swing as widely. This is high variance: right on average, but each estimate jumps. The next reel calms it.

reinforce:14.t: Your turn. Drag the step size alpha. Each setting reruns 100 runs of 300 walks with the same dice. The thick line is their average return; the thin lines are runs 1 to 5. Small alpha learns slowly but steadily. Big alpha learns faster at first, but watch the count of runs that end up stuck.

reinforce:15.t: Too big a step. With alpha equals 1, 8 of 100 runs get stuck. Run 15’s early walks hit the cat 7 times, never the cheese; big pushes turned most arrows left or down, away from it. From walk 52, all 249 walks hit the 100-move stop: return 0, no nudge. No chance is exactly 0, so an ending is possible, just unlikely. Big steps on noisy estimates can wreck a policy.
