reinforce:16.t: Where it is used. Ronald Williams published REINFORCE in 1992. AlphaGo, described in 2016, improved its policy network this way: games against earlier versions of itself, with each move nudged by whether the game was won or lost. REINFORCE-style updates are still used today, for example to fine-tune language models on a reward score, usually together with the noise-calming tricks of the next reels.

reinforce:17.t: Recap. REINFORCE learns a policy from complete episodes. After each one, every action’s log-probability is nudged by step size times the return that followed it. Rare choices get bigger nudges, so on average the nudges follow the true gradient. But one episode’s luck colours every action, so single updates are noisy, and big steps can wreck the policy.

baseline:0.t: Baselines  and  Advantage. Not “was it good?” but “was it better than usual?”

baseline:1.t: A crumb behind the worst door. Door room, plain REINFORCE, 14 picks in. B’s crumbs made B the favourite, though C is better. Now Pip opens A, the worst door: a crumb, reward 1. A pays only 2 times in 10, yet becomes more likely. An empty door, reward 0, changes nothing. So a picked door only goes up or stays; it loses chance slowly, only when other doors pay.

baseline:2.t: Better than usual?. Think of grading on a curve. A score of 75 is great if the class usually gets 60, and poor if it usually gets 90. What matters is the score against what is usual. So Pip keeps a baseline, a yardstick for a usual reward, and nudges by reward minus yardstick, not the reward itself. Better than usual: push up. Worse: push down.

baseline:3.t: The advantage. Reward minus yardstick is the advantage: how much better this try went than usual. A simple yardstick: the average of Pip’s rewards so far this run. With each door at one third, crumbs come about half the time, so it starts near 0.5. A crumb from A: advantage 1 minus 0.5 equals plus 0.5. An empty door: 0 minus 0.5 equals minus 0.5, a push down.

baseline:4.t: Same direction, on average. Does a yardstick bend Pip’s learning direction? No: it is the same whatever Pip picks. Door A, yardstick 0.5: Picked, a third of the time, A’s preference loses 0.5 times 0.67 equals 0.33. Not picked, two thirds of the time, it gains 0.5 times 0.33 equals 0.17. Averaged: a third of 0.33 minus two thirds of 0.17 is 0. Same for every door, any yardstick.

baseline:5.t: Smaller spread. So the average nudge stays minus 0.10, 0, plus 0.10, the exact gradient. What changes is the spread: how far a single nudge typically lands from that average, measured in preference units. Here each dot is one possible single-try nudge to C’s preference; its size shows how often it happens. Combining all three doors, the spread is 0.56 plain and 0.38 with the yardstick.

baseline:6.t: Less spread, faster learning. Now 500 runs of 200 picks, with and without the average-reward yardstick, alpha equals 0.5, same dice. Along the bottom: picks. Up the side: Pip’s chance of picking C. Lines: the average over runs. Shaded: the middle 80 percent of runs. After 50 picks the chance of C averages 0.78 plain and 0.84 with the yardstick, and the band is much narrower.

baseline:7.t: Fewer stuck runs. Look at single runs at pick 200. Plain REINFORCE leaves 32 of 500 runs with C’s chance still below one half: a few lucky crumbs from A or B pushed them the wrong way, and empty doors change nothing; only C’s crumbs slowly pull them back. With the yardstick, 3 of 500. Empty doors now push down, so a wrong lead gets corrected.

baseline:8.t: Your turn. Drag the yardstick: a fixed number from 0 to 1, or Pip’s running average. Each reruns the same 500 runs. Any yardstick from 0.25 to 1 beats none here. A yardstick of 1 mirrors plain REINFORCE: crumbs change nothing, empty doors push down. It helps less: 0.83 after 50 picks, against 0.85 with 0.75. The running average is not best, but needs no tuning.

baseline:9.t: One yardstick is not enough. Back to the maze: REINFORCE, same alpha equals 0.2. One average won’t do: late in training, Pip’s usual return is about 0.46 from the start, 0.99 from beside the cheese. The numbers: Pip’s yardsticks after 300 walks, learned as shown next. So each cell gets a yardstick: its value V of s, the usual return from that cell under current chances, from the values reel.

baseline:10.t: Learning the yardsticks. Pip learns V of s like the Monte Carlo reel, from returns, with no rulebook: after each walk, each visited cell’s yardstick moves a tenth of the way toward the return that followed. Each move is nudged by its advantage: return minus its cell’s yardstick, using the yardsticks from before the walk; only then are they updated. Preferences and yardsticks learn side by side.

baseline:11.t: Better or worse than usual. Walk 201: Pip steps from the cell left of the cheese straight onto it. Return 1, yardstick there 0.99: advantage plus 0.01, a gentle push up. Walk 202: in that same cell Pip’s dice pick left, then right, right: cheese on the third move, return 0.81. Advantage minus 0.18: that move gets pushed down. Plain REINFORCE would push it up, since its return was positive.

baseline:12.t: How much calmer?. Freeze everything after walks 50, 150, 300; run 2,000 walks each. Measure the variance of one walk’s nudges, with and without yardsticks: the average squared distance from their mean, summed over 64 preferences. After walk 50, poor young yardsticks make it worse: 2.43 to 3.25. After 150 they divide it by 3.5, after 300 by 8.3. The average direction holds; poor ones just add noise.

baseline:13.t: An honest result. Over 100 runs, average curves almost overlap: last 25 walks, 0.45 plain, 0.45 with yardsticks. Run-to-run spread, the standard deviation of last-25 averages, shrinks slightly: 0.034 to 0.024. Why so little? Most learning is early, with returns near 0 and yardsticks poor. The door room’s big effect came from a usual reward far above 0. Baselines help most when returns share a large common level.

baseline:14.t: Where it is used. Nearly every modern policy gradient method subtracts a baseline. Actor-critic methods, A 2 C and P P O among them, learn V of s with a second network and nudge by an advantage: return minus V of s, or a refinement of it. For language models, methods like RLOO and G R P O sample several answers to the same question and use their average reward as the yardstick: the door-room idea, almost exactly.

baseline:15.t: Recap. A baseline is a yardstick for the usual return. Nudging by return minus baseline, the advantage, pushes up only what went better than usual and down what went worse. It changes only the noise, not the average direction. It helps most when returns share a big common level; a common yardstick is the state’s value V of s, which the next reel learns step by step.

actorcritic:0.t: Actor-Critic. One network acts, another grades every move.

actorcritic:1.t: Pip’s chances, again. Same maze: stepping onto the cheese pays plus 1, onto the cat minus 1, and either ends the walk. gamma (gamma) is 0.9. A walk stopped after 100 steps scores 0. Pip has no rulebook. In every cell Pip keeps four preference numbers, one per move; softmax turns them into chances. All start at 0, so every arrow is a quarter. Arrow length shows the chance.

actorcritic:2.t: The long wait. REINFORCE with a baseline learns only when the walk is over. Here is Pip’s first walk: 15 steps, then the cat. Until that last step, nothing was learned. Then every move is judged by the return that followed it, which includes the luck of every later move. The very first step up gets blamed for a cat met 14 moves later.

actorcritic:3.t: An actor and a critic. Split Pip in two. The actor is the chances: it picks the moves. The critic is a value notebook: for each cell, a guess of the return to expect from there with the current chances. Think of an athlete and a coach. The athlete tries a move; the coach says at once, better than I expected, or worse. Both keep learning.

actorcritic:4.t: The critic learns by T D. Same rule as the T D reel. After each step, target equals reward plus 0.9 times guess where Pip landed; if the walk ended, just the reward. Target minus the guess where Pip was is the T D error delta (delta). The guess moves a fifth of the way, plus 0.2 times delta. It starts blank, all 0, and must keep up as Pip’s chances change.

actorcritic:5.t: delta grades the move. The critic expected its guess for Pip’s cell. After the move, Pip has one real reward plus the landing cell’s guess. If more, delta is positive: better than expected, so make the move more likely. Negative: less likely. The actor pushes as in REINFORCE, delta replacing return minus yardstick: the critic’s guess stands in for the rest of the walk. It happens at once.

actorcritic:6.t: One step, in numbers. Walk 1’s last step: up, onto the cat. Reward minus 1, guesses 0: delta equals minus 1. Up’s preference changes by 1 times delta times (1 minus 0.25), to minus 0.75; others rise 0.25. Chances: up 0.11, others 0.30. That 1 is the actor’s step size, the REINFORCE reel’s alpha: it moves chances clearly, not all at once. Others come later. The critic’s guess there drops to minus 0.20.

actorcritic:7.t: Quiet until the end. The first 14 steps of walk 1? Each had reward 0 and landed where the guess was 0, so delta equals 0: no push. On walk 1 actor-critic is even quieter than REINFORCE, which pushed every move once the walk ended. A blank critic needs news from the cheese or cat, which spreads back slowly, one walk at a time. Hence a slower start.

actorcritic:8.t: Learning mid-walk. Walk 11. The cell right of the cat has guess minus 0.20, from past meetings. Step 18 moves up into it: delta equals 0.9 times ( minus 0.20) minus ( minus 0.03) equals minus 0.15. A push away, mid-walk. Dots mark delta beyond 0.01 either way, gold better, rose worse; 6 before the cheese. Leaving that cell again lifted its guess to minus 0.17; the cheese’s delta: 1 minus ( minus 0.17) equals 1.17.

actorcritic:9.t: After 300 walks. Let the pair learn for 300 walks. The arrows straighten along the short path, and the critic’s numbers fill in behind them. After walk 300, the critic’s guess for the start is 0.52. The best possible return is 0.9 to the power 6, 0.53: seven steps to the cheese. 7 of Pip’s last 10 walks took exactly 7 steps.

actorcritic:10.t: Two signals for one move. Freeze Pip after walk 50: from the start it goes up with chance 0.44. Take 40 walks starting with up. Each dot is what REINFORCE with a baseline would use for that move: the walk’s return minus a yardstick, here the critic’s start guess, 0.13. The dots spread from 0.01 to 0.41: each one carries the luck of the rest of its walk.

actorcritic:11.t: Steady but biased. The critic’s delta for that move: 0.9 times 0.23 minus 0.13 equals 0.08. Moves on this dry floor never slip and the critic is frozen, so delta never changes: no noise. The dots average 0.30, not 0.08. That average estimates the true grade. delta leans on the cell above’s guess, which lags Pip’s progress: bias. Returns: unbiased but noisy. delta: steady but can be wrong.

actorcritic:12.t: A fair race. A race over 300 walks: actor-critic against REINFORCE with a baseline. Both use actor step 1, up from the baseline reel’s 0.2, so it fits. Yardstick step 0.1 and critic step 0.2, as in their own reels. 100 runs each; run k shares a seed. Across: walks. Up: return from the start, averaged over runs and 10 neighbouring walks. Dashed: the best possible, 0.53.

actorcritic:13.t: Slow start, strong finish. REINFORCE with a baseline gets going sooner: after 50 walks it averages 0.33, actor-critic 0.23. The blank critic is the reason: its delta stays near 0 until news from the cheese has spread back to the start. From walk 69 on, actor-critic leads. After 300 walks: 0.52 against 0.50.

actorcritic:14.t: Calmer, too. Each dot is one run: average return over its last 100 walks. Dashed line: 0.4; big dark dots: runs below it. REINFORCE with a baseline: 4 of 100 runs below 0.4. In 3, Pip wanders: 90 or more of its last 100 walks hit the step limit, scoring 0, so return minus yardstick is about 0 and pushes fade. Actor-critic: 0 below 0.4, lowest 0.50.

actorcritic:15.t: Fair step sizes?. The yardstick learned with step 0.1, the critic with 0.2, and step sizes matter. So we swapped the two steps. REINFORCE with a baseline and yardstick step 0.2: 0.32 after 50 walks, 9 runs below 0.4. Actor-critic with critic step 0.1: 0.10 after 50 walks, 0 runs below 0.4. Same picture either way: REINFORCE with a baseline starts faster and leaves more runs behind.

actorcritic:16.t: Your turn. Drag the actor step size and rerun both methods on the same seeds. The chart title counts the runs that end below 0.4. Big steps learn fast but trust each push more. Watch which method copes with step 2, and which one is quicker with small steps.

actorcritic:17.t: A rushed critic. The critic is only a guess, and how fast it learns matters. With critic step 0.5 it spreads news faster, 0.34 after 50 walks against 0.23 at 0.2. But each walk now jerks the guesses and grades around, and 7 of 100 runs end below 0.4. At 0.05 the critic is calm but slow: 0.05 after 50 walks. A wrong critic steers the actor wrong.

actorcritic:18.t: Where you’ve seen this. In 1983, Andrew Barto, Richard Sutton and Charles Anderson balanced a pole on a cart with two learning parts: one chose the pushes, an adaptive critic graded them. The actor and the critic. Today A 2 C, A 3 C, P P O, D D P G, T D 3 and sack are all actor-critic methods, with neural networks in both roles. Next: many workers at once, and better grades than a single step.

actorcritic:19.t: Recap. Actor-critic splits Pip in two: the actor holds the chances, the critic learns a value notebook by T D. After every step, the critic’s T D error grades the move, and the actor nudges it up or down. No waiting for the walk to end, and steady grades instead of noisy returns. The price: a critic that is wrong, or still blank, grades wrongly. That is bias.

gae:0.t: n-step Returns  and  G A E. How far should you look before trusting the critic’s guess?

gae:1.t: How far should Pip look?. Same maze: plus 1 for the cheese, minus 1 for the cat, either ends the walk; gamma (gamma) is 0.9. Pip’s actor needs a grade for each move: how much better it went than the critic expected. Actor-critic graded with one real step plus the critic’s guess. REINFORCE with a baseline used the whole real return. Is there something in between, and is it better?

gae:2.t: Two grades, one move. Actor-critic reel again: Pip frozen after walk 50, going up from the start. Now 2,000 walks, not 40. The one-step grade, the T D error, is 0.08 every time. Whole-walk grade, return minus start guess: average 0.294, but it swings; 40 walks shown as dots. Gold line: the true grade, 0.297: up’s exact value under these chances, from the rulebook, minus the start guess.

gae:3.t: Bias and noise. The one-step grade has no noise: on the dry floor up never slips. But it is always 0.22 too low: the guess for that cell lags. Leaning one way every time is bias. The whole-walk grade is right on average: 0.294 against 0.297; the gap is just luck over 2,000 walks. But each walk’s luck moves it: spread 0.13. That jumping is variance, or noise.

gae:4.t: n steps, then the guess. From the traces reel, the n-step target: the next n real rewards, discounted 0.9 per step as in a return, plus the critic’s guess where Pip is then, discounted n times. Grade: target minus the start guess. n equals 1 gives the T D error. If the walk ends sooner, no guess: just the whole return minus the start guess. Between, n is a dial.

gae:5.t: Turning the n dial. Grades for n equals 1, 2, 4, 8 and the whole walk. As n grows, the average nears the true grade, 0.08 to 0.27 at n equals 8; spread grows from 0 to 0.16. More real steps: less bias, more noise. n equals 8 is noisier even than the whole walk, spread 0.13: it adds the guess after 8 moves, and guesses differ by cell.

gae:6.t: G A E: mix every n. Why one n? Generalised advantage estimation, G A E, averages them all with fading weights; its grade is the baseline reel’s advantage. n equals 1 gets 1 minus lambda; each next n, lambda times the last. They add up to 1, so it stays an average; weight past the walk’s end goes to the whole-walk grade. lambda (lambda), between 0 and 1, sets how fast they fade.

gae:7.t: A neat shortcut. The mix has a simple form. Number the walk’s T D errors delta zero, delta one, and so on. A two-step grade is delta zero plus 0.9 delta one, because the guess in between cancels. Mixing all n weights each later delta by another 0.9 lambda. Later surprises count less, like the traces reel’s fading marks. This walk, lambda equals 0.9: grade 0.28. One move, delta three, bumped into the wall.

gae:8.t: Your turn. Drag lambda and watch the grades of the same move. Gold is the true grade, teal the average of all the walks. At 0 the dots stack on one wrong spot; at 1 they centre on the truth but spread wide. The typical miss combines both: the square root of bias squared plus spread squared, how far one grade usually lands from the truth.

gae:9.t: Which lambda is best?. Across: lambda from 0 to 1. Rose: the bias, blue: the spread, black: the typical miss, which combines both. Lower is better. With this critic, frozen after walk 50, the typical miss keeps falling all the way, so it is smallest at lambda equals 1: 0.13, against 0.22 at lambda equals 0. The critic still lags, so trusting it less pays.

gae:10.t: A better critic. Freeze Pip after walk 80. The critic caught up: one-step grades miss by only 0.02. Pip’s chances improved, up 0.82, not 0.44, so walks wander less and long grades calm: spread 0.07 at lambda equals 1. Best lambda: 0, typical miss 0.02, against 0.07 at lambda equals 1. The critic wins despite calmer walks: the best lambda depends on how much you trust the critic.

gae:11.t: Learning with G A E. Now Pip learns with G A E: after each walk, every move gets its grade. The actor is nudged by it, step 1; the critic moves toward grade plus its guess, step 0.2. 100 runs per lambda, same dice. Chart: return from the start, averaged over runs and 10 neighbouring walks. After 50 walks: 0.24 at lambda equals 0, 0.37 at 0.5, 0.34 at 1.

gae:12.t: Middle ground. lambda equals 0 starts slowest: its grades lean on a blank critic. lambda equals 1 starts fast, stays noisy: 7 runs below 0.4, against 1 for lambda equals 0. At walk 50, lambda equals 0.5 is fastest. lambda equals 0.9 is no better than 1: 8 runs against 7. lambda equals 0 ends best, 0.52: the critic is good by then, as at walk 80.

gae:13.t: The price: waiting. A G A E grade needs the T D errors of the moves that come after, so Pip cannot grade a move the moment it makes it. Here Pip waits for the end of each walk. Real systems cut experience into chunks, a few hundred or a few thousand steps, and let the critic’s guess stand in for whatever comes after the cut.

gae:14.t: In practice. G A E was introduced by John Schulman and colleagues in 2015. With neural networks as actor and critic, lambda equals 0.95 together with gamma equals 0.99 became a common default; the P P O paper used exactly that. So G A E is the same dial as T D(lambda) in the traces reel, now used to grade moves for the actor instead of to update values.

gae:15.t: Recap. An n-step grade adds n real rewards, then trusts the critic: small n is steady but biased when the critic is off, large n is unbiased but noisy. G A E mixes every n with weights that fade by lambda, which is the same as summing T D errors weighted by (0.9 lambda) per step. The best lambda depends on how far the critic can be trusted.

ppo:0.t: P P O. Improve the policy, but not too much at once.

ppo:1.t: Pip starts from scratch. Same maze, dry floor: cheese plus 1, cat minus 1, both end the walk; gamma (gamma) is 0.9. Walks still going after 100 steps are stopped, scoring 0. Pip’s arrows, its move chances, start at a quarter each. Of 1000 test walks: 179 cheese, 643 cat, 178 stopped. Its score, the expected return from the start, computed exactly from the rulebook, is minus 0.03; the best is 0.53.

ppo:2.t: One update. Each update, Pip walks 10 times: a batch. Each move’s advantage is the return that followed it minus the critic’s value of the cell. The critic here is exact, so we watch the actor alone. The move made gains alpha (alpha) times advantage times (1 minus its chance); the others lose alpha times advantage times their chance; divided by the 10 walks. alpha equals 3.

ppo:3.t: Walks are precious. This batch cost ten walks, used once and thrown away. In a real game or robot, collecting walks is the slow, expensive part; computing is cheap. So learn more from each batch: go over the same walks 10 times, 10 passes, each an update with alpha equals 3. But ten passes can push up to ten times as far as one, unless something stops them.

ppo:4.t: The ratio. After one pass the chances have changed, but the walks came from the old ones. So P P O weighs each move by the ratio: its new chance divided by old chance in that cell. Take the cheese step from the cell to its left. Old chance 0.25; after one pass 0.321, so the ratio is 1.285: new Pip makes that move about 1.29 times as often.

ppo:5.t: What each pass climbs. Each pass raises an objective: the average of ratio times advantage over the batch. The walks came from old Pip; weighting by new divided by old chance turns their average into an estimate for new Pip: moves it makes more often count more. At ratio 1, the slope of new divided by old equals that of log(new chance), so the first pass is exactly the ordinary update.

ppo:6.t: Ten passes, no brakes. Pip takes 10 passes over its first batch, pushing ratio times advantage each time, with no brake. Of 1000 test walks, not one now ends: Pip wanders and bumps until it is stopped, meeting neither cat nor cheese. So the score goes from minus 0.03 to 0.00. That looks harmless. It is not: watch what happens next.

ppo:7.t: Why never finish?. The batch: 5 hit the cat, 1 the cheese, 4 stopped at 100 steps, return 0. The critic expected below 0 everywhere, down to minus 0.54 beside the cat. So all 400 stopped-walk moves had positive advantage, averaging 0.05. Pushed ten times, “keep wandering” beat “reach the cheese”. One ordinary pass pushes them once: the score barely moves, to minus 0.01, and later batches can correct it.

ppo:8.t: Stuck for good. Now every walk is stopped. In the next batch, 10 of 10 walks stop at 100 steps, every return is 0, and the critic, exact for a Pip who never finishes, says about 0 everywhere. The largest advantage is 0.0002. With no surprises there is nothing to learn from. The chart shows this run’s score after each update: forty updates later it is still 0.00.

ppo:9.t: Clip the ratio. P P O, Proximal Policy Optimization, adds a brake: clip the ratio to between 1 minus epsilon and 1 plus epsilon. epsilon (epsilon, not the epsilon-greedy one) is usually 0.2, so 0.8 to 1.2. With positive advantage, the objective follows ratio times advantage up to 1.2, then stays flat: no reward for pushing further. Below 0.8 the line continues: making a good move rarer is still penalised.

ppo:10.t: When the advantage is negative. For a move with negative advantage, it mirrors: lowering the ratio helps only down to 0.8, then the objective goes flat. But raising that bad move’s chance still costs, with no cap. P P O keeps whichever of the two numbers, clipped or not, is lower. It removes the reward for going too far, never the penalty.

ppo:11.t: Flat means stop. On a flat stretch the objective has no slope, so that move stops pushing. The cheese step, over 10 passes: unclipped, its ratio climbs to 2.50. With epsilon equals 0.2 it overshoots on the first pass, to 1.29, then stays. The first pass starts at ratio 1, inside the band, so the clip cannot hold it yet. Nothing else in that cell moves it afterwards.

ppo:12.t: The same batch, with the brake. Same batch, 10 passes, now clipped at 0.2. Score minus 0.01; 457 of 1000 test walks still end, fewer than the blank policy’s 822. The brake limits the bad advice but does not undo it. Average K L divergence, how far old and new chances differ: 0.015, against 0.544 unclipped. Later batches correct it: the clipped run, blue, reaches 0.46 after 10 updates, 0.52 after 40.

ppo:13.t: Fifty runs. 50 runs, different dice, 40 updates each, averaged. Teal: one ordinary pass. Rose: 10 passes, unclipped. Blue: 10 passes, clipped at 0.2. No clip: 11 of 50 got stuck. One pass: 0.32 after 10 updates, 0.50 after 40. Clipped passes: 0.39 and 0.52, none stuck. Even counting crashes, unclipped passes lead early. All compared per walk collected; ten passes cost ten times the computing.

ppo:14.t: Ten passes, one big step?. Ten unclipped passes at alpha equals 3 can push about as far as one at alpha equals 30. Teal: ten passes at alpha equals 0.3, a tenth each. Rose, that one pass: 20 of 50 stuck, the too-big step again. Teal is as safe and slow as one ordinary pass: 0.31 against 0.32 after 10 updates. The clip lets ten passes through: 0.39, none stuck.

ppo:15.t: Your turn. Drag epsilon. Each setting reruns the same 50 runs: 10 passes per batch, alpha equals 3. The line is the average score; the card counts runs stuck near 0. A tight band is safe but learns slowly. A wide band lets more through. With no clip, 11 of 50 runs get stuck.

ppo:16.t: A brake, not a wall. The clip only stops a move from pushing itself further. Other moves in its cell still shift its chance. After the clipped update, 172 of the batch’s 769 ratios lie outside 0.8 to 1.2, from 0.30 to 1.43. So P P O is a soft limit, not a guarantee. Practical versions often also stop passes early once average K L exceeds a small threshold, such as 0.015.

ppo:17.t: Where it is used. Schulman’s team at OpenAI introduced P P O in 2017. Easy to code and tune, it became a common default. A scaled-up P P O trained OpenAI Five, which played Dota 2 from 2018, beating the world champions in 2019. In 2022, InstructGPT used P P O for R L H F’s reinforcement step, steering a language model toward answers people preferred. A cell is the text so far; a move, the next word.

ppo:18.t: Recap. Reusing a batch for several passes squeezes more learning out of each walk, but unchecked passes can push the policy far past what the batch supports, and a wrecked policy may never recover. P P O clips the ratio, new chance divided by old chance, to 1  plus or minus  epsilon, so a move stops earning credit once it has moved enough.

sac:0.t: Entropy  and  Soft Actor-Critic. Reward the agent for keeping its options open.

sac:1.t: Back in the door room. The door room from the policy gradient reel. Behind doors A, B and C a crumb, reward 1, appears with a hidden chance: 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8. Pip picks one door per visit, and the visit ends. Pip’s policy is a pie of chances made from three preferences by softmax. It starts at a third each.

sac:2.t: A critic for each door. Pip is an actor-critic. The critic keeps a score per door, starting at 0. After each pick it studies 8 random picks among the last 200, D Q N’s replay idea, each nudging its door’s score a tenth closer to its crumb. The actor uses every score via the policy gradient nudge: chance times (score minus the pie’s average), with step 3. No sampled returns needed.

sac:3.t: Why old picks still count. REINFORCE and P P O judged moves by Pip’s recent returns, so walks under an older policy were stale. This critic learns what each door pays, like D Q N’s Q-values. A crumb behind C is evidence about C, whoever picked it, whenever. The actor trains against the critic’s scores, not its own returns, so old picks can be replayed: the method is off-policy. sack works the same way.

sac:4.t: An unlucky start. Pip’s first run. First 30 picks: A 2 times, B 28 times, C never. B pays 14 crumbs: its score climbs, C’s stays at 0. After B’s first crumbs the actor quickly raised its chance, so Pip tried the others even less. Luck decided the first picks; the rule did the rest. We chose this run to show getting stuck; later steps show how often.

sac:5.t: Stuck on B. By pick 400, B’s chance is 1.00. In all 400 picks Pip never tries C, so C’s score stays 0.00, far below its true 0.8. The critic only learns about doors Pip picks. A’s score dates from 2 early tries; B’s jumps, as each study moves it a tenth. Pip gets about half a crumb per visit, not 0.8, with almost no way out.

sac:6.t: Not one unlucky run. Run it 200 times with different dice. In 36 of the 200 runs, by pick 400 Pip’s favourite door is not C. It is the trap from the Exploration versus Exploitation reel: a learner that stops trying a door never finds out it was wrong. Pip needs a reason to keep trying doors it currently rates low.

sac:7.t: How spread out?. A door’s surprise is minus log of its chance: a door Pip almost never picks would be very surprising, a sure door not at all. Entropy is the average surprise. It measures how spread out the chances are. A third each: entropy 1.10, the most possible for three doors. Chances 0.1, 0.1, 0.8: 0.64. Always the same door: 0.

sac:8.t: A bonus for staying spread. Now Pip aims for average reward plus alpha times entropy. alpha (alpha) is the temperature: how many crumbs one unit of spread is worth. Not earlier reels’ step size. For the actor a door is worth score plus alpha times surprise; the nudge uses worth, not score: exactly uphill for the new aim. Rare doors earn a bonus, so their preferences do not sink forever.

sac:9.t: Why not random picks?. Why not pick a random door 1 time in 5, as epsilon-greedy does? The actor’s own aim would still push its pie toward certainty, and random picks would go to good and bad doors alike, forever. With the bonus, staying spread is part of the aim. The actor keeps spare chances where they cost little: on doors scoring close to the best.

sac:10.t: Turning the temperature. Given the crumb chances, the best pie at temperature alpha makes each door’s chance proportional to e to the power of crumb chance divided by alpha. At alpha equals 0.2: A 0.04, B 0.18, C 0.79. That is softmax of crumb chance divided by alpha, where the actor’s rule settles once the critic is right. Cold, near 0: always C. Hot: closer to a third each.

sac:11.t: Same dice, with a bonus. Rerun Pip’s first run with alpha equals 0.2. Same dice, so it starts the same way, but once its chances differ the picks drift apart. The bonus keeps C in play: by pick 400 C’s chance is 0.85 and its score 0.83. Over 200 runs, the favourite at pick 400 is not C in 2 runs, against 36 without the bonus.

sac:12.t: Curiosity has a price. Even after finding C, Pip keeps a few percent on A and B. Averaged over 200 runs, stuck ones included, C’s chance at pick 400 is 0.79, against 0.82 without. Crumbs per visit tie: 0.72 and 0.72. So for now, alpha equals 0.2 curiosity roughly pays for itself; a cooler alpha equals 0.1 is ahead, at 0.75. The bigger payoff comes when the world changes.

sac:13.t: The world changes. After pick 400, door A suddenly pays a crumb 95 times in 100. The certain Pip picks A not once in the next 600 picks and never finds out. The curious Pip tries A 306 times; A leads its pie from pick 550. Over 200 runs, A is the favourite at pick 1000 in 190 runs with the bonus, 5 without.

sac:14.t: Your turn. Drag the temperature alpha and rerun the 200 runs. The pie is the best pie for that temperature if Pip knew the chances; the numbers are what learning Pips actually did. Too cold and Pip gets stuck and misses the change; too hot and it wastes visits on bad doors. Which alpha collects the most after the change?

sac:15.t: A jump instead of doors. New task, from the policy gradient reel. Pip on a ledge picks a jump strength: metres flown, any number. The cheese lies 0.7 metres out. Landing on it pays 1; a miss pays less along the curve, about 0.37 for 0.15 metres. With no menu, the policy is a bell curve: a centre, the strength Pip aims for, and a spread, how far jumps scatter.

sac:16.t: Bell curves too. A bell’s entropy grows by 0.69 each time its spread doubles. Without a bonus the bell narrows toward one strength; with it, the bell keeps the width where reward lost by spreading balances the bonus. Strengths stay between 0 and 1.2 metres. Exactly, for a bell centred on the cheese: alpha equals 0.01 keeps a spread of 0.01 metres, 0.03 keeps 0.02, 0.1 keeps 0.04.

sac:17.t: Soft values. In longer tasks the bonus joins the reward at every step, so the critic’s values count future bonuses too. A spot with several good ways on outranks one with a single way, so the agent learns to keep options open. Why “soft”? The best pie is a softmax of the values, a soft maximum; as alpha shrinks to 0 it becomes the hard maximum.

sac:18.t: Soft Actor-Critic. sack, by Haarnoja, Zhou, Abbeel and Levine in 2018, brings this to continuous actions. Unable to list every strength, its actor samples a few from its bell, asks the critic which way to move each, then reshapes it. It keeps two critics, trusting the lower: the actor seeks spots a critic overrates by luck, and two rarely share a lucky error. alpha was later auto-tuned.

sac:19.t: Where it’s used. sack is a standard choice for continuous control, simulated and real. Its authors taught a four-legged robot, Minitaur, to walk with about two hours of real experience: short for real hardware, where every trial costs time and wear. They also taught a robot hand to turn a valve. Entropy bonuses are common elsewhere: many policy gradient methods add a small one to keep exploring.

sac:20.t: Recap. Entropy measures how spread out the chances are: the average surprise. Adding alpha times entropy to the reward keeps Pip curious, so an unlucky start or a changed world does not trap it. The temperature alpha sets the price of curiosity. sack puts this bonus into an actor-critic for continuous actions.

ddpg:0.t: Continuous Control: D D P G  and  T D 3. D Q N for steering wheels and robot joints.

ddpg:1.t: How hard to jump?. Back to the jump from the sack reel. Pip stands on a ledge and picks a jump strength: how many metres it flies. Any number will do: 0.5, 0.71, 0.7034. The cheese lies 0.7 metres out. Landing right on it pays 1; a bit short or long pays less, following the curve below. The reward is paid on landing.

ddpg:2.t: A row of ledges. The cheese ledge is narrow, 0.4 to 1.0 metres. Miss it: Pip falls in the stream, reward 0, run over. Land on it: from its front edge, the next crumb is again 0.7 metres out. Wind shifts each landing a few centimetres. Crumbs vary from nothing to double, 1 on average, so reward is curve times crumb: real rewards are noisy too. gamma (gamma): 0.9.

ddpg:3.t: No menu to pick from. D Q N kept one Q-value per move and took the biggest: up, right, down or left, four numbers to compare. Here the move is a number, and there are endlessly many of them. Taking the max means searching them all, at every jump. Chop strengths into steps? A robot arm with 7 joints and 10 settings each has 10 million combinations to compare, every single step.

ddpg:4.t: A critic for any strength. The critic scores any strength: Q of s, a, the reward expected from jumping a now and the actor’s clean answer ever after, each later jump times another 0.9. Here s is always a gap’s edge. Dashed: the true Q if the actor answers 0.7. Jumping 0.7 is worth 9.06; past the cliffs at 0.4 and 1.0 Pip falls. The critic must learn this curve.

ddpg:5.t: An actor that just answers. The actor answers each situation with one strength. No chances, no dice: same situation, same answer. A deterministic actor. Earlier reels needed chances so a small nudge made a small change; a strength is a smooth number, so nudging it already does. In real tasks the actor is a network, situation in, action out; here, one number, starting at 0.3 metres. Pip falls.

ddpg:6.t: Teaching the critic. Like D Q N, the critic’s target equals reward plus 0.9 times its score for the next jump. But the next jump comes from the actor, not the best move. A fall’s target is its reward, 0. Jump 217: Pip jumps 0.81, lands 0.74: reward 0.94 times crumb 1.14 equals 1.07. Next jump: 0.68, scored 2.10. Target 2.96 beats the critic’s 2.51, so its curve rises there.

ddpg:7.t: Try a little around it. Always the same answer means the critic sees only one strength and cannot tell whether harder or softer is better. So in training, every jump gets random noise: a bell curve with a spread of 0.1 metres around the actor’s answer. D D P G explored like this too. Noise is only for the jumps Pip makes; the target’s next jump uses the actor’s clean answer.

ddpg:8.t: Climb the critic’s slope. How can the actor improve without trying every strength? It asks the critic: if I jumped a little harder, would your score rise? That is the slope of the critic’s curve at the actor’s strength. It steps uphill: new strength equals old plus 0.01 times slope. At jump 45 of the first run: actor 0.47, slope there 2.77, so the actor moves to 0.50.

ddpg:9.t: Many knobs. Real actors are networks of many knobs. Multiply two slopes: the critic’s, score per metre of strength, and each knob’s, strength moved per turn. The product, by the chain rule, is how much each knob raises the score; backpropagation computes it; each knob moves a small step times it. So it is still a policy gradient. Our one-number actor makes the knob’s slope 1.

ddpg:10.t: Borrowed from D Q N. Two Deep R L tricks keep this steady. A replay buffer: after each jump the critic studies 8 random stored jumps, not just the latest. Target networks: the next jump is scored by slow copies, moved 2 percent toward the real ones per jump, so targets hold still under the critic. The actor gets a slow copy too: the target asks it for the next jump.

ddpg:11.t: D D P G. Actor climbing a critic, plus replay, target copies and noise: D D P G, Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient, by Lillicrap and colleagues, 2015. Pip’s first run, sped up. Of the first 50 jumps, 35 end in the stream. By jump 100 the actor says 0.70, and stays near 0.7. In jumps 100 to 400 Pip falls only once: exploring noise can still send it off.

ddpg:12.t: The critic catches up. Gold: critic’s score of the actor’s jump; dashed: true worth. The actor found 0.7 by about jump 100; the critic about 1250: a worth near 9 builds one reward plus 0.9 times an older guess at a time, as in T D, and the slow copy slows it more. Dips: the actor drifted, to 0.59 at jump 11250, paying less. Finally: critic 9.02, truth 8.80.

ddpg:13.t: Too optimistic. From jump 4000 on, this critic is too high by 0.41 on average, believing in reward that never comes. At jump 9650: critic 9.48, truth 9.06. Why? The actor seeks the critic’s highest point, including spots too high by sampling luck. Every target leans on that inflated score, copying the error back, jump after jump. Double D Q N saw this: the max picks lucky guesses.

ddpg:14.t: Not just bad luck. Run D D P G 8 times with different dice. The chart: the critic’s score of its own jump minus true worth, averaged over the 8 runs, from jump 4000 to 12000, once the critics have caught up. Above the dashed zero line the critic is too optimistic, below too pessimistic. D D P G stays above zero: too high by 0.39 on average, and in 8 of the 8 runs.

ddpg:15.t: T D 3, fix one: two critics. In 2018, Scott Fujimoto, Herke van Hoof and David Meger proposed T D 3, Twin Delayed D D P G: three fixes. First: train two critics, each studying its own random old jumps, and build one shared target from the smaller of their scores. The actor climbs the first critic. Both rarely share a lucky high guess. Over the same 8 runs, the average gap shrinks from 0.39 to minus 0.03.

ddpg:16.t: Fix two: let the critic settle. Second: update the actor and slow copies only every second jump; the critics learn every jump. Why? The actor chases the critic’s peak; if the critic still wobbles, the actor chases the wobble. In this small task it changes nothing visible: the gap is minus 0.03, same as two critics alone. The T D 3 authors aimed it at large networks, whose critics take longer to settle.

ddpg:17.t: Fix three: blur the target. Third: jiggle the target’s next jump by a spread of 0.03 metres, at most 0.06, so a narrow false peak cannot lift the target. All three fixes read minus 0.22, mostly by design: the critic values a jiggled, clumsier jumper, truly worth 0.26 less. Against that, T D 3 is off by less than 0.01, the dashed line. Its authors called a small underestimate safer anyway.

ddpg:18.t: Your turn. Drag to add T D 3’s fixes one at a time: thin lines: the 8 runs; thick: their average. T D 3’s gap is measured against the jiggled jumper it really values. Each run’s average gap: D D P G 0.18 to 0.60, two critics minus 0.14 to 0.09. Pip jumps about equally well in all four: with one hump, false optimism has nowhere to lure the actor. In big tasks it can.

ddpg:19.t: Where it’s used. D D P G (2015) learned over 20 simulated physics tasks, like swinging up a pole, grasping, walking and driving, many straight from camera pixels. T D 3 (2018) clearly beat it on standard simulated robot benchmarks like Hopper and HalfCheetah. Today T D 3 is a common starting point for continuous control, robot arms included. Soft Actor-Critic, in its own reel, also uses two critics, but a policy with spread.

ddpg:20.t: Recap. When actions are numbers, no max over them all is possible. D D P G: a deterministic actor climbs the slope of a critic Q of s, a, with exploring noise, a replay buffer and slow target copies. The actor seeks the critic’s peaks, so the critic turns optimistic. T D 3 takes the smaller of two critics, which removed the optimism here, delays the actor and blurs the target action.

modelbased:0.t: Model-Based R L. Learn how the world works, then plan in your head.

modelbased:1.t: No rulebook. Pip’s maze again. Stepping onto the cheese pays plus 1, onto the cat minus 1, and either ends the walk. Other steps pay 0, a bump leaves Pip in place, and gamma (gamma) is 0.9. Pip has no rulebook: it cannot tell where a move will land. In the Q-learning reel it learned from experience alone; its first four walks took 24, 20, 28 and 31 steps.

modelbased:2.t: One walk, one number. That first walk again, sped up. Pip keeps four numbers per cell, one per move, all starting at 0, so each update nudges 0 toward 0 plus 0.9 times 0 and nothing moves. Only the last step, onto the cheese, changes a number: “up” below the cheese, from 0 to 0.2. Pip saw 24 steps of the maze; the other 23 left no trace.

modelbased:3.t: Write it down. What if Pip also noted what each move did? In this cell, this move landed there and paid this much. Bumps count too: pushed up, stayed put. After walk 1 the notebook holds 14 entries, from the 7 cells Pip visited, out of 64 cell and move pairs; some moves repeated. The notebook is a learned model: Pip’s copy of part of the rulebook.

modelbased:4.t: Counting. Pip’s floor stays dry: one look per move is enough. On the M D P reel’s wet floor, “right” from the start was tried 1000 times: 795 moved right, 102 slid up, 103 stayed. Count divided by tries guesses each chance: 0.795, 0.102, 0.103, near the true 0.8, 0.1, 0.1. Planning would weight landings by these chances; an imagined step would draw one with them.

modelbased:5.t: Planning in the notebook. Plan with it, as in the value iteration reel: value of a cell equals the best, over moves, of reward plus 0.9 times value where that move lands. Start from zeros and sweep. One difference: Pip uses only moves in its notebook, since it has no idea where untried ones lead. Here 7 sweeps change something; sweep 8 changes nothing, so the planning stops.

modelbased:6.t: A route after one walk. Taking the best noted move in each cell, Pip walks from the start to the cheese in 7 steps, the shortest possible. Its real experience so far: one walk of 24 steps. After that same walk, plain Q-learning knew one move, the one below the cheese. Writing things down got far more out of the same experience: better sample efficiency, learning per real step.

modelbased:7.t: Planning costs thinking. Planning is not free. That plan took 8 sweeps over 14 entries: 112 updates. Each new walk adds entries, and a fresh plan would sweep them all again. Here that is cheap. In a world with millions of states, sweeping everything after every step is not. Richard Sutton’s Dyna spreads the planning thin instead: a little after each real step.

modelbased:8.t: Dyna-Q, part one: a real step. Dyna-Q runs Q-learning as usual. After each real move, the target is the reward plus 0.9 times the biggest number in the landing cell, and the move’s number goes a fifth of the way toward it: alpha (alpha) equals 0.2. Pip still takes the biggest number, with one move in five random: epsilon (epsilon) equals 0.2. New: it also notes the move in its notebook.

modelbased:9.t: Part two: imagined steps. Before its next real move, Pip practises in its head 10 times: pick a random entry, read its landing and reward, and apply the same update as if it were real. Imagination takes no real step and replays only tried moves. Unlike a replay memory of every move made, the notebook keeps one entry per cell and move: a rulebook Pip could also plan with.

modelbased:10.t: The first walks. Walk 1 is the same 24 steps for both methods: every number is 0, so imagining changes nothing until the cheese is found. Walk 2 also takes 20 steps for both. But by its end Q-learning has 2 nonzero numbers and Dyna-Q has 16. On walk 3, Q-learning wanders 28 steps; Dyna-Q walks 7.

modelbased:11.t: The race. One run can be lucky, so race on 20 runs with different dice, seeds 1 to 20; both methods get the same 20. In the chart, across is the walk number, 1 to 30. Up is the number of steps that walk took, averaged over the 20 runs. Grey is Q-learning, teal is Dyna-Q with 10 imagined steps per real one.

modelbased:12.t: Real steps saved. Over the first 10 walks, Q-learning used 642 real steps on average and Dyna-Q 319, about half. In walks 21 to 30 both average about 9 steps a walk, not 7, because one move in five is still random. The price is thinking: Dyna-Q made 10 imagined updates for every real one, about 5500 updates per run against about 900.

modelbased:13.t: The catch: the world changes. After 50 walks with Dyna-Q, Pip’s arrows take the bottom route and the start’s best number is 0.53. Then the cat wakes up and moves to the bottom row, right onto that route. The notebook does not know. It still says the bottom row is safe, and the numbers built from it agree. Pip follows its confident plan and meets the cat after 3 steps.

modelbased:14.t: Real steps fix it, slowly. Its entry is overwritten: “right here lands on the cat, minus 1”. On walk 2, Pip bumps up and down in that cell 11 times: their numbers, 0.59 and 0.58, date from the old cheese route. A bump’s target is 0.9 times the cell’s best number, so they shrink slowly. Once below “left”, a random move hits the cat again. After walk 2, the arrows go over the top.

modelbased:15.t: A belief nobody checks. 3 notebook entries, the rose minus 1 tags, still say stepping into the old cat cell costs minus 1. The plan keeps away, so only a random move could check, and imagination keeps replaying those entries, reinforcing the mistake. A known fix, Dyna-Q+ in Sutton and Barto’s textbook, adds a small bonus to moves not tried for a long time, so Pip goes back to check.

modelbased:16.t: Your turn. Drag the number of imagined steps per real step. 0 is plain Q-learning. The chart reruns the same 20 runs and compares with Q-learning in grey. Watch the first walks shrink as Pip imagines more, then stop shrinking: once the notebook is mostly learned, extra imagining adds little, and the random moves remain.

modelbased:17.t: Where it came from. Richard Sutton introduced Dyna in 1990: learn a model, and mix real updates with imagined ones. Learned models matter most where real experience is slow or costly, like robots. PILCO, in 2011, learned to swing up a real cart-pole within a handful of trials. The next reels search ahead with a model (tree search, AlphaZero, MuZero) or learn a model from pictures (World Models, Dreamer).

modelbased:18.t: Recap. A model says, for each state and action, where you land and what it pays. If nobody hands you one, learn it by writing down, and counting, what really happened. Then plan with it, or use it for imagined practice between real steps, as Dyna does. In Pip’s maze that halved the real steps. But a wrong model gives confident wrong plans.

mcts:0.t: Monte Carlo Tree Search. Grow a search tree toward the most promising moves.

mcts:1.t: Pip versus the cat. Pip and the cat play noughts and crosses: a 3 by 3 board, three in a row wins. Pip goes first and draws cheese; the cat draws paws. A full board with no line is a draw. We keep score in Pip’s points: a win is 1, a draw  one half, a loss 0. The cat wants Pip’s points low.

mcts:2.t: Pip’s move. Another game, two moves in: Pip took the middle right, the cat answered in the top left corner. Now it is Pip’s turn, with 7 empty squares. Pip knows the rules exactly: where each move puts a mark and when a game ends. That rulebook is a model of the game, so Pip can play moves out in its head before choosing one.

mcts:3.t: A tree of futures. Under the current board, a branch for each of Pip’s 7 moves; under each, the cat’s 6 replies, and so on until the games end. This is a search tree; each spot is a node. Counting every partial game, even repeats from different move orders, the tree has 6,900 nodes, few enough to check. Go, with about 250 moves per turn, is not.

mcts:4.t: Play it out at random. A cheap way to judge a move: play it, then let both sides make random moves until the game ends. That is a playout. Here Pip tries bottom left, and the random game ends in a win: 1 point. One playout is a coin flip. The average over many playouts estimates how good the move is. Averaging random trials is what Monte Carlo means.

mcts:5.t: Averages from playouts. So run 2000 playouts after each of Pip’s 7 moves. Each number on the board is the average of Pip’s points over the 2000 random games that start with a move there. The centre looks best, 0.69. Top right comes second at 0.65; bottom middle is worst at 0.43. Should Pip play the centre?

mcts:6.t: The careless cat. Checking every line backwards from its end, with Pip taking most points, the cat fewest, only top right wins. Centre and bottom left draw; the other four lose, even bottom right, which the playouts rated 0.60. Top right threatens the right column, the cat must block, then Pip’s centre makes two threats. Playouts missed it: their cat rarely defends. Moves must survive a careful opponent.

mcts:7.t: Let the tree think for both. Monte Carlo Tree Search (M C T S) grows a tree over playouts. Both sides pick by U C B: each node a cheese arcade, its moves the machines. The cat uses cat’s points, 1 minus Pip’s. Imagined pulls are free; U C B still aims loops where choices are decided. Growing trees make averages drift, breaking the arcade’s guarantee; a 2006 proof shows M C T S still finds best play, given enough loops.

mcts:8.t: One loop, four steps. Each node keeps n, its loop count, and the total of Pip’s points. Average equals total divided by n, a Monte Carlo estimate. Select: from the top, follow top U C B scores to an untried move. Expand: add it as a node. Simulate: one random playout. Back up: add its points along the path. A walk ending at a finished game backs up its real result instead.

mcts:9.t: The first seven loops. At first the top node has untried moves, so each loop simply adds one of Pip’s moves, in random order, and plays it out once, like trying each arcade machine once. Results, left to right in the picture: top middle  one half, top right 1, middle left 0, centre  one half, bottom left 1, bottom middle 1, bottom right 0. Pip’s points, from one coin flip each.

mcts:10.t: Loop 8: U C B chooses. Every move has n equals 1; the top, N equals 7. Each bonus is the square root of (2 times log 7 divided by 1) equals 1.97. The three winners tie; the tie goes to the earliest added, so loop 8 goes to bottom left. It adds a random untried reply, the cat in the centre, whose playout the cat wins. Bottom left now shows n equals 2, average 0.5.

mcts:11.t: The tree grows. Loop after loop, the same four steps. Under each move, brown dots are the cat’s replies; bigger means visited more. Deeper levels are bars, gold for Pip’s moves, brown for the cat’s: wider bar, more nodes at that depth. Moves that keep scoring well get walked often, so their branches grow deeper. Weak moves still get an occasional look: their bonus creeps up while ignored.

mcts:12.t: After 1000 loops. Top right was visited 292 times, the centre 202, no other over 138. It also averages best, 0.67 against 0.63. M C T S plays the move it visited most. A rare move’s average can be lucky; visits pile up only on moves that keep scoring. Averages include exploring loops and playout blunders, so even a sure win averages below 1. It can stop anytime with an answer.

mcts:13.t: Where the effort went. 1000 loops built 796 nodes, top one included, out of 6,900. 205 loops reached finished games and added none, 108 under top right. Top right’s branch has 184 nodes, 5 moves deep; bottom middle’s only 62, 3 deep. Value iteration also plans with a model, but sweeps everything. M C T S goes deep where it matters, shallow elsewhere, so it handles games too big to search fully.

mcts:14.t: How many loops are enough?. Is 1000 loops luck? Run the search 100 times, with different random playouts, for several budgets. Left to right: loops per decision, 10, 30, 100, 300, 1000 and 3000. Upward: how many of the 100 runs chose that move. Gold: top right, the winning move. With 10 loops, only 13 runs: about a random guess among 7. With 1000 loops, 80; with 3000, 100.

mcts:15.t: The tree first agrees with the playouts. In teal, the centre. M C T S picks it more up to 300 loops, 70 of 100 runs: a shallow tree’s averages, in the table, are playout averages, near the playouts’ 0.65 and 0.69. Deeper trees reach the cat’s replies: under the centre, its one good answer, middle left; under top right, Pip’s plan. At 3000 loops top right leads, below 1 as exploring and playouts blunder.

mcts:16.t: Your turn. Drag the number of loops per decision. The board shows one search: the share of loops that went through each move, with the move it would play highlighted. Below, the result over 100 searches. With few loops the visits spread out. The centre peaks at 300 loops, chosen in 70 of 100 searches. By 3000, every one of the 100 searches plays top right.

mcts:17.t: The weak spot: random playouts. Random playouts judge crudely: they rated the centre above the only winning move, costing M C T S about 1000 loops. Even in this tiny game, 3000 loops built 1,098 nodes, a sixth of the tree. In Go, random games say little about who leads, and the tree covers only a sliver. Programs added handmade rules for less random playouts. The next reel learns a replacement.

mcts:18.t: Where it is used. In 2006 Rémi Coulom named Monte Carlo tree search in his program Crazy Stone, and Kocsis and Szepesvári published UCT, the U C B rule at every node used here. MoGo soon used UCT for Go. For a decade the strongest Go programs used M C T S. They reached strong amateur level, losing to top professionals on the full board. AlphaGo, in 2016, kept tree search, adding learned networks.

mcts:19.t: Recap. M C T S grows a search tree from the current position, at most one node per loop: select by U C B, expand, simulate a random playout, back up the result. Both sides choose by U C B inside the tree, so the search learns to expect good replies. It goes deep where moves look strong, and plays the most visited move. Its weak spot is the random playout.

alphazero:0.t: AlphaZero. Self-play plus tree search plus one neural network.

alphazero:1.t: A better judge. Back to Pip’s puzzle from the tree search reel: cat in the top left corner, Pip on the middle right, Pip to move. Only top right wins. Random playouts rated the centre higher, 0.69 against 0.65, and the search needed about 1000 loops to see past them. What if Pip could learn to judge a position, instead of playing it out at random?

alphazero:2.t: One network, two answers. AlphaZero uses one small neural network. It reads the board, which squares hold cheese, which hold paws and whose turn it is, and gives two answers. The value: Pip’s expected points from this position. The prior: for each empty square, how promising that move looks, as shares adding up to 100 percent. Ours has 32 hidden units and 970 knobs; before training they are random.

alphazero:3.t: A judge inside the search. The search loop stays: select, expand, back up. But there is no random playout. When a loop reaches a new node, the network looks at it once: its value is backed up the path, and its priors are stored for the node’s moves. If the loop reaches a finished game, the real result is backed up instead: the rules say who won.

alphazero:4.t: The prior steers the bonus. AlphaZero swaps in a bonus using the prior, shown on screen. The average still uses the chooser’s points, and c equals 1.5 weighs the bonus. A move the network likes gets tried early; one it dislikes waits, but its bonus grows while ignored. Untried moves count as a draw,  one half. Unlike U C B, this rule has no proof; it was chosen because it works.

alphazero:5.t: Where the lessons come from. No human games, no hints. The network plays against itself, network plus search choosing every move for both sides: self-play. Games start from the empty board. To make games differ, the first moves are drawn at random, weighted by visits, and noise is mixed into the top priors, where the move is chosen, so disliked moves still get tried. Later moves take the most visited.

alphazero:6.t: What one game teaches. Game 1, untrained network. Under each board: the visit share of the move played. The cat’s 13% move ignores Pip’s diagonal: a random opening draw. It ends in a Pip win. Each position becomes a lesson: the visit shares, pi (pi), and the result, z. Training shrinks the value’s miss on z and the cross-entropy, a standard mismatch score for shares, between prior and pi.

alphazero:7.t: Search as a teacher. Why copy the search? Because search plus network chooses better than the network alone: it looks ahead, and checks the network’s guesses against positions further down. Training the prior toward pi makes the network’s instinct more like its own careful thinking. The value head learns what a position is worth from how whole games turned out, z: a Monte Carlo target, not a T D one.

alphazero:8.t: The loop. One generation: play 50 self-play games, then train on the lessons of the last 4 generations, shown 8 times each, each randomly rotated or mirrored. Older games, played by a clumsier network, are dropped. The new network plays the next 50 games. We run 12 generations, 600 games in all. Each nudge changes the knobs a little toward the lessons, like earlier reels’ gradient steps.

alphazero:9.t: Watching it learn. Our answer key lists the best moves in all 3,191 positions where the choice matters. The chart: how often the prior’s favourite is a best move. Untrained: 40%. After generation 4: 73%. It peaks at 87% after generation 8, ending at 85%. Nobody showed it a good move. Truth enters through the rules: finished games report real results, in search and as z.

alphazero:10.t: Its instinct on our puzzle. After training, the network looks at Pip’s puzzle. Its prior gives top right 39%, the centre 23% and bottom right 20%. Its value: 0.63 of a point for Pip; the truth is 1, a sure win. So the instinct already leans the right way, but the value is unsure. Next, the search checks it.

alphazero:11.t: The search checks the instinct. With 50 loops, the first only asks the network about the current board; the board shows where the rest went. Top right gets the most, and its average climbs to 0.86. Random playouts needed about 1000 loops. Why so few? The value head judges each new position directly. After bottom right, the prior gives 52% to the cat’s only non-losing reply, the top right corner.

alphazero:12.t: The teacher stays ahead. Take 300 random positions where the choice matters; the bars count best moves found by the trained network, alone and with search. Untrained, the gap was wider: 120 alone, 285 with 40 loops. Visit shares are the better target, and that gap keeps the loop improving. Caveat: only 20 of the 300 have six or more empty squares, so 40 loops often reach the end.

alphazero:13.t: Against perfect play. It plays a perfect player, 30 games on each side. Perfect play draws. Untrained, even with 40 loops, it lost 19 of 30 as the cat and 0 as Pip. Its search did well on random positions, but here one wrong early move loses. Trained, losses almost vanish. The card’s error rate is overall; in these games it erred in 1 of 142 such positions.

alphazero:14.t: Your turn. Drag through the generations. The board shows the network’s prior on Pip’s puzzle; the chart marks how often its favourite is a best move overall. At generation 0 the prior is close to even. Watch when top right takes the lead, and when the search with 40 loops starts to pick it.

alphazero:15.t: The catch. Even this toy took 600 games with 40 loops per move. Go needs vastly more: AlphaZero played tens of millions of self-play games each for chess, shogi and Go, on thousands of special chips. Every loop, the search plays moves by the rules to reach new positions. AlphaZero needs the rules. Atari games and the real world have no rulebook. That is the next reel.

alphazero:16.t: AlphaGo to AlphaZero. In 2016 DeepMind’s AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, a top Go player, 4 games to 1. It learned from human games first and used playouts. In 2017 AlphaGo Zero dropped both, learned by self-play alone, and beat that AlphaGo 100 games to 0. Then AlphaZero, preprint 2017, journal paper 2018: given only the rules, the same method learned chess, shogi and Go, and beat leading programs.

alphazero:17.t: Recap. AlphaZero replaces random playouts with a network that gives a value and a prior for each position. The search uses the value at new nodes, and the prior to decide which moves to try. It learns by self-play: the value learns how games ended, the prior learns the search’s visit shares. Better network, better search, better lessons. It still needs the rules.

worldmodels:0.t: World Models  and  Dreamer. Learn to dream the game, then practise inside the dream.

worldmodels:1.t: Back in the meadow. Pip is now in the open meadow. Its position is two numbers, x and y. A move goes 0.15 up, right, down or left, plus a small random wobble. The cheese circle pays plus 1, the cat circle minus 1, and either ends the walk. gamma (gamma) is 0.9. The D Q N reel used 8000 real moves. For a robot, each one costs time and wear.

worldmodels:2.t: Too big for a notebook. In the model-based reel, Pip noted what each move did in each cell: a learned model, its own copy of the rulebook. Then it practised in its head. Here Pip never stands on the same spot twice, so no notebook can list them all. The fix, as for values in the function approximation reel: a network that guesses for spots it has never seen.

worldmodels:3.t: A world model. Pip’s world model is two small networks. The move predictor takes Pip’s four measurements and the move, one switch per move, and guesses the change in x and y. The change is nearly the same everywhere, so it is easier to learn than the new position. The reward predictor guesses the reward from the landing spot’s four measurements. Together they are a learned simulator.

worldmodels:4.t: Learning from 500 real moves. First, real experience: Pip wanders with random moves from random spots, 500 real moves in all. Only 4 of them landed on the cheese and 7 on the cat. Each network is trained as in the function approximation reel: guess, compare with what really happened, nudge every knob a little toward the truth, thousands of times over these same moves.

worldmodels:5.t: How good are its moves?. Teal arrows: the move predictor’s guesses for “right” from a few spots. Grey: the move without wobble. Near the right fence they poke past it: few of the 500 moves showed that bump. On 2000 fresh real moves it is off by 0.029 on average, against 0.022 for a perfect predictor of the average move: the wobble cannot be predicted. A move is 0.15.

worldmodels:6.t: How good are its rewards?. Squares show the reward predictor: gold where it says cheese, a guess above 0.5, rose where it says cat, below minus 0.5. Its cheese covers 64 percent of the real circle, its cat only 34 percent. Caveat: “to cheese” and “to cat” are computed from their positions, so the layout comes free. The predictor only learns how near counts, from 4 cheese and 7 cat landings.

worldmodels:7.t: Dreaming. Now Pip can dream. From the start it picks a move, asks the move predictor where it lands, then repeats from that guessed spot, with no real step taken. Dashed: a dream of ten fixed moves, up four times, then right, then up. Solid: the same moves for real. Reality reaches the cheese after 10 moves; the dream says after 9.

worldmodels:8.t: Dreams drift. From 200 random spots, make 15 random moves, real and dreamed. Teal: the learned model’s average gap. Grey: a perfect predictor of the average move, missing only the wobble. After 1 step the gap is 0.030; after 15, 0.137, against 0.074 for grey. Each dream step builds on the last guess, so errors pile up. Grey grows too, as the wobble adds up.

worldmodels:9.t: Practice in the dream. Train the D Q N reel’s Q-network, same settings, in the dream: 8000 dreamed moves, zero real. Each starts where Pip really was and lasts at most 15 moves, since long dreams drift. Steps pay 0 until the reward predictor says cheese or cat, ending the dream. Of 860 dreams, 271 stray past the fence, where real Pip never goes: the move predictor never quite learned it.

worldmodels:10.t: Waking up. Time to wake up. The dream-trained network now steers the real Pip, always taking its best move, from the D Q N reel’s 30 test spots. It reaches the cheese from 27 of the 30 spots and meets the cat 3 times. All it ever saw of the real meadow were those 500 random moves.

worldmodels:11.t: A fair test. Luck? Four runs, different dice. D Q N alone on the 500 real moves, allowing only 400 updates, reaches the cheese from 7, 1, 0, 3 of the 30 spots. Dream-trained Pip: 27, 30, 26, 29. A Q-network fed those moves directly, with the dream run’s 7900 updates: 1, 1, 0, 0. So it is not just more updates: the model fills gaps those few moves left.

worldmodels:12.t: The catch: a flawed dream. The dream’s cat covers only a third of the real one. In run 3, dream-trained Pip met the real cat from 4 of 30 spots. At 2 of these 4 landings the dream predicted minus 0.44 and minus 0.38: not below minus 0.5, so grass, and practice never warned against them. At the other 2 it did predict the cat; network mistakes or the wobble did the rest.

worldmodels:13.t: Your turn. Drag the number of real moves the move predictor learns from, and watch its dream of the ten fixed moves and the drift chart. Retraining takes a moment. From 30 real moves, the dream is off by 0.75 after 15 steps, about 5 moves’ length. From 2000, by 0.09. More real experience makes the dream more trustworthy, but grey shows a floor no model beats.

worldmodels:14.t: From pictures. Real agents often see pictures, not positions; predicting every pixel is wasteful. In 2018, David Ha and Jürgen Schmidhuber’s World Models squeezed each frame into a short list of numbers, a latent state, and learned to predict the next list. In VizDoom, the controller, which picks actions, trained only in that dream yet worked for real. Pip’s four measurements act as its latent state.

worldmodels:15.t: Dreamer. Danijar Hafner and colleagues’ Dreamer (2019) learns such a latent model from pixels. It trains an actor, a policy network, and a critic, a value network, on 15-step dreams from real moments, like Pip’s. It keeps collecting real experience and retraining the model, so the dream is checked against reality. DreamerV3 (2023) used one setting for many tasks and collected diamonds in Minecraft from scratch.

worldmodels:16.t: Recap. Too big for a notebook? Learn a world model with networks: where a move lands and what it pays. Then the policy practises in the dream, almost for free. Keep dreams short, since errors pile up, and check them against reality: the policy inherits the dream’s mistakes. In bigger problems a policy may even exploit the dream’s errors, a known risk not shown here.

shaping:0.t: Reward Shaping. Add hints so the agent isn’t searching in the dark.

shaping:1.t: A bigger maze. Pip has a bigger maze, so the cheese is harder to find: 8 cells across, 6 up, five rocks, cheese top right, start bottom left. No cat, to keep it simple. Rules as before: plus 1 for the step onto the cheese, which ends the walk; every other step pays 0; gamma (gamma) equals 0.9. A walk still without cheese after 1000 steps is called off.

shaping:2.t: The learner. Pip learns with Q-learning, as in that reel: four numbers per cell, one per move, all starting at 0. It takes the move with the biggest number, ties broken at random; one move in five is random. After each move, its number is nudged a fifth of the way, alpha (alpha) equals 0.2, toward the reward plus 0.9 times the best number where Pip landed.

shaping:3.t: Searching in the dark. Every number starts at 0, so every choice is a coin toss. Pip’s first walk took 207 steps. Each update said “0 stays 0”. Only the last step, onto the cheese, changed anything: one number out of 168 rose to 0.2. All that wandering taught Pip nothing. A reward that almost never shows up is called a sparse reward.

shaping:4.t: How slow is slow?. To see the speed, run 20 Pips, each with its own luck, for 30 walks each. The chart’s line goes across from walk 1 to walk 30; its height is how many steps that walk took, averaged over the 20 Pips. Lower is better: the shortest way takes 12 steps. Without hints, the first 10 walks average 151 steps. By walk 30 it is 16.

shaping:5.t: Give hints: hot and cold. We, the designers, know each cell’s distance to the cheese: columns plus rows, since no rock makes the real way longer here. Pip does not know this. So we add a hint to the reward, like the game hot and cold: plus 0.1 for a step closer, minus 0.1 for a step away, 0 for a bump. Adding such extra rewards is called reward shaping.

shaping:6.t: Much faster. The teal line is the same 20 Pips with hot-and-cold hints. Their first 10 walks average 20 steps instead of 151. Why? Every step now carries a little news, so the numbers start pointing toward the cheese long before Pip ever reaches it.

shaping:7.t: A tempting shortcut. A designer thinks: why punish steps away at all? Just reward progress, and make it stronger: plus 0.3 for every step closer, nothing otherwise. It sounds like the same hint. Watch what Pip learns.

shaping:8.t: Pip dances. After 30 walks, Pip follows its biggest numbers from the start, no random moves. It runs toward the cheese, then steps back and forth beside it. It would never eat. 16 of 20 Pips dance: 8 beside the cheese, the rest farther away, their learning unfinished. Even early, this hint slows learning: 271 steps per walk over the first 10, against 151 without hints.

shaping:9.t: Why dancing pays. Beside the cheese, Pip has two plans. Eat now: plus 1, plus 0.3 for stepping closer, then nothing: 1.3. Or dance: step away free, plus 0.3 back, repeated. With the 0.9 discount, the dance is worth 1.42. Here the hint did not just speed things up. It changed what is best. Pip is not broken; it found how best to collect our hints, called farming a reward.

shaping:10.t: Why hot and cold was fine. With hot and cold, a step away takes back what the step closer gave: plus 0.1, then minus 0.1. Out and back sums to nothing, or plus 0.01 with the discount, too little to beat the cheese. A cell’s potential: minus a tenth of its distance. Each hint is new potential minus old, so along any walk the middle terms cancel: only start and end count.

shaping:11.t: The safe recipe. In 1999, Andrew Ng, Daishi Harada and Stuart Russell made this exact. Give each cell any potential, 0 once the walk ends. Pay hint equals 0.9 times new potential minus old potential. Discounted, any walk’s hints from a cell sum to minus its potential, loops included. So every move number there shifts equally, keeping their ranking: the best plan stays best. This is potential-based shaping.

shaping:12.t: Choosing a potential. Any potential is safe; a good one also helps. A natural choice: a rough guess of reward to come. Ours: 1 minus distance over 12. That is 0 at the start, 12 steps away, 0.92 beside the cheese. The walk ends on the cheese, so its potential is 0. The step onto it pays plus 1 reward and a minus 0.92 hint: the guess is cashed in.

shaping:13.t: What the hints feel like. From a cell 8 steps away: a step closer pays plus 0.042, a bump minus 0.033, a step away minus 0.108. Getting closer pays, wasting a step costs a little, going back costs more. These costs do not change the plan like a step cost would: the cheese step repays them, so every plan totals the same. What matters is the recipe’s form, with 0.9 built in.

shaping:14.t: Same total, every time. Check from the start, where the potential is 0. Three walks: the shortest route, Pip’s first wandering walk with these hints, 53 steps, and 1000 steps of dancing beside the cheese. Their discounted hints add up to 0, 0 and 0. Dancing earns nothing extra. Only the reward differs: the route’s cheese is worth 0.31 from the start, the dance 0.

shaping:15.t: Fast and safe. Gold: 20 Pips with the potential hint. Their first 10 walks average 21 steps, almost as fast as hot and cold, and all 20 end on a 12-step route. Pip’s best numbers head for the usual ones minus the cell’s potential. At the start, potential 0, that is 0.31, as without hints. The teal hot-and-cold line hides under the gold one.

shaping:16.t: Safe is not the same as fast. The guarantee ignores speed. Use hot and cold’s potential, minus a tenth of distance, in the exact recipe. Even a bump now earns a little, so tried moves beat untried ones. First 10 walks: 412 steps, slower than no hints. It differs from ours mostly by a constant, which cannot change the best plan, but since Pip’s numbers start at 0, it changes learning speed.

shaping:17.t: Your turn. Pick one of four hints: none, hot and cold, plus 0.3 per step closer, or the potential hint. The picture shows one Pip after 30 walks, following its biggest numbers with no random moves. The card gives averages over all 20 Pips. Which hints speed Pip up, and which one teaches it the wrong thing?

shaping:18.t: In the real world. The word comes from animal training: B. F. Skinner taught pigeons by rewarding small steps toward a trick. In R L, Jette Randløv and Preben Alstrøm in 1998 rewarded a simulated bicycle for nearing a goal, never penalising riding away. It learned to ride in circles, collecting reward every loop, like Pip’s dance. That helped motivate the 1999 recipe. Hand-made hints remain common in robot learning.

shaping:19.t: Recap. Sparse rewards make learning slow: most steps teach nothing. Shaping adds hints so every step carries news. Careless hints change what is best and get farmed. Hints of the form gamma times potential(new) minus potential(old) can never change the best plan; a good potential also makes learning fast.

hacking:0.t: Reward Hacking. You get what you reward, not what you meant.

hacking:1.t: A chore for Pip. Back in Pip’s maze: cheese plus 1, cat minus 1, both end the walk, gamma (gamma) equals 0.9. Today there are also three crumbs lying around. We want Pip to tidy up: pick up the crumbs, then go to the cheese. Pip, as always, knows nothing of what we want. It only feels the rewards we hand out.

hacking:2.t: Writing the reward. We have a crumb sensor, so we write: plus 0.2 for every step that ends on a crumb. Cheese and cat stay as before, and a walk stops after 50 steps. The sensor only checks where Pip stands, so a crumb never disappears. Pip learns with Q-learning, as in the Q-learning reel: one move in five random.

hacking:3.t: What Pip learned. After 100 walks, Pip follows its biggest numbers from the start, no random moves. It walks 2 steps to the crumb on the left, and then bumps into the rock beside it, again and again. Each bump is a step that ends on a crumb: plus 0.2, every single step. Pip never goes near the cheese.

hacking:4.t: Why bumping wins. Bump forever on the crumb: 0.2 every step. With the 0.9 discount, worth 2. From the start: 1.8. Going straight to the cheese along the bottom, over two crumbs: only 0.84. Even beside the cheese, the best move is to turn away. Left of it, eating is worth 1, returning to the left crumb 1.46. Below it, the right crumb is next door: 2.

hacking:5.t: Reward hacking. Pip broke no rule. It found the best way to collect exactly what we rewarded: steps that end on a crumb. What we meant, tidy up and then eat, was never in the numbers. When an agent scores well by a route its designers did not intend, it is called reward hacking, or specification gaming.

hacking:6.t: High score from the first walk. Each bar is one training walk, as high as its points, the plain sum of rewards; gold if it reached cheese. Scores are high from walk 1: once the crumb paid plus 0.2, that move had the only number above 0, so Pip repeated it. Only 1 of the first 10 reached cheese, the last on walk 6. Last 50: 8.7 points per walk, 0 cheeses.

hacking:7.t: Goodhart’s law. Economists know this as Goodhart’s law. In Marilyn Strathern’s words: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Touching crumbs was a fine sign of tidying, as long as nobody optimised it. Once Pip optimised it, the sign and the goal came apart.

hacking:8.t: Patch the reward. Fix the loophole: each crumb pays plus 0.2 once, then is gone. Pip’s state now includes which crumbs are left, since that decides whether a cell pays. A longer run, 300 walks: eight times as many states. Pip takes 2 crumbs en route, skips the left one, eats in 7 steps. That is best here: all three are worth 0.73, against 0.84; the detour delays cheese.

hacking:9.t: Patches don’t scale. Patching worked because we watched Pip and saw the trick. In a big world we cannot list every loophole ahead, and a hard-searching agent finds the ones we missed. A patch also changes the problem: Pip had to track which crumbs were left. Each fix is a new reward with its own gaps: ours still does not say “collect every crumb”, so Pip skipped one.

hacking:10.t: A boat that never finished. This happens with real agents. In 2016, OpenAI trained an agent on the boat racing game CoastRunners, where points come from hitting targets along the course. It found a lagoon where three targets kept coming back, and circled there, crashing and catching fire, never finishing the race. It still scored more than finishing would. Like Pip, it was rewarded for points, not for the race.

hacking:11.t: More from the list. Victoria Krakovna and colleagues at DeepMind keep a public list of such cases. A simulated robot arm, rewarded for the height of a block’s bottom face, flipped the block over instead of stacking it.
