A simulated hand, judged by people watching through a camera, hovered between camera and ball so it looked like grabbing. A Tetris program paused the game forever, so it never lost.

hacking:12.t: Why it matters more for strong agents. Pip found its trick in 20 cells. A stronger agent searches more, finding gaps weaker ones miss. In 2022, Alexander Pan, Kush Bhatia and Jacob Steinhardt found more capable agents exploited badly specified rewards more. Chatbots tuned with a reward model, a network predicting which answers people prefer, face the same pull: an answer can score well with it yet be no better for people.

hacking:13.t: What helps. No complete cure exists. Watch what the agent does, not just its score. Test it in situations it never trained on. Patch loopholes you find. Don’t push too hard on a reward you do not fully trust. In chatbot tuning, a penalty usually keeps the new model’s answers close to the untuned model’s, so they cannot drift toward odd answers only the reward model likes.

hacking:14.t: Your turn. Choose what each crumb step pays. After 100 training walks, Pip follows its biggest numbers from the start. How small before Pip goes for the cheese? Bumping is best only above about 0.07. Below that Pip still bumps: the crumb came long before the cheese, and rare random moves never carry it far enough to learn better. Not hacking: unfinished exploration, from the bandit reels.

hacking:15.t: Recap. An agent optimises exactly what you reward, not what you meant. Gaps between the two get found: Pip bumped a rock on a crumb, a boat circled for points. When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. The stronger the optimiser, the more this matters: watch behaviour, test widely, and patch.

curiosity:0.t: Curiosity  and  Intrinsic Motivation. Reward the agent for being surprised.

curiosity:1.t: A much bigger maze. Pip moves to a big maze: 12 columns by 9 rows, 108 cells, with walls between them. The cheese is top right, 21 steps away by the shortest route. No cat here. Same rules: plus 1 on the step onto the cheese, then Pip restarts at the bottom left. Other steps pay 0. Bumping a wall leaves Pip in place but still counts as a step.

curiosity:2.t: A reward that almost never comes. Until Pip first steps onto the cheese, every step pays 0: a sparse reward, as in the shaping reel. Why not add hints? With walls everywhere, "closer as the crow flies" can point into dead ends, and the designer may not know the maze at all. So Pip learns nothing until it stumbles onto the cheese once. Everything depends on how it explores before that.

curiosity:3.t: Pip’s learner. Pip keeps a guess per cell and move. Each step moves that guess halfway toward the reward plus 0.9 times the new cell’s best guess: Q-learning, gamma (gamma) 0.9. One move in 10 is random, the rest are best-guess: epsilon-greedy, epsilon (epsilon) 0.1. Step size and epsilon differ from earlier reels. Guesses start at 0 and stay 0 without reward; ties are broken at random.

curiosity:4.t: Wandering in circles. Watch 1000 steps of this random walk, sped up. Shading shows how often Pip stood in a cell: the darker, the more visits. After 1000 steps Pip has seen only 57 of the 108 cells. It stood on the start cell 52 times and on one cell nearby 64 times. Random steps keep undoing each other, so Pip circles near home.

curiosity:5.t: Found, eventually. Pip keeps wandering. It finally steps onto the cheese at step 2274, more than a hundred times the 21 steps of the shortest route. Was this run unlucky? A bit, but it was typical. Over 101 runs with different luck, the middle run, the median, needs 1738 steps to find the cheese the first time.

curiosity:6.t: A reward from inside. Children explore because new things are interesting, not for pay. Give Pip the same drive: an intrinsic reward, a bonus Pip pays itself for going somewhere new. The cheese is an extrinsic reward, from the world. Pip learns from the sum, with the same learner. Doesn’t a bonus change what is best, as in the shaping reel? Yes, on purpose. We come back to that.

curiosity:7.t: Counting visits. The simplest novelty bonus: Pip counts its visits to each cell. On arrival it pays itself 0.1 divided by the square root of the count, this visit included. The bars show the first ten visits: 0.1 on the first, 0.05 on the fourth. The hundredth pays 0.01. Familiar cells get boring, but slowly; unvisited cells keep the full 0.1.

curiosity:8.t: Untried moves look promising. An untried move starts with the guess 1, not 0. Why? Endless new cells, each paying 0.1, are worth 0.1, plus 0.9 times 0.1, plus 0.81 times 0.1, and so on: exactly 1. So "untried" means "maybe fresh ground": optimism, as in the bandit reels. The surprise explorer later starts at 1 too. The cheese-only random walker started at 0.

curiosity:9.t: The counting explorer. Same maze, same luck seed. Now each visit makes a cell a little more boring, so Pip’s guesses point toward the least visited parts of the maze, and the shading spreads like a flood. This Pip steps onto the cheese at step 348, after seeing 64 cells. By that step the random walker had seen 18; it needed 2274 steps for the cheese.

curiosity:10.t: A chart of exploring. One run proves little, so here are averages over 101 runs. The chart: left to right, steps taken. Upward, how many of the 108 cells Pip has seen at least once by then. A line that reaches the top has seen the whole maze. The grey line shows the fastest possible case, one new cell per step.

curiosity:11.t: Counting covers the maze. Gold, the random walker: after 1000 steps it has seen 50 cells on average. Teal, the counting explorer: 97, almost all of them. The random walker is still at 68 after 2000 steps. Being pulled toward rarely visited cells turns wandering into a sweep.

curiosity:12.t: Time to the first cheese. Now the race to the first cheese. Each bar is the median over 101 runs. Random walker: 1738 steps. Counting explorer: 314, more than five times faster. Is it just the hopeful start of 1? With that start but no bonus, the median is 560: it helps, but those hopes fade once each move is tried. The bonus keeps pulling Pip onward.

curiosity:13.t: Curiosity as surprise. Pathak and colleagues, in 2017, paid for surprise instead. For each cell and move, Pip keeps chances for what it sees next, here the cell it lands in. The prediction error is 1 minus the chance given to what it saw. Bonus: 0.1 times that. Each move’s chances shift halfway toward the outcome. A new move has error 1, then 0.5, 0.25, 0.125.

curiosity:14.t: Surprise works too. Same seed, the surprise explorer finds the cheese at step 738. Its median over 101 runs: 769 steps, slower than counting’s 314, far faster than the random walker’s 1738. Moves here are not random, so surprise is a count per cell and move, halving each try. It likely lags because it fades faster than the square root and is kept per move, not per cell.

curiosity:15.t: The noisy TV. A TV now sits 6 steps from the start, showing static: one of 64 random patterns each time. There Pip must also predict the picture, and no chance beats 1 in 64. So the error stays near 1: the bonus there averages 0.099 forever. Pip reaches the TV at step 103 and mostly stays: each wall bump keeps it there, with a fresh picture.

curiosity:16.t: Trapped by noise. In 3000 steps this Pip spent 2333 on the TV cell, saw only 46 cells, and never found the cheese. Over 101 runs of 5000 steps, median time to cheese: 2724, with the 28 failed runs counted as over 5000. Counting is not fooled: it counts cells, not pictures. Counting each picture as a new place would make static always new, and trap counting too.

curiosity:17.t: Can a bonus be farmed?. After the hacking reel, a fair question: can Pip farm its own bonus? A count bonus fades: the hundredth visit pays only 0.01. Farming pays less and less, so in the end the cheese’s plus 1 wins. A surprise bonus fades only if the world is predictable. Noise never is, so it pays about 0.099 forever. The noisy TV is reward hacking of an inner reward.

curiosity:18.t: Your turn. Tap a cell to put the TV there. The slider picks the explorer: left is surprise, right is counting; its name shows beside the slider and above the maze. Pip replays 3000 steps, same seed, sped up. Try the TV far away, or in a dead end. When does surprise get hooked, and does counting ever care?

curiosity:19.t: Where you meet this. Pathak and colleagues’ prediction-error curiosity let agents explore Doom and Super Mario Bros games with little or no game reward. Their Mario agent cleared part of level one on curiosity alone. Bellemare and colleagues stretched count bonuses to game screens in 2016, with big gains on Montezuma’s Revenge, the Atari game where D Q N scored 0. In 2018 Burda and colleagues demonstrated the noisy TV trap.

curiosity:20.t: Recap. When reward is sparse, random exploring wanders in circles. An intrinsic reward for novelty sends the agent toward fresh ground. Count visits and pay more for rare places, or pay for prediction error. Beware the noisy TV: pure randomness stays surprising forever. Next: what to do when places never repeat, so there is nothing to count.

imitation:0.t: Imitation Learning. Skip the reward: just copy an expert.

imitation:1.t: Meet Mo. This is Mo, an old mouse who has lived in Pip’s maze for years. In every cell, Mo knows a good move. Pip could learn by trial and error, as in earlier reels, but that takes many walks and many meetings with the cat. Here is a shortcut: watch Mo, and copy. That is imitation learning.

imitation:2.t: Two kinds of paws. The floor is wet, as in the M D P and policy reels. Pip’s moves go as intended 8 times in 10 and slide sideways 1 in 10 each way. Mo’s old paws grip: Mo never slides. Rewards as usual: plus 1 for stepping onto the cheese, minus 1 onto the cat; either ends the walk. But a copier never looks at rewards, only at what Mo does.

imitation:3.t: Recording a demonstration. Mo walks from the start to the cheese while we write down every step as a pair: the cell Mo was in, and the move Mo made. Cell 16, up. Cell 11, up. And so on. One recorded walk is a demonstration. Mo’s takes 7 steps: up the left side, then along the top.

imitation:4.t: Three demonstrations. Mo walks the route 3 times. Mo never slides, so every walk is the same: 21 examples, all in the same 7 cells. In the other 9 cells, nobody has ever seen Mo. Those cells get a grey question mark.

imitation:5.t: Behaviour cloning. Each example is like a quiz question with its answer: “in cell 16, which move?” “Up.” Learning a rule from questions with known answers is called supervised learning. Used on demonstrations, it is behaviour cloning: in each cell, give Mo’s answer. Had Mo answered differently on different visits, Pip would take the most common answer.

imitation:6.t: Cells without examples. But Pip’s rule must answer in every cell. Our copier’s simple stand-in for a trained network: an empty cell copies the nearest cell with an example, counting steps across the grid. Ties go to the lower-numbered cell. These answers are guesses. 5 of the 9 push into a rock or a wall. In cell 8, beside the cat, the guess “right” steps onto the cat.

imitation:7.t: Looks just like Mo. Pip walks with its copy. Walk 3: no slides, 7 steps, cheese. On Mo’s route the copy is perfect, because every cell there holds Mo’s example. If Pip never slid, cloning would be all it needs.

imitation:8.t: One slide. Walk 194. On its very first move Pip tries up and slides right, into cell 17. Mo never stood there, so the copy guesses: “up”. Up leads to cell 12? No: Pip slides again, into cell 18. There the guess “up” pushes into the rock. Bump, bump. Then a slide back into cell 17.

imitation:9.t: Errors pile up. Pip bumps a rock in cell 12 until a lucky slide returns it to Mo’s route. Near the end it slides into cell 8; the guess says right, onto the cat. That is compounding error: a slip reaches a cell Mo never showed, guessing there leads further off, and nothing shows the way back. 9 of Pip’s 15 steps were in cells without an example.

imitation:10.t: A thousand walks. Now 1000 walks per rule from the start, same dice. In each bar, gold reached the cheese, rose the cat, grey stopped at 100 steps. Top: Pip with Mo’s whole rule card, perfect everywhere. Bottom: the clone. The card reaches the cheese 861 times, the clone 784. 293 clone walks entered a cell without an example; only 156 of those reached the cheese.

imitation:11.t: More of Mo won’t help. Would more demonstrations help? Thirty walks by Mo give 210 examples, but still the same 7 cells, because Mo never leaves the route. The clone is exactly the same, and so is its score: 784. The trouble is not how much data, but where it comes from. Mo’s examples cover Mo’s cells; Pip’s slides take it to its own. This mismatch is called distribution shift.

imitation:12.t: dagger: ask about Pip’s cells. In 2011, Stéphane Ross, Geoff Gordon and Drew Bagnell proposed a fix: let the learner walk, and ask the expert about the cells the learner actually reaches. Mo watches Pip and says, for every cell Pip stood in, “here, I would go ...”. Add those answers to the examples, clone again, repeat. The method is called dagger, short for Dataset Aggregation.

imitation:13.t: Round 1. Pip walks 5 times with its clone, slides and guesses included: 62 steps. Mo labels every one, so there are now 83 examples. 4 cells get Mo’s answer for the first time: cells 8, 12, 17 and 18. With them, the clone reaches the cheese 857 times in 1000, up from 784.

imitation:14.t: Round by round. Round 0 is plain cloning; dashed is Mo’s whole card. Rounds 2 and 3 add examples but no new cells: no change. In round 4 all 16 cells hold Mo’s answer; the clone scores 861, exactly the card’s score. The ceiling: a copier matches its teacher, never beats it. Mo’s card suits gripping paws: from cells 4, 10 and 14, one slide hits the cat.

imitation:15.t: The price of asking. The cost: an expert on call for places it never goes; for driving, slowly labelling a learner’s drives. The learner practises for real, mistakes included. In return, a better guarantee. One early slip can strand a clone for good: in the worst case its mistakes beyond the expert’s grow with the walk’s length squared. Trained on its own cells, dagger’s grow only in proportion.

imitation:16.t: Your turn. Slide through the dagger rounds, from 0, plain cloning, to 4. Plum arrows are Mo’s examples; gold arrows with a dot are the clone’s guesses. Tap a cell to drop Pip there and watch one walk with that round’s clone, slides and all. Each tap rolls new dice.

imitation:17.t: Where it is used. Around 1990, Carnegie Mellon’s ALVINN learned to steer a van from camera images by copying a human driver. In 2016, NVIDIA trained a car to steer from about 72 hours of human driving, adding off-centre camera views labelled with the steering that leads back: dagger’s recovery idea, without an expert on call. Robots often learn from remote-control demonstrations, and chatbots begin by imitating human-written text.

imitation:18.t: Recap. Behaviour cloning turns an expert’s demonstrations into examples and copies the expert’s move in each state: plain supervised learning, no rewards needed. Its weak spot: small mistakes lead to states the expert never showed, and the errors compound. More expert walks don’t reach those states. dagger asks the expert about the states the learner actually visits.

irl:0.t: Inverse R L. Watch the expert, figure out what they want.

irl:1.t: What does Mo want?. Last reel, Pip copied Mo’s moves cell by cell. Copying has a second weakness: it breaks when the maze changes, since Mo’s arrows point where the cheese used to be. Pip asks a deeper question: not “what does Mo do?” but “what does Mo want?” Normal R L goes from reward to behaviour. Inverse R L goes backwards, from behaviour to the reward that explains it.

irl:2.t: Why the goal travels. Think of a friend who always takes the longer road home. You might guess they care more about avoiding traffic than about distance. That guess is a reward, and it is useful: in a new city, you can predict their route without ever having seen it. Moves belong to one place. A goal can be reused anywhere.

irl:3.t: Mo’s walk, dry floor. The floor is dry here, so every move goes where it points. Mo walks from the start to the cheese in 7 steps, up the left side and along the top. Pip knows the maze: where each move leads. It does not know the rewards. Inverse R L usually assumes this: the learner can plan, but must find out what is worth planning for.

irl:4.t: Rewards from features. Pip describes every step with three features: does it reach the cheese, does it reach the cat, and that a step was taken. A guessed reward is one weight per feature. A step’s reward equals cheese weight if it lands on the cheese, plus cat weight if on the cat, plus the step weight, always. The usual rewards are weights plus 1, minus 1 and 0.

irl:5.t: Adding up a walk. Sum each feature over the walk, discounted: one more 0.9 per step of delay. Mo reaches the cheese on step 7: cheese total 0.9 to the sixth equals 0.53. Cat total 0. Step total 1 plus 0.9 plus ... plus 0.9 to the sixth equals 5.22. Under any guess, a walk’s return is the sum of weight times total. Usual weights give 0.53, the familiar return of a 7-step cheese walk.

irl:6.t: Many rewards fit. Which rewards make Mo’s walk a best walk? The usual ones, and “only cheese counts”. So does all zero: every walk scores 0, so Mo’s is as good as any. All zero explains every behaviour at once. Rewarding steps does not fit: the best walk would never end. Andrew Ng and Stuart Russell framed inverse R L in 2000 and pointed out this ambiguity.

irl:7.t: Pick the clearest win. Pip’s rule: grow a list of rival behaviours and pick the reward under which Mo beats them all by the widest margin. All zero gives margin 0, so it is out. Walks matching Mo’s feature totals tie Mo under every guess, so never count as rivals. Doubling all weights doubles every gap without changing any choice, so the squared weights must add up to 1.

irl:8.t: Round 1: Mo against the Wanderer. Start with one rival: the Wanderer, every move random. Its exact totals from the rules: cheese 0.01, cat 0.04, steps 9.54. Mo takes far fewer steps. The widest-margin reward says mostly “steps are bad”: cheese plus 0.12, cat minus 0.01, step minus 0.99. The cheese weight is tiny partly because step totals are about 5 while a cheese total is at most 1: feature scaling sways the choice.

irl:9.t: Planning with guess 1. Pip plans the best walk under guess 1. With steps that costly, the quickest ending wins: Pip runs to the cat in 5 steps instead of reaching the cheese in 7. That is not what Mo does, so guess 1 is wrong. But it is useful: the cat run joins the list of behaviours Mo must beat.

irl:10.t: Round 2: beat both. Now Mo must beat both the Wanderer and the cat run. Widest margin: cheese plus 0.71, cat minus 0.70, step minus 0.08, a win of 0.75 against each. Planned with guess 2, the route has exactly Mo’s feature totals. Mo’s route ties with the bottom-and-right route: both take 7 steps. The planner tries up first, so it takes Mo’s. Nothing is left to beat: the search stops.

irl:11.t: What Pip found. Scaled to cheese plus 1, guess 2 is cat minus 0.99, step minus 0.11: near the real plus 1 and minus 1, plus a small dislike of steps that Mo’s walk cannot rule out. Why stop at a match? A plan with Mo’s feature totals earns Mo’s return under every reward built from these features, Mo’s true one included. Pieter Abbeel and Andrew Ng built their 2004 method on this.

irl:12.t: A new maze. The maze changes: cheese bottom right in cell 20, cat in cell 18, rocks in cells 7 and 14. Mo has never walked here. Copying Mo’s card fails. Pip goes up and along the top to cell 5. It held the old cheese, so even Mo’s full card has no arrow there; the nearest arrow says right: into the wall, again and again until stopped.

irl:13.t: Plan with what Mo wants. Pip plans in the new maze with guess 2. The plan goes up and around the cat: 8 steps to the cheese, through cells 11, 12, 13, 8, 9, 10, 15. A route through cell 17 is just as short; the planner tries up first. It is exactly the best route under the maze’s real rewards. The moves did not transfer; the goal did.

irl:14.t: Your turn. Pick a reward guess; tap a cell to move the cheese. Pip plans with that guess in its usual maze and walks it. Guess 1 runs for the cat whenever the cat is nearer; all zero has no reason to go anywhere. Guess 2 finds the cheese anywhere in this small maze. In a bigger maze, a far-off cheese could lose to a nearby cat.

irl:15.t: Noisy experts: maximum entropy. Real experts vary routes. Brian Ziebart and colleagues’ 2008 maximum entropy inverse R L assumes the most random behaviour matching the expert’s feature totals. So each walk’s chance grows like e to the power of its return under the guess. Weights are tuned until walks match the expert’s totals on average. From taxi GPS traces, his team learned how drivers weigh road types, speeds and turns.

irl:16.t: Where it is used. Around 2007 to 2010, Pieter Abbeel’s team flew aerobatics with a model helicopter, using apprenticeship learning, built on inverse R L, from a pilot’s demonstrations. Inverse R L also models drivers and pedestrians. Costs: a planner inside every round, hand-picked features, and lingering ambiguity. gale (2016) skips writing the reward: a second network tells expert moves from the learner’s, and the learner earns reward for fooling it.

irl:17.t: Recap. Inverse R L watches behaviour and works out the reward behind it. A reward is a reusable description of the goal: plan with it in a new maze, where copied moves fail. Many rewards explain the same behaviour, even all zero, so a rule must choose: the widest margin, matching feature totals, or maximum entropy.

offline:0.t: Offline R L. Learn from a fixed log of data, with no new trials.

offline:1.t: Learning without walking. In the on/off reel, Pip learned from the Wanderer’s diary without taking a single step itself. Now make that the whole rule: a fixed record of old experience, and no new walks, ever. This is offline R L. It matters wherever trying things is costly or dangerous: you cannot test random treatments on patients, but hospitals keep years of records.

offline:2.t: Pip’s old diary. Pip once walked 50 times with Mo’s rule card on the wet floor, where a move goes where it points 8 times in 10 and slides to each side 1 in 10. Each step was logged: cell, move, reward, landing cell. 433 steps; 46 walks reached the cheese, 4 the cat. Slides reached all 16 cells, but each holds only one move: Mo’s arrow.

offline:3.t: With a table, no harm done. Replay with a table, as in the on/off reel: four numbers per cell, drawn as triangles, updated by Q-learning over many readings. Untried moves stay 0. Harmless here: every tried move scores above 0, so Pip follows Mo’s arrows: cheese 861 times in 1000 tests. The start’s number, 0.38, beats the true 0.33 only because this diary was lucky: 46 of 50 reached the cheese.

offline:4.t: Big problems need a network. In big problems a table is impossible, as the function approximation reel showed. A network instead computes the numbers from a description of the state. Pip’s tiny network takes the column and row, scaled to between minus 1 and 1, passes them through 8 hidden units, and gives four numbers, one per move: 60 knobs in all. Every move gets a number, tried or not.

offline:5.t: Replaying with the network. As with the table, each round every diary step gets a target: the reward plus 0.9 times the biggest of the network’s four numbers at the landing cell, or just the reward if the walk ended there. Then, with targets held fixed, all the knobs take 60 small steps toward them. 30 rounds in all. Nothing else changes; Pip never takes a new step.

offline:6.t: Numbers that cannot be true. After 30 rounds, the start cell’s numbers are: up 2.20, right 1.63, down minus 0.69, left 2.88. Only “up” appears in the diary. But no walk can earn more than 1: the cheese pays plus 1 once, and the discount only shrinks it. Under the best possible rule, the start is worth 0.33. The untried “left”, 2.88, is pure invention.

offline:7.t: How the error grows. Across: rounds 0 to 30; round 0 is random knobs. Up: the start’s biggest number. Dashed lines: 1, the most any walk can earn, and the true best value. It climbs past 1, to 2.88. Why? Each target’s max takes the landing cell’s biggest number, including untried moves’ made-up ones. It finds the most optimistic invention, and the next round builds on it: extrapolation error.

offline:8.t: Nobody ever checks. Online, the mistake would fix itself: Pip would try “left”, bump the wall, earn nothing, and lower the number each try. Offline, nobody tries it. Following the biggest numbers, Pip pushes into the wall at the start again and again. It reaches the cheese 0 times in 1000 tests. In 10 of 16 cells it picks a move the diary never tried.

offline:9.t: Stay close to the data. The fix sounds simple: don’t trust moves the diary never tried. If the data says nothing about a move, assume it is not great. Offline methods do this in different ways. Some only ever pick moves that look like the diary’s. Others lower the numbers of untried moves, so the max stops finding inventions. The next step shows one of those.

offline:10.t: Conservative Q-learning. C Q L, from Aviral Kumar, Aurick Zhou, George Tucker and Sergey Levine in 2020, adds a penalty at each diary step: a soft maximum of the cell’s four numbers, minus the diary move’s. Lowering it pushes all four down, the biggest hardest, and the diary’s move back up. Targets hold tried moves up; untried ones only sink. Dial alpha (alpha), here 0.5, sets how hard.

offline:11.t: After C Q L. Same diary, knobs and rounds, with C Q L. Start: up 0.44, right minus 2.12, down minus 4.96, left minus 3.06. The diary’s move is on top, above its real worth, 0.33, and far below 1. The new line stays down. Pip reaches the cheese 845 times in 1000, against 0 without C Q L. One invention survives: up in cell 14, into the cat, so it trails the diary’s rule, 861.

offline:12.t: How hard to push. At alpha 0.05, inventions survive: cheese 141. At 0.5 numbers are sane, but cell 14’s invention costs walks: 845. At 5 Pip copies the diary, 861, but the start’s number, 1.27, tops 1 again. Strong pushes win walks, middle ones honest numbers. With one move per cell, C Q L cannot beat the diary’s rule. Offline R L’s promise, combining the best of varied walks, is not shown.

offline:13.t: Your turn. Slide alpha, the strength of C Q L’s push, from 0, plain offline Q-learning, to 5. Each setting trains its own network on the same diary. Rose arrows are choices the diary never tried. Tap a cell to drop Pip there and watch one walk with that network’s choices, slides and all.

offline:14.t: Other ways to stay close. I Q L, implicit Q-learning, by Ilya Kostrikov, Ashvin Nair and Sergey Levine in 2021, ignores untried moves: its targets use only logged moves. Where a cell has several, it learns which did best and leans toward those. Earlier, BCQ, batch-constrained Q-learning, in 2019, kept the learner to moves like the data’s. All share one idea: offline, do not trust what the data does not show.

offline:15.t: Where it matters. Offline R L is studied wherever logs are plentiful and experiments are costly: treatment records in healthcare, logs of what people clicked in recommendation systems, and recorded runs of robots. Often it gives a careful warm start, followed by a little cautious practice in the real world. The toy here shows the main danger, not how large systems behave.

offline:16.t: Recap. Offline R L learns from a fixed record, with no new trials. With a network, untried moves get made-up numbers, and Q-learning’s max hunts down the most optimistic: extrapolation error. Nothing corrects it, because nobody tries those moves. The cure is to stay close to the data: C Q L pushes untried moves down, I Q L never asks about them.

rlhf:0.t: R L H F. How chatbots are tuned with human preferences.

rlhf:1.t: Bot, the answer machine. Pip asks Bot a question: how do I get to the cheese? Bot is a tiny stand-in for a language model. A real one writes word by word; Bot just picks one of eight whole answers, each with a chance. Bot learned these chances by copying example answers that people wrote, as in the imitation reel. Some are good, many are not.

rlhf:2.t: What is a good answer?. From the start, the way is up three, then right four, just above the cat. So some answers help, some do not. Could a rule in code judge them? Counting words fails: the longest answer repeats itself, and people dislike it. Direction words fail too: Down, then left, has them and is wrong. For real questions, coding helpful and honest is far harder.

rlhf:3.t: Easy to compare. But people can easily say which of two answers they prefer. Bot answers twice, a person picks one. Here the people are simulated; Mo, the old mouse with glasses, stands in for them. Each answer has a hidden taste score that drives their choices. Bot never sees it, only the comparisons.

rlhf:4.t: How people choose. People are noisy. Our simulated person picks answer A with chance 1 divided by (1 plus e to the minus gap), where the gap is A’s taste minus B’s: the Bradley–Terry model. The chart shows this curve: across, the taste gap; up, the chance of picking A. Equal taste gives 0.5. The two answers above differ by 3, so A wins with chance 0.95, not always.

rlhf:5.t: 400 comparisons. Bot answers twice, 400 times over, and the simulated people pick. Most pairs are two of Bot’s common answers. Bot’s rare repeated answer, the last row, turns up in only 11 of the 400 pairs. It wins 4 and loses 7. Keep an eye on it.

rlhf:6.t: A reward model. Now we build a reward model: a program that scores any answer, trained to agree with the comparisons. Real ones are large networks reading the whole text. Ours counts three things and gives each a weight: every word, every up or right, every down or left. Score equals the sum. Training picks the weights that make the people’s choices most likely under the same curve.

rlhf:7.t: Scores for every answer. Trained weights: 0.084 per word, 0.910 per up or right, minus 0.337 per down or left. The good answers score 2.24 and 2.41, above the rest. It matches 60% of choices: low, but people’s own hidden taste matches only 60%, since in 97 pairs both tasted the same. The repeated answer scores highest, 4.31: it says up and right four times, and the scorer just counts.

rlhf:8.t: Practice with P P O. Now the reward model is the judge, scoring thousands of answers at no cost. Bot improves with P P O, from the P P O reel. Each update Bot answers 32 times. An answer’s advantage is its reward minus the batch average. Bot takes 4 passes over the batch, ratio clipped to 0.8 to 1.2. Answers are one step long, so the batch average serves as the critic.

rlhf:9.t: Two ways to keep score. Two charts will track Bot. Top: the average reward-model score of Bot’s answers, what P P O is pushing up. Bottom: people’s verdict, the chance a person prefers the new Bot’s answer over the original Bot’s. 0.5 means no better. We can compute it exactly from the hidden taste. Bot cannot. Both start at the dot.

rlhf:10.t: Leash off. Run P P O with only the reward-model score as reward. At first both lines rise: Bot learns the good answers, and by update 34 people’s verdict is 0.87. Rarely, Bot gives its repeated answer, which scores higher still, and P P O piles on. By update 100 the score is 4.30, the repeated answer comes 99.6 times in 100, and people’s verdict is 0.37: worse than the original.

rlhf:11.t: Reward hacking. The reward model learned that up and right are good, and that is true in Bot’s usual answers. Repeating them is not, but in its 11 comparisons there was too little to learn from, and three weights cannot say repeating is bad. Maximising a learned score finds exactly such gaps. This is reward hacking: a high score, a worse answer.

rlhf:12.t: A leash. The fix, a leash to the original Bot: each reward loses beta (beta) times log of new over old chance. Averaged over new answers, that is the K L divergence: how far Bot has moved. Bot settles where leashed rewards tie: original chance times e to the score over beta, rescaled to sum to 1. At beta 1, the repeated answer grows only from 1 in 100 to 0.22.

rlhf:13.t: Leash on. Same run with beta equals 1. The score rises less, to 2.15. People’s verdict rises to 0.65: people now prefer the tuned Bot’s answer about 65 times in 100. The good answers climb to 0.27 and 0.23. The repeated one still grows, from 0.01 to 0.22: the leash holds it back, it does not erase the blind spot.

rlhf:14.t: Your turn. Drag beta, the strength of the leash. Each setting reruns P P O for 100 updates. The bars show Bot’s final chances, the card the reward-model score and people’s verdict. Too loose, and Bot hacks the scorer. Too tight, and Bot barely changes. Of these settings, beta equals 1 does best with people, 0.65.

rlhf:15.t: Not a cure. The best Bot here, always the good answer with the cat warning, would earn 0.91. The leash got 0.65: safer, not perfect. A reward model is only as good as its comparisons. So teams collect fresh comparisons on the tuned model’s answers and retrain the reward model. Unable to see hidden taste, real teams pick beta, and when to stop, from people’s ratings.

rlhf:16.t: Where it is used. Christiano and colleagues, in 2017, taught simulated robots and Atari players from people comparing short video clips; a backflip took about 900 comparisons. In 2022, InstructGPT (Ouyang and colleagues) tuned GPT-3 with comparisons, a reward model, and P P O with a K L penalty. People preferred a 1.3 billion parameter InstructGPT to the 175 billion parameter GPT-3. This recipe, R L H F, shaped later chat assistants.

rlhf:17.t: Recap. When a good answer is hard to write down, ask people to compare two answers. Fit a reward model so that bigger score gaps mean more reliable preferences. Then tune the model with P P O against that score, on a K L leash to the original, because a learned scorer has blind spots that an unleashed optimiser will find.

pomdp:0.t: Partial Observability (P O M D P). What to do when you can’t see the whole picture.

pomdp:1.t: A maze built for fog. A new maze, built to show one problem: a corridor of seven cells, numbered 1 to 7, with three rooms below: the cheese under cell 4, cats under cells 1 and 7. The usual rules: plus 1 for stepping onto the cheese, minus 1 onto a cat, either ends the walk, gamma (gamma) 0.9. Each walk starts in one of the seven cells, picked at random.

pomdp:2.t: Fog. Now the fog comes in. Pip sees only its own cell, and even there only which sides are walls and which are open. No cheese, no cats, no cell numbers. What Pip senses is its observation. Where it really is, the cell, is still the state, but Pip cannot see it.

pomdp:3.t: Only four feelings. Walking the corridor, Pip can feel only four different things. Cell 1: a wall on the left, an opening below. Cell 7: the mirror image. Cell 4: open left, right and below. And cells 2, 3, 5 and 6 all feel exactly the same: walls above and below, open on both sides. Call that feeling corridor.

pomdp:4.t: Twins that need opposite moves. Cells 3 and 5 feel identical, yet from cell 3 the cheese is to the right, and from cell 5 to the left. Likewise cells 2 and 6. So what Pip feels does not tell it what to do. In the M D P reel’s words, the observation is not Markov: what happens next depends on more than what Pip can sense.

pomdp:5.t: A name for it: P O M D P. Underneath, nothing changed: states, moves, rewards and gamma are still an M D P. Add one thing, which observation each state gives, and you have a partially observable M D P: a P O M D P, said “pom-dee-pee”. The true state is still Markov. It is just hidden behind the observations.

pomdp:6.t: A rule from what Pip feels. The simplest policy maps the current observation straight to a move. It has no memory, so it is called memoryless. Three entries are easy: left end, go right; junction, go down; right end, go left. But a memoryless rule has one entry for “corridor”, so all four corridor cells must get the same move.

pomdp:7.t: Corridor means right. Try “corridor: go right”. Cells 1 to 4 work. But start in cell 5: right to 6, right to 7, the right end says left, back to 6, which feels like corridor: right again. Pip shuttles forever. So it reaches the cheese from 4 of 7 starts. “Corridor: go left” fails on the other side, also 4 of 7. Up and down only bump.

pomdp:8.t: Roll a die?. One trick helps a little: in the corridor, flip a coin: left or right. Now every start reaches the cheese, with dithering. Average return over the 7 starts: 0.62, against 0.49 for “always right”. Seeing its cell, Pip would go straight: 0.84. No memoryless rule can. With the full state a fixed rule always suffices; under fog, a random one can beat every fixed one.

pomdp:9.t: Fix one: remember. Give Pip a one-item memory: the move it just made. Now “corridor, going right” and “corridor, going left” are different situations, each with its own entry. Rule: in the corridor keep going the way you were; with no memory yet, go right. From cell 5: right, right, the end turns it around, then left, left, left, down. Cheese in 6 steps.

pomdp:10.t: Learning in the fog. Can Q-learning find them? Same settings: one move in five random, alpha (alpha) 0.2. Across: walks. Up: return, averaged over the last 20 walks and 20 runs. Grey dashed: Pip seeing its cell. Lines start below 0: early walks often meet a cat. Rose, learning from feelings, stalls near 0.37: its one corridor entry mixes opposite-move twins, and a greedy rule cannot flip a coin.

pomdp:11.t: Memory pays, slowly. Teal learns from what Pip feels plus its last move. At first no better, with more situations to fill; then it pulls ahead: 0.54 against 0.37 over the last 100 walks. After 300 walks, the rose runs’ best moves reach the cheese from 3.5 of 7 starts on average; the teal runs’, 6.85. All lines include random exploring moves, so even grey stays below 0.84.

pomdp:12.t: Fix two: a belief. Fix two needs more knowledge. Give Pip the map: where each move leads and what each cell feels like, but not its own position. Then it can keep a belief: its chance of each cell, shown as shading. At first, 1 in 7 per cell, about 0.14. Then Pip feels “corridor”, which only cells 2, 3, 5 and 6 feel like: 1 in 4 each.

pomdp:13.t: Move, then look. Pip moves right. Not knowing from where, it shifts every chance one cell right: cell 2’s to 3, cell 6’s to 7, and so on. Then it feels corridor again. Cells 4 and 7 do not feel like that, so their chances are wiped out. Cells 3 and 6 remain, scaled back up to add to 1: one half each.

pomdp:14.t: Certain. Pip moves right again: chances shift to 4 and 7. It feels the right end, unique to cell 7: now Pip is certain. The map’s plan: left, left, left, down. Moving right led away from the cheese, but bought information: 6 moves in all, as many as the memory rule. “Go right until sure” was hand-made; generally, planning from a belief is its own problem.

pomdp:15.t: Shaky whiskers. Say each feeling is right 9 times in 10, else a random other one; moves never skid. Looks now lower chances, not wipe them out. Same readings: 0.96 sure of cell 7. Had the middle reading wrongly said “junction”, cell 7 still gets 0.66: starts in 5 or 6 explain it, as right from 7 bumps. Cell 5 gets 0.33: a start in 3, only the last reading wrong.

pomdp:16.t: Your turn. Pip starts in a hidden random cell, any of 1 to 7. Tap left, right or down to move it, and watch the belief after each move and feel. Down ends the walk where there is a room. Tap the card for a new walk. Use the slider to make the whiskers unreliable, and see how much longer it takes to be sure.

pomdp:17.t: Memory or belief?. Built with the map from every move and look, a belief holds all history says of Pip’s place, so choosing from it is Markov again. But it needs the map, and one number per state: hopeless for big worlds. Memory needs no map: deep R L often uses a recurrent network, like an LSTM, reading one observation at a time; ordinary training shapes what it keeps.

pomdp:18.t: Where you meet fog. In poker you cannot see the other cards, so good players and programs reason about what an opponent might hold, given their bets: a belief. A self-driving car that loses sight of a cyclist behind a bus must remember the cyclist is probably still there. In the D Q N reel, the Atari player took in four recent screens: a short memory, so motion could be seen.

pomdp:19.t: Recap. In a P O M D P the agent gets observations, not the state. Different states can look the same, so a rule on observations alone can fail, as Pip shuttled in the corridor. Two fixes: memory of recent observations and moves, which Q-learning can learn without a map; or a belief, chances over states, updated after every move and look, which needs the map.

hrl:0.t: Hierarchical R L. Think in sub-goals, not individual muscle twitches.

hrl:1.t: A bigger maze. Pip moves into a house: four rooms of 5 by 5 cells, joined by four doors, A to D. Walls are shaded. Pip starts in room 1’s top-left corner; the cheese sits in door D, between rooms 3 and 4. Rules as before: plus 1 for stepping onto the cheese, which ends the walk, gamma (gamma) 0.9. No cat. The shortest route takes 13 steps.

hrl:2.t: Tiny steps, a long way. First, plain Q-learning, as in its reel: a number for each move in each cell, one move in five random, alpha (alpha) 0.2. All start at 0, so walk 1 is pure wandering. Here walk 1 took 840 steps to stumble onto the cheese; over 20 runs with different seeds, 665 on average. Dots mark the cells Pip passed.

hrl:3.t: Think in big steps. You don’t plan a trip to the kitchen one footstep at a time. You think: leave this room, go down the hall, into the kitchen. Each big step hides many small ones. For Pip: from room 1, go to door B; from door B, go to door D. Two big steps instead of thirteen small ones.

hrl:4.t: An option. A big step needs its own little policy. Here is “go to door B”: an arrow in every cell of room 1 and door A, all leading to door B. It can start anywhere there, and stops at door B. A mini-policy with a start zone and a stopping rule is an option. We hand-drew 8, one per door of each room.

hrl:5.t: A bigger menu. The menu: 4 moves plus options that can start here: 2 inside a room, and in a doorway one per room it joins, like “go to door A” or “go to door D” in door B. Picking one is one decision: Pip follows its arrows until it stops. Random picks happen only at decisions, and nobody says which choice is good: options are just extra choices.

hrl:6.t: Learning numbers for options. Stopping after k steps, its target is the discounted reward en route, plus 0.9 to the k times the best move or option number at the stop. Only the chosen option’s number changes. Walk 1 ends with “go to door D”: its plus 1 comes on step 4, worth 0.9 to the 3: 0.729. alpha 0.2 moves the number a fifth of the way: 0.146.

hrl:7.t: Walk 1, side by side. Same seed, same rules, walk 1. Plain Q-learning, gold, wanders for 840 steps. With options, teal, Pip needs 39 steps and 16 decisions. Why so much faster? A random option carries Pip a whole room at a time, so even pure wandering crosses the house quickly. Over 20 runs, walk 1 takes 35 steps with options on average, against 665.

hrl:8.t: Sixty walks. Now 60 walks per run. Across is the walk number; up is the steps that walk took, averaged over the same 20 seeds for both learners. The dashed line is the shortest route, 13. Gold, plain Q-learning, needs many walks to come down. Teal, with options, is near the bottom almost at once. Over all 60 walks: 6,714 steps against 1,060.

hrl:9.t: Manager and worker. After 60 walks, follow the best choices. Plain: 13 decisions, one per step. With options: 2 decisions, “go to door B” then “go to door D”, over the same 13 steps. Think of a manager that picks the next big step, and a worker, the option’s arrows, that takes the small steps. The manager’s problem is tiny: a few decisions per walk.

hrl:10.t: Why news travels faster. In plain Q-learning, the cheese’s plus 1 creeps back about one cell per walk, so the start learns of it only once a chain of 13 numbers fills in. Over the 20 runs, the start’s best number first rose above 0 after about 23 walks. With options the chain has two links: start to door B, door B to cheese. Average: about 5 walks.

hrl:11.t: When options get in the way. Move the cheese to room 4’s far corner, seven steps from any door. Same options and seeds; walk 1 capped at 5,000. Plain Q-learning averages 974 steps; with options, 19 of 20 runs hit the cap. One choice in three is an option, and each ends at a door, yanking Pip back. Finding the cheese, it slowly recovers. With options versus plain: walk 20, 1,915 to 260; walk 60, 44 to 26.

hrl:12.t: The hard part. Options help only when their stopping points suit the task. We drew ours knowing where the doors were. Making an agent discover good options itself is the hard, still open problem of hierarchical R L. Some methods seek bottlenecks like doorways, which many good routes pass through. Others, like option-critic (2017), learn options and stopping rules from reward alone.

hrl:13.t: Other ways to split the work. Options come from Sutton, Precup and Singh, 1999. Others split the work differently. In feudal designs, dating to Dayan and Hinton, 1993, a manager hands out goals and is rewarded by the task, while the worker is rewarded only for reaching them. In goal-conditioned versions, the manager picks a target state, like “be at door B”, and one worker policy learns to reach any target.

hrl:14.t: Your turn. Slide to move the cheese: door D, door C, the middle of room 4, or its far corner. Both learners rerun, 10 seeds, 30 walks each, walks stopped at 3,000 steps. Where do the options shine, and where do they hurt? Look at how close the cheese is to a door.

hrl:15.t: Where it is used. Robots often combine skills like reach, grasp and place, hand-written or learned one at a time, with a higher-level policy picking the next. DeepMind’s FeUdal Networks, in 2017, used a manager setting goals for a worker in Atari games like Montezuma’s Revenge. It helps most when tasks are long, rewards rare, and sub-goals fit the task.

hrl:16.t: Recap. Hierarchical R L plans with big steps and small ones. An option is a mini-policy with a start zone and a stopping rule; picking one is a single decision that may take many steps. With options that fit the task, Pip explored and learned far faster. With ill-fitting options it did worse. Finding good options automatically is the hard part.

marl:0.t: Multi-Agent R L. When several learners share one world.

marl:1.t: Not alone any more. In every reel so far, Pip was the only one learning. The cheese, the cat, even the wet floor followed fixed rules: the same move in the same cell gave the same chances, every time. Now meet Tam, a second mouse in the same maze, with a pink bow. Tam learns too. Several learners sharing one world: that is multi-agent R L.

marl:2.t: The others are part of the world. From Pip’s point of view, Tam is part of the world, like the floor: what happens after Pip’s move can depend on what Tam does. And for Tam, Pip is part of its world. But the floor never changes its habits. Tam does, as it learns. So the chances in Pip’s world keep shifting. A world like that is called non-stationary.

marl:3.t: One room, two doors. Shrink the maze to one room. Each round, Pip and Tam each pick a door at once, without seeing the other’s choice. The big door is heavy: it opens only if both push, and then each gets a big cheese, worth 1. Pushing alone gets nothing. The small hole always has a crumb, worth 0.3, for each mouse there. The round ends, paid at once.

marl:4.t: The payoff table. Rows: Pip’s door. Columns: Tam’s. Each box shows Pip’s payoff, then Tam’s. Both do best together at the big door, 1 each, so they are a team. But the big door is a gamble: it pays only if the other comes too. The hole is safe. This is a stag hunt: two hunters catch a stag only together, while a hare is safe alone.

marl:5.t: How each mouse learns. Each mouse keeps two numbers, its payoff guess for each door, both starting at 0. It takes the bigger-numbered door, a coin toss on ties; one round in five it picks at random, to keep trying both. After the round, it moves its door’s number a fifth of the way toward the payoff. Neither knows the other is learning: these are independent learners.

marl:6.t: The first rounds. Round 1: all numbers are 0; both toss coins and pick the hole. Each gets 0.3, and its hole number goes from 0 to 0.06. Now the hole leads, so both stay. Round 6: one of Pip’s random rounds sends it to the big door. Tam is at the hole, so the door stays shut: payoff 0, and Pip’s big-door number stays 0.

marl:7.t: The big door, alone. Before round 100, Pip tried the big door 11 times, all at random, each time with Tam at the hole: 0. Is Pip wrong? Not really. Tam goes to the big door only in its random rounds, half of one in five: one round in ten. So it pays 0.1 on average, less than the crumb’s 0.3. Given Tam’s habit, the hole really is better.

marl:8.t: A lucky round. Round 100: both happen to make a random choice, and both pick the big door. It opens! Each number for the big door jumps from 0 to 0.2. Then each happens to try it once alone, and drops to 0.16. Round 112: another random double. 0.16 plus 0.2 times 0.84 equals 0.33, just above the hole’s 0.3. Now both prefer the big door.

marl:9.t: Same door, different world. The world from Pip’s side. Across: rounds 1 to 200. Up: the chance the big door pays Pip, which is Tam’s chance of picking it. Round 1: 0.5, Tam’s first coin toss. The door never changed; Tam did: it jumped from 0.1 to 0.9 after round 112. On the wet floor, chances stayed fixed; here Pip’s lessons can go stale any time.

marl:10.t: A hundred pairs. 100 pairs, each with its own dice, play 200 rounds. Dots are pairs: gold if both prefer the big door, teal if both the hole, grey otherwise. After 50 rounds, 66 pairs share the hole; after 200, still 47, and 53 reached the big door. A pair at the hole is stuck sensibly: whoever switches alone gets 0. Only a lucky double frees them.

marl:11.t: Now against the cat. Teammates share a goal. Opponents do not. New game: Pip runs to one of two doors, with cheese behind each, and the cat waits at one door. Same door: caught, Pip gets minus 1, the cat plus 1. Different doors: Pip eats, plus 1, and the cat gets minus 1. What one wins, the other loses. This is called zero-sum: pure competition.

marl:12.t: Chasing each other. Pip and the cat learn like the two mice: two numbers each, one round in five random. The strips show each one’s favourite door before every round: gold for left, teal for right. The cat learns Pip’s favourite and waits there, so that door starts to cost Pip, and Pip switches. Then the cat follows. Pip’s favourite changed 19 times in 200 rounds. Neither settles.

marl:13.t: No resting point. Best play here is the policy reel’s rock, paper, scissors answer: a coin toss. If both do, neither gains by changing alone: nothing left to learn. Such a resting point is an equilibrium; so was the pair at the hole. Our learners never hold it: each has a favourite, taken nine rounds in ten, which the other exploits. Pip went left 98 of 200 times: near half, but only on average.

marl:14.t: Your turn: be the cat. You are the cat: tap a door to wait there. Pip keeps learning; its two numbers are below. A cat always at the left door caught this Pip just once in 30 rounds; against 1000 other Pips, 3.4 on average, mostly in Pip’s random rounds. A coin-tossing cat catches about half: Pip escaped 515 of 1000 in our run. Can you catch Pip more often?

marl:15.t: Train together, act alone. One popular fix: centralised training with decentralised acting. During training a helper, often called a critic, learns a number for each pair of doors, like the payoff table, seeing what neither mouse can: the big door pays 1 when both come. Each mouse is nudged toward doors the helper rates highly. Acting, each mouse decides alone, helper gone. MADDPG (2017) is one, not run here.

marl:16.t: Playing against yourself. When both sides share the rules, like chess, an agent can train against copies of itself. As it improves, so does its opponent, so practice is never too easy or hopeless. This self-play taught AlphaZero chess and Go. An uneven game, like runner against cat, needs both roles trained. Self-play can still circle, as our learners did, so big systems also play older copies.

marl:17.t: Out in the world. In April 2019, OpenAI Five, five copies of one network trained mostly by self-play, beat OG, the reigning Dota 2 world champions. That year DeepMind’s AlphaStar reached Grandmaster level in StarCraft II, training a league: many agents, old and new, playing each other. Both took enormous practice. This reel’s shifting world is one reason multi-agent training is hard.

marl:18.t: Recap. In multi-agent R L, several learners share a world. To each one, the others are part of that world, and because they keep learning, the world is non-stationary. Teammates can get stuck on a safe but poor habit; opponents can chase each other forever. Helpers that see everything during training, and self-play, are common ways to cope.

sim2real:0.t: Sim-to-Real  and  Domain Randomisation. Train in simulation, then deploy on a real robot.

sim2real:1.t: Practice is expensive. Pip has a new job: a real running track, with cheese at the end. Practising on the real track is slow, and a mistake can be painful: the cat sleeps just past the cheese. So the engineers build a simulator: a computer copy of the track. In it, Pip can practise thousands of walks in seconds, many copies at once, and nobody gets hurt.

sim2real:2.t: The rules of the track. Cells run 0 to 7; Pip starts on 0. Each step it walks one cell or runs two. Reaching the cheese, cell 6, pays plus 1. Overshooting lands on the cat, cell 7: minus 1. Either ends the walk. Each delay step multiplies the reward by 0.9, the discount gamma (gamma), giving the walk’s return: three runs give 0.9 times 0.9 equals 0.81, six walks only 0.59.

sim2real:3.t: A dry simulator. In the simulator the floor is perfectly dry: a run always goes exactly two cells. Practice walks start in random cells, so Pip learns every cell. Its habit is one choice per cell. The best dry habit: run everywhere, except next to the cheese, where a run would overshoot; where walking is no better, Pip runs. From cell 0: run, run, run, 0.81.

sim2real:4.t: The real floor is polished. The real track is polished. A run sometimes skids one cell further, and Pip needs an extra step to get back up. The lost step counts even when the skid lands on the cheese or cat. Walking never skids. The slip chance is unknown: engineers only guess it lies between 0 and 0.4. The difference between copy and real thing is the reality gap.

sim2real:5.t: One skid, at the worst moment. Pip takes its dry habit onto the real track. Say the real slip chance is 0.2. Run, run: fine. From cell 4 it runs again, which in the simulator always landed exactly on the cheese. This time it skids one cell further, past the cheese, onto the cat. The habit never had to plan for a skid, because the simulator never made one.

sim2real:6.t: A thousand real walks. One walk could be bad luck, so the engineers test 1000 walks at slip chance 0.2. Each dot is one of the first 100: gold reached the cheese, rose met the cat. 133 of the 1000 walks met the cat. The average return is 0.58, far below the 0.81 the simulator promised.

sim2real:7.t: Tuned to one exact world. The dry habit is not stupid. It is perfect for its practice floor, squeezing out every step: it counts on each run landing exactly two cells on. That is the trouble with one exact simulator: whatever the copy gets slightly wrong, the habit may rely on. Engineers can make the copy more accurate, but never perfect.

sim2real:8.t: Randomise the simulator. A different idea: domain randomisation. Before each practice walk, the simulator picks a random slip chance: 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 or 0.4. Pip is not told which. Now the best habit has the best average over all those floors, so it cannot rely on any one. We find it by scoring all 64 possible habits on them, standing in for a learner.

sim2real:9.t: The randomised habit. The winner: run until two cells from the cheese, then walk. From cell 4 a run might skid past the cheese, so it walks; from 3 a skid lands on it, so it runs. On dry floor caution costs one step: 0.73 not 0.81. As in the fog reel, Pip can’t see the floor; remembering skids would not help: two clean runs don’t prove a dry floor.

sim2real:10.t: Back on the real track. 1000 real walks at slip chance 0.2. None meets the cat. Average return: 0.73, against 0.58 for the dry habit. In this toy, any single practice slip chance above about 0.05 gives the same safe habit; below that, running from cell 4 is still worth the risk. Randomising matters because nobody knows which value matches reality, and real worlds differ in many ways at once.

sim2real:11.t: Your turn. Drag the real slip chance; both habits face 1000 real walks. Across: slip chance; up: average return; shaded: the practised range. On a dry floor the dry habit wins, 0.81 to 0.73; from 0.1 on, the randomised one wins. The dry habit recovers a little on slick floors: early skids often carry it past cell 4, the only cell where a skid hits the cat.

sim2real:12.t: Not a free lunch. Why is the randomised line flat, even beyond 0.4? Walking never skids; a skid moves Pip three cells in two steps, so every walk takes four steps. Real robots aren’t: outside the randomised range, a policy can break. Too wide a range can cost too, though not here: slips up to 0.9 give the same habit. In real tasks it can make policies slow and cautious, or hard to learn.

sim2real:13.t: Real robots. In 2017, Josh Tobin and colleagues trained a network to locate objects using only simulated images, randomly coloured, textured and lit: not an R L policy, but the same idea. It worked on unseen real images, enough for a robot to grasp them. In 2018 and 2019, OpenAI trained a robot hand in randomised simulation to turn a block, then a Rubik’s cube. The real hand succeeded, though not always.

sim2real:14.t: Recap. A simulator makes practice fast, cheap and safe, but it never matches the real world exactly. A policy tuned to one exact copy can rely on details reality does not share: the reality gap. Domain randomisation practises on many randomised versions, so the real world is just one more of them. The price is some caution, and the range must cover reality.

rainbow:0.t: Rainbow: Dueling  and  Distributional D Q N. Six fixes for D Q N, stacked into one strong agent.

rainbow:1.t: Six upgrades. Pip’s D Q N has a replay memory, a frozen copy for the targets and, from the last reel, the Double D Q N trick. Each came from a different paper. In 2017 Matteo Hessel and colleagues at DeepMind stacked six such upgrades into one agent: Rainbow. This reel opens up two new ones in the meadow, dueling heads and distributional learning, then lists all six.

rainbow:2.t: Does the move matter?. Pip’s D Q N-reel network, run 1, after 8000 moves, no Double trick: at the bottom-left start its Q-values are 0.39, 0.32, 0.31, 0.34. Close: from out here, every move leaves a long way to go. Over the 30 test spots the best Q-value spans 0.41 to 0.95, but best and worst moves typically differ by only 0.17. Where Pip stands often matters more than which move.

rainbow:3.t: Spot plus move. Split each Q-value into a spot part, V, and a move part, its advantage A: Q equals V plus A. Shifting 0.1 between V and the A’s changes no Q, so the split needs a rule. The rule: subtract the four A’s average. V then equals the four Q’s plain average, the value of a random first move; not the values reel’s V, which weights moves by Pip’s choices.

rainbow:4.t: Two heads. A dueling network builds this into its shape (Ziyu Wang and colleagues, 2016). One hidden layer feeds two heads: one output for V, four for the advantages. Then Q equals V plus A minus average A. Trained like Pip’s D Q N, same seeds, it starts at V equals 0.39; the four A’s average minus 0.03. The Q-values come out 0.44, 0.35, 0.35, 0.41, averaging 0.39: the V.

rainbow:5.t: Why bother?. Each replay card is about one move: where Pip stood, which move, what followed. In a plain Q-network, it teaches that move’s output; shared hidden knobs nudge the other three only indirectly. In a dueling network, V sits inside every Q-value, so every card trains V directly, whatever the move. The advantage head only learns the differences, small in most of the meadow.

rainbow:6.t: Two maps. Dueling network, run 1, 8000 moves. Left: V at every spot, rising toward the cheese, lowest just below and left of the cat, where every route goes the long way round. Right: how much the move matters, largest advantage minus smallest. Strongest around the cat, where one wrong step costs a lot; palest bottom left and in a band below the cat, where moves are about equally good. The heads split the question as hoped.

rainbow:7.t: A fair race. Does it learn faster? Eight runs each, same seeds for starts, wobble and random moves, same 30 test spots, tested every 500 moves. After 8000 moves: 26.6 of 30 for plain, 27.9 for dueling. Single runs spread widely, so this gap is within the noise: about equal with four moves. Wang and colleagues saw clearer gains on Atari, with up to 18 moves.

rainbow:8.t: One spot, many futures. Now the second upgrade. From one spot, below and right of the cat, Pip walks 1000 times, following its network, one move in five random. Each walk ends on the cheese, the cat, or after 60 moves. A walk’s return is the final plus 1 or minus 1, discounted by 0.9 per move before it: cheese after 3 moves gives 0.81. Drawn: six cheese walks, two cat walks. Same spot, same habit, different luck.

rainbow:9.t: A histogram of returns. Now sort all 1000 returns into a histogram. Across: the return, minus 1 to plus 1, in slices 0.1 wide. Height: how many walks landed in that slice. Gold bars are walks that reached the cheese: 935 of them, spread by how many moves they took. Rose bars on the far left are walks that met the cat: 65. None ran out of time.

rainbow:10.t: The average hides it. A Q-value keeps just one number: the average return, here 0.56. Only 249 of the 1000 walks came within 0.1 of it; the rest scattered, the cat walks far off on the left. And it hides the risk: 7% of walks from here end on the cat. A single number cannot say whether 0.56 is a sure thing or a gamble.

rainbow:11.t: Same average, different risk. Force the first move from the same spot, then carry on. Up first, past the cat’s edge: average 0.50. Down first, away from it: 0.47. Almost the same. But up meets the cat in 11% of walks, down in only 4%. Nearly equal averages, very different risks. Unforced, the network goes right here; down averages slightly lower because its way round is longer.

rainbow:12.t: Learning a histogram. Distributional R L learns the whole histogram for every move (Marc Bellemare, Will Dabney and Rémi Munos, 2017). Their C 51 network gives each move the chances of 51 fixed return values. Target: Pip moved right, reward 0; take the landing spot’s histogram, squeeze it toward 0 by 0.9, add the reward. Ours come from walks; real C 51 learns them, using the best move where it landed.

rainbow:13.t: Back onto the bins. The squeezed bars no longer sit on the fixed return values. So each is split between its two nearest fixed values, more to the nearer. Now the target is again one chance per fixed value. The network’s histogram for that move is then nudged toward the target. The loss, cross-entropy, measures how far apart the histograms are, as squared error did for two numbers.

rainbow:14.t: Why it helps. Pip still picks moves by the average, which the histogram contains. Yet on Atari, learning the whole shape scored clearly better than the average alone. Why is still debated; perhaps the histogram is a much richer lesson per card. It also opens the door to risk-aware choices, like preferring the move that rarely meets the cat, though C 51 itself did not do that.

rainbow:15.t: Your turn. Tap any spot on the meadow. Pip walks from there 400 times, following its network with one move in five random, and the histogram of returns appears below, with its average. Try spots in open grass, then spots touching the cat’s circle, then spots right next to the cheese. Where is the average a fair summary, and where does it hide a cat?

rainbow:16.t: All six. You have seen four of the six: Double D Q N, dueling heads, distributional learning, and prioritised replay, mentioned in the replay reel. The other two: multi-step targets use three real rewards, discounted, then 0.9 cubed times a guess. Noisy networks add random wiggles to the knobs, learn how big they should be, and pick greedily on the wiggled Q-values, instead of one random move in five.

rainbow:17.t: What mattered. On 57 Atari games, Rainbow beat every one of its parts alone, and needed much less experience than D Q N to reach D Q N’s final scores. Removing one part at a time, prioritised replay and multi-step targets hurt most, distributional learning next. Dueling and Double D Q N changed the median game little (scores scaled to a human player’s), though some games cared. Small, compatible upgrades can add up.

rainbow:18.t: Recap. A dueling network splits each Q-value into the value of the spot, V, and the advantage of each move, A, with the average advantage subtracted so the split is unique. V learns from every card. Distributional R L learns the whole histogram of returns, which an average hides. Rainbow combined six upgrades to D Q N, and together they worked better than any one alone.

a2c:0.t: A 2 C  and  A 3 C. Many players learning at once beats one player alone.

a2c:1.t: One Pip, one maze. Same maze as the actor-critic reel: plus 1 for the cheese, minus 1 for the cat, either ends the walk, gamma (gamma) 0.9, and a walk is stopped after 100 moves. Pip is an actor, its chances, and a critic, its notebook. After every move the critic’s T D error grades that move. Everything Pip learns comes from one walk at a time, one move after another.

a2c:2.t: Look-alike moments. Consecutive moves look alike: Pip is still in one corner. In 8 moves in a row it visits only 3.7 different cells on average, chances still all a quarter. So successive updates push the same few cells. In Pip’s table, with separate numbers per cell, that is mild. In a neural network, where all situations share numbers, look-alike updates can drag it one way.

a2c:3.t: Copies of the maze. The fix: run many copies of the maze at once. Each has its own Pip, a worker, with its own dice: here 8. But all workers share one set of chances and one critic. Whatever one worker’s moves teach, every worker uses from then on. A worker whose walk ends just starts anew and plays on.

a2c:4.t: A varied batch. Now take one move from each worker at the same moment. The workers drift apart, so their cells differ: on average 5.8 different cells among 8 moves, against 3.7 for one worker’s 8 moves in a row. Each update then mixes many situations at once. That is the first reason for workers: varied data.

a2c:5.t: A 2 C: play, wait, update. In A 2 C, each worker plays 5 moves with the shared chances and waits; the 40 moves are pooled. Each move’s push uses its T D error, with the critic from the round’s start. One update averages the workers’ summed pushes: chances move by step 4, the critic by 0.4. A 2 C means advantage actor-critic: the T D error plays the baseline reel’s advantage. This lock-step version is synchronous.

a2c:6.t: Why average?. One worker’s 5 moves carry one walk’s luck; averaging 8 workers cancels much of it, steadying each update’s direction. So steps can be big: actor 4, critic 0.4, pushes summed over each worker’s 5 moves. Alone, one worker is the actor-critic reel’s method, updated every 5 moves at about four times its step: too big, as the next charts show. With eight it works; one worker with smaller steps is steadier but slow.

a2c:7.t: Two clocks. For a clock: a move takes one tick, but one move in four takes two: 1.25 ticks on average. Eight workers on eight computers: at most 6.4 moves per tick. In A 2 C the fast also wait for the slowest, 19 percent of the time, leaving about 5.2. Top: a 4-worker run’s first 30 ticks; bars moving, dots waiting. Chart: across, ticks; up, the start’s expected return, computed with the rulebook Pip never sees.

a2c:8.t: One worker against eight. 100 runs each, same dice. With step 4, one worker (grey) reaches 0.31 on average after 2500 ticks, and 42 of 100 runs are still below 0.4. Eight workers (teal): 0.52, 0 runs below 0.4. Dashed: one worker with both steps four times smaller. It is steadier but slow: 0.06 after 2500 ticks. On this clock, eight workers end far higher, and steadier.

a2c:9.t: Count moves, not ticks. Same runs, but across is moves gathered by all workers together, up to 2,000. By then one worker with step 4 is at 0.31 on average; eight workers have only reached 0.03. So workers do not make Pip learn from fewer moves. They buy clock speed, moving in parallel, and steadier updates, but need many computers or cores.

a2c:10.t: Your turn. Drag the workers: 1, 2, 4 or 8, all A 2 C with step 4, 100 runs each, on the tick clock. Watch the curve and the runs below 0.4. 1 to 2 workers helps a lot, 4 more still; 8 gains nothing here: 4 workers end at 0.53 with 14% waiting, 8 at 0.52 with 19%. Averaging 20 moves is already steady enough, and 8 workers make each round a little longer.

a2c:11.t: A 3 C: no waiting. A 3 C, asynchronous advantage actor-critic (Mnih and colleagues, 2016), never waits. Each worker copies the shared numbers, plays its 5 moves, and sends its update the moment it is done, then copies the latest numbers and goes on. Top: A 2 C, 4 workers: bars are a worker’s 5 moves, dotted lines waiting, black lines shared updates. Bottom: A 3 C, each black dot one worker’s update.

a2c:12.t: Stale copies. The catch: while a worker plays, others update, so its copy goes stale. White numbers count missed updates: 3.0 on average with 4 workers, 7.0 with 8. Why does A 3 C work, when one worker’s push was too big? Each push uses step 4 divided by 8 workers: 0.5. Eight small pushes make about one A 2 C update, arriving one by one. With 8 workers: A 3 C ends at 0.527, A 2 C at 0.525, best 0.531; at 1,000 ticks, 0.32 against 0.15.

a2c:13.t: A 2 C or A 3 C?. A 3 C ran its workers on one ordinary computer’s cores, no graphics card, and on Atari beat earlier graphics-card agents in about half their training time. A year later OpenAI found synchronous A 2 C did as well, its one big batch per update suiting graphics cards. Our toy has none, so it shows only the costs: A 2 C’s waiting, A 3 C’s stale copies. Real speed depends on hardware.

a2c:14.t: Where it went. Running many copies of the world in parallel became standard. P P O, the next big method in this track, is usually trained exactly this way, with anything from 8 copies on a laptop to thousands in large labs. The asynchronous style lives on in large distributed systems such as IMPALA (2018), which corrects for the stale chances its workers act with.

a2c:15.t: Recap. Workers run copies of the world in parallel and share one actor and one critic. Their moves are more varied, and averaging their pushes steadies each update. A 2 C waits for all workers and makes one update per round. A 3 C lets each worker update on its own, with slightly stale copies. Workers save time on the clock, not moves.

trpo:0.t: T R P O: Trust Regions. Improve the policy, but never jump too far at once.

trpo:1.t: Pip’s policy, as chances. Same maze, dry floor: plus 1 onto the cheese, minus 1 onto the cat, both end the walk, gamma (gamma) 0.9. Walks still going after 100 steps stop and score 0. Pip holds four chances per cell, the arrows. After 10 ordinary updates from blank, its score, the expected return from the start, from the rulebook, is 0.36. The best: 0.53, seven steps straight to the cheese.

trpo:2.t: One update. Each update, Pip walks 10 times with its current chances: a batch, where REINFORCE used one walk. For each move it asks: did things go better than usual from here? That is the move’s advantage: the return after the move minus the critic’s value of the cell, the simplest grade. The critic here is exact, so we watch the actor alone.

trpo:3.t: What the batch says at the start. At the start Pip moved up 10 times. Twice, that walk later met the cat: advantages minus 0.59 and minus 0.79. Down and left both bump a wall, wasting a step, yet after 5 of 8 down bumps the walk went better than usual by luck. So: less up, more of two useless moves. Summed: up minus 0.55, down 0.31, left 0.19. Right was never tried.

trpo:4.t: A normal step. For each batch move, the move made gains alpha (alpha) times advantage times (1 minus its chance) in preference; each other move loses alpha times advantage times its chance. Divide by the 10 walks. Usual step: alpha equals 3. At the start, up drops from 0.55 to 0.49, down rises from 0.24 to 0.28, and other batch moves make the top row surer of right. Score: 0.36 to 0.39.

trpo:5.t: Why not a bigger step?. If a small step helps, a bigger one should help more and learn faster. Same batch, same direction, but alpha equals 100: about 33 times bigger. At the start, up falls from 0.55 to 0.00 and down climbs to 0.85. Pip now mostly walks into the wall. The score crashes from 0.36 to 0.01.

trpo:6.t: Bump, bump, bump. With the new chances, Pip bumps into the bottom wall again and again. In its next batch, 8 of 10 walks hit the 100-step limit and score 0. After the normal step, none did. The wrecked policy now collects poor walks, and poor walks are what it must learn from next.

trpo:7.t: Climbing back is slow. Both policies now keep learning with the usual alpha equals 3. The chart shows the score after each update: teal continues from the normal step, rose from the big one. The dashed line is the best possible, 0.53. The teal line reaches 0.51 after 40 updates. The rose line stays below 0.1 for 3 more updates, and is still only at 0.41 after 40.

trpo:8.t: The batch is a local map. Why did the batch mislead? Its advice is a slope: which way to nudge each preference, measured at the old policy. A slope is reliable only near where it was measured, and all its walks came from the old policy. The chart steps along that direction by different sizes, scored exactly. Small steps help, up to about alpha equals 5; further out the same advice hurts: at 100 the score is 0.01.

trpo:9.t: How far is too far?. So limit how far one update may move. But measure it in behaviour, not in preference numbers. In a cell with all preferences 0, adding 2 to up lifts its chance from 0.25 to 0.71. If up’s preference is already 10, the same plus 2 leaves its chance at 1.00. What matters is how different the chances become.

trpo:10.t: Surprise. First, a way to score one choice. The surprise at a choice is minus the log of its chance. A sure thing, chance 1, surprises 0. Chance one half gives 0.69, one quarter 1.39, one tenth 2.30. Rarer choices surprise more, without limit as the chance shrinks to 0. The curve shows surprise against chance.

trpo:11.t: K L divergence. The batch came from old Pip. How much less likely is new Pip to make old Pip’s moves? Per move, log of old chance over new; averaged by old Pip’s chances, that is the K L divergence, 0 for identical policies. At the start, new Pip almost never goes up, which old Pip did 0.55 of the time: that term alone is 4.01. The others add minus 0.18; single terms can be negative, never the total. K L 3.83; after the normal step, 0.007.

trpo:12.t: The trust region rule. T R P O, Trust Region Policy Optimization (Schulman and colleagues, 2015), turns this into a rule: improve as the batch suggests, but keep the K L under a limit, commonly 0.01. The K L is computed in each visited cell, then averaged over visits. Here the big step’s average K L is 3.47. Even the normal step, 0.026, is over, though harmless: 0.01 is a large-network habit, stricter than this maze needs.

trpo:13.t: Halve until it fits. Real T R P O computes a step that just fits, with heavier maths. Our toy halves the big step until the K L fits and the batch still predicts a gain: the sum of each move’s advantage times new chance divided by old chance must beat the old policy’s. Here: six halvings, from 100 to 1.56, K L 0.008. Score 0.36 to 0.38, a bit below the plain alpha equals 3 step: safety costs some speed.

trpo:14.t: Forty updates, fifty runs. From a blank policy, 40 updates, averaged over 50 runs with different dice. Rose: plain alpha equals 100. Teal: plain alpha equals 3. Blue: T R P O, limit 0.01, halving from 100. Big plain steps: 46 of 50 runs stuck near 0. Small ones: 0.32 after 10 updates, 0.50 after 40. T R P O starts slower, 0.17 after 10, as early on only steps of about 1 to 3 fit. It ends at 0.53, every run within 0.02 of the best, none stuck.

trpo:15.t: Which part does the work?. T R P O here halves the step and checks the K L. Which prevents the crashes? Rose keeps the halving and gain check but drops the K L check. Without the K L check, 46 of 50 runs get stuck, as bad as plain big steps. The batch predicts a gain even for huge steps: on the first update, 50 of 50 took the full alpha equals 100. The K L limit does the work.

trpo:16.t: Your turn. Drag the K L limit. Each setting reruns the same 50 runs of T R P O from a blank policy, always halving from alpha equals 100. The line is the average score; the card counts runs stuck near 0. Tiny limits are safe but crawl. Big limits let the big steps through: at limit 1, 15 of 50 runs get stuck.

trpo:17.t: A limit that adapts, at a price. A fixed small alpha also worked here, but the safe alpha changes as Pip learns. In run 0 the first 10 updates fit only steps of 0.78 to 3.13; later the full 100 fit, as chances near 0 or 1 make the (1 minus chance) factors and advantages small. The cost: at the old policy the K L is 0 and flat, so its curvature sets its growth. Real T R P O computes that curvature with second-order maths, slow and fiddly for big networks.

trpo:18.t: Where it was used. In 2015 T R P O trained simulated robots to swim, hop and walk, and played several Atari games straight from the screen pixels. Its steady improvement made it a standard baseline. In 2017 Schulman and colleagues, now at OpenAI, introduced P P O, which keeps the “don’t move too far” idea with a much simpler trick. P P O then largely replaced T R P O in practice.

trpo:19.t: Recap. A step that is too big can wreck a good policy, and the wrecked policy then collects poor walks to learn from. A batch’s advice is a local map: trust it only near the old policy. T R P O measures how far a step goes by the K L divergence between old and new chances, and only accepts steps within a limit.

muzero:0.t: MuZero. Plan like AlphaZero, without being told the rules.
