muzero:1.t: Searching without a rulebook. Look again at AlphaZero’s search. Every loop, it plays moves by the rules to reach a new position, and the rules say when a game is won. Pip held the rulebook. Atari games, robots and most real problems come with no rulebook. Can Pip still search ahead? MuZero says yes: learn your own model of what moves do, and search inside it.

muzero:2.t: What should the model predict?. Predicting the next board exactly would mean every pixel of a game screen, mostly irrelevant details. MuZero predicts only what the search uses: the reward a move pays, the value of where it leads, and a prior over next moves. Like the world-models reel it plans in a learned model, but never predicts the board, and a search uses it, not a dream-trained policy.

muzero:3.t: Three small networks. h reads the real board once and turns it into a hidden state: here 18 numbers, bars above the line positive, below negative. g, the dynamics, takes a hidden state and a move and imagines the next one, plus that move’s reward. f, the prediction, takes any hidden state and gives a prior and a value, like AlphaZero’s network. Ours: 5,519 knobs in all.

muzero:4.t: Rewards and values here. A game-ending move pays its result as a reward: 1 for Pip’s win,  one half for a draw, 0 for a cat win; other moves pay 0. The value is the points still to come: 0 after the game. A move’s worth is reward plus the value where it leads, undiscounted; at the cat’s turns the search uses 1 minus that. AlphaZero’s value held the final result; MuZero must predict it as a reward.

muzero:5.t: Imagining a line. From Pip’s puzzle, h reads the board; g imagines five moves: Pip top right, cat bottom right, Pip centre, cat middle left, Pip bottom left. MuZero never sees those boards; we draw them faded. Predicted rewards: 0.00, 0.00, 0.02, 0.00, then 0.95 on the last move, which really completes Pip’s diagonal; then value 0.00. Earlier values stay below 1 on this sure win: f learned from a half-random player’s games.

muzero:6.t: Searching inside the model. MuZero runs AlphaZero’s search with the model in place of the rules. Each new node: hidden state and reward from g, prior and value from f. Only the top is real: there the game says which squares are empty, as in the paper. Deeper, all 9 moves are allowed. Never told when an imagined game ends, the model should predict reward and value near 0 after a win, so further moves add nothing.

muzero:7.t: How the model learns. Replay a recorded position’s next 3 real moves inside the model, from h. Each imagined step is checked against reality: the reward paid, how the game ended, the move played. Past a game’s end, targets are reward 0 and value 0. Errors flow back through f, g and h, with cross-entropy for move shares, as in AlphaZero. So the hidden state holds whatever predicts those three things; nobody says what its 18 numbers mean.

muzero:8.t: Our toy is simplified. Real MuZero learns from its own search’s games, as AlphaZero did; too slow in a browser. So this toy learns from 3,000 recorded games by a player perfect half the time, random otherwise; the move played is the policy target. Training ran beforehand: 960,000 lessons of 3 unrolled moves, weights stored in the reel. Beyond legal moves at the top, it never sees the rules.

muzero:9.t: Did it learn what matters?. For every Pip move in every position: of 1,834 instant wins, g predicts reward above one half for 1,550; of 6,717 non-ending moves, below one half for 6,345. The other 372 are imagined wins the search may chase. The 80 draws average 0.50. Untold what three in a row is, it learned most of it from which moves ended games, since that helped predict rewards.

muzero:10.t: The puzzle, searched in its head. The search runs 50 loops inside the model: 18 through top right, 8 through the centre, 11 through bottom right, which loses against best play. All 50 go through a move; the top is judged first. It plays top right: average 0.81, with the centre close at 0.76. Every position below the top was imagined: no rules, no real boards. Still, it finds the winning move, as the real-rules searches did.

muzero:11.t: How good is it?. On 200 random positions where the choice matters, f’s prior alone picks a best move in 138; 50 loops in the model, 148. Model or imitation training to blame? Same h and f searching real rules instead of g: 197. Against a perfect player: 17 losses of 60 in the model, 2 with real rules. So model errors are the main cost; its search even lost the prior’s right move in 19 positions, fixing 29.

muzero:12.t: Your turn. Tap squares to imagine moves from Pip’s puzzle, Pip and cat taking turns. Each tap runs g once: you see the predicted reward and the value after it. The faded board, unseen by MuZero, shows what really happens. Try the winning line, or a move onto a taken square. The model was never told that is impossible. Tap the reset note to start again.

muzero:13.t: Where it is used. MuZero came from Julian Schrittwieser and colleagues at DeepMind, in Nature in 2020 after a 2019 preprint. Given legal moves but not rules, it matched AlphaZero in chess, shogi and Go, and set a new best on 57 Atari games, priors over joystick moves, rewards in game points. Later versions learned from fixed records of past play, and one was trialled compressing YouTube videos.

muzero:14.t: Recap. MuZero searches like AlphaZero, but inside a model it learned. h turns the board into a hidden state, g imagines a move’s next state and reward, f gives a prior and a value. The model is trained only to predict rewards, results and moves, never to draw the board. So it keeps what matters for choosing moves, and the search trusts it, errors included.

successor:0.t: Successor Features. Know where you’ll go, and new goals cost almost nothing.

successor:1.t: Back in the maze. Same maze, habit and rules as the T D reel: dry floor, arrows plus one random move in five, plus 1 for cheese, minus 1 for cat, gamma (gamma) 0.9. T D’s 200 walks gave this notebook: 0.98 left of the cheese, 0.34 at the start: how good each cell is under this habit, for this cheese. Noisy: the true values are 0.87 and 0.40, and that noise follows us all reel.

successor:2.t: What if the cheese moves?. Tomorrow someone swaps the cheese and the cat. Walls, habit, the two ending cells: all the same. Only what the ending cells pay has changed. Pip’s notebook is now wrong almost everywhere, because each number mixes two things together: where Pip tends to go, and what it finds there. Plain T D would have to unlearn and relearn, walk by walk.

successor:3.t: Two questions. So keep the two apart. Question one: from here, where will I go? That depends only on the maze and Pip’s habit. Question two: what does each cell pay? That is the part that changed. Like knowing your town’s streets: whether today you want the bakery or the pool, the streets you would walk are the same. Only the errand changes.

successor:4.t: Counting future visits. Answer question one by counting. Walk 1: Pip steps into cell 11, then 6, reaching the cheese on step 7. Score each cell stepped into: 1 for the next step, 0.9 for the one after, 0.81 next, one more 0.9 per step. That is reward discounting. The cheese cell gets 0.9 multiplied 6 times: 0.53. Ending cells count too; then the walk is over.

successor:5.t: Pip’s map from the start. One walk is luck. Averaged over all walks from the start, these scores are Pip’s map: 1.12 above the start, over 1 since Pip can return, 0.43 at the cheese, 0.03 at the cat. This is Peter Dayan’s 1993 successor representation. The start gets 0.17, from walks wandering back; counting begins at the next step, matching “reward on arrival”. Computed with the rulebook, as a check.

successor:6.t: Value from the map. Now question two. Each cell’s pay on arrival: cheese plus 1, cat minus 1, others 0; this works because pay depends only on the landing cell. Multiply each cell’s visits by its pay, and add up. From the start: 0.43 times 1 plus 0.03 times ( minus 1) equals 0.40. That is exactly the start’s value under this habit, the number the sweeps found in the earlier reels.

successor:7.t: Learning the map by T D. Without the rulebook, Pip learns the map by T D, a row of 18 per open cell. After each step, the left cell’s row moves toward 1 at the landing cell plus 0.9 times the landing row, or just the 1 if the walk ended. It is T D with “I arrived” as reward. First step: Pip lands in cell 11, whose row is all 0, so the start’s entry for it moves a fifth of the way to 1: 0.2.

successor:8.t: 200 walks later. After the same walks, the start row: 1.23 above the start, 0.41 at the cheese, 0.07 at the cat; near the rulebook’s map on the usual route, rougher elsewhere. Times the pays, every cell matches the T D notebook exactly: 0.34 at the start. Same walks, same alpha, and a linear update: it equals T D’s term by term. With fixed rewards the map buys nothing; it pays off when rewards change.

successor:9.t: The swap. Cheese and cat trade places. Habit and walls are unchanged, so Pip keeps its map and only rewrites the pays: plus 1 at the old cat cell, minus 1 at the old cheese, and multiplies again. With no new walk: the start reads minus 0.34, the cell left of the old cheese minus 0.98. The pays just swapped, so every value flips sign; the next example is less tidy.

successor:10.t: Relearning, the slow way. Plain T D has only its old notebook; let it walk 200 more times. Gold: its average distance from the true new values under the old habit. Dashed teal: instant re-weighting, 0.26 off. T D starts 0.96 off; its start value turns negative only after walk 34; after 200 walks it is 0.29 off. Both share a fixed alpha’s noise; the map got there at once.

successor:11.t: Any new reward. Rewards can change anywhere, not only at ending cells. Restore cheese and cat, and add a crumb in cell 6, on Pip’s usual route: plus 0.5 each time Pip steps on it, and the walk goes on. Same map, new pays: the start’s value jumps from 0.34 to 0.86 at once, as the map says Pip visits that cell often and early. The rulebook says 0.89.

successor:12.t: Your turn. Tap a cell to put a crumb there, worth plus 0.5 each time Pip steps onto it. Tap it again to take it away. Pip’s values come straight from its learned map times the new pays, with no new walks. Crumbs on the usual route lift many cells; crumbs in corners Pip rarely visits barely matter, because the map gives them few visits.

successor:13.t: The catch. The map belongs to the habit. After the swap, Pip’s arrows still march to the old cheese corner, now the cat’s. A better habit would take other routes, and a new habit means a new map, relearned at least in part. To improve the habit without the rulebook, keep a map per move, like Q-values, as Q-learning does. The successor representation makes new rewards cheap, not new habits.

successor:14.t: Successor features. Big worlds have too many cells to map. Successor features (André Barreto and colleagues, 2017) map future amounts of a few features, like food or water; a task weights each feature, and value is map times weights. Keep several old habits’ maps. For a new task each value comes instantly; at every spot, follow the best-looking habit. This generalised policy improvement beats or ties every old habit.

successor:15.t: A map in the brain?. The hippocampus holds place cells: neurons that fire when an animal is in a particular place. Kimberly Stachenfeld, Matthew Botvinick and Samuel Gershman (2017) proposed they hold a predictive map like Pip’s, firing for where the animal will likely go, not just where it is. This fits some recordings, like place fields stretching backward along a habitual path. How far it goes is still debated.

successor:16.t: Recap. The successor representation splits value into a map of where Pip will go, discounted future visits to every cell under its habit, and what each cell pays. Value is visits times pay, added up. The map is learned by T D, with “I arrived here” in place of the reward. When rewards change, new values come instantly; when the habit changes, the map must be relearned.

contextual:0.t: Contextual Bandits. Same slot machines, but now you know who’s playing.

contextual:1.t: Open late. The cheese arcade now stays open 10 am to 10 pm, with one new rule: the chances drift with the hour. Pulls happen in its 12 opening hours, 10:00 to 21:00. At 10:00 they match the earlier reels: A 30, B 55, C 70, D 15 percent. C fades through the day, D wakes up; by 21:00, A 25, B 45, C 25, D 80.

contextual:2.t: Who is best, and when. The four chances through the day: across, the hour; up, the chance of a crumb. Each machine’s line runs straight from morning to night. Dots mark the best machine each hour: C until 14:00, B at 15:00, D from 16:00. Pulling the best one every hour would drop a crumb on 63 percent of pulls.

contextual:3.t: One winner for everyone?. Each pull now comes at a random opening hour. A plain bandit ignores the clock and hunts the single best machine on average: B, at 50 percent, with C and D close behind at 48 percent. Even finding B perfectly gives crumbs on 50 percent of pulls, against 63 percent for the best-for-the-hour plan. One winner for everyone leaves crumbs on the table.

contextual:4.t: Look at the clock first. Information seen before choosing is the context: here, the hour, like a state your pulls cannot change. A contextual bandit sees the context, picks an arm, gets a reward, and learns the best arm for each kind of situation. One thing stays simple: Pip’s pull doesn’t change when the next pull happens. When actions shape future situations, you need full reinforcement learning.

contextual:5.t: A row for each part of the day. The simplest fix: keep separate tallies for each context. Split the day into two rows, 10:00 to 15:00 and 16:00 to 21:00, and run U C B in each row on its own, as if each were its own arcade. Each row starts from scratch: it first pulls every machine once, then follows estimate plus bonus, using only that row’s pulls.

contextual:6.t: Each row settles. After 1000 pulls in this visit, the morning row pulled C 297 times out of 480, and the evening row pulled D 380 times out of 520. Each row found its own winner. Within a row the hours still differ: at 15:00 B is best, but only by one percentage point over C, so lumping 15:00 in with the morning costs very little.

contextual:7.t: Keeping score. Regret now compares pulls with the best machine at that hour: a pull of D gives up 0.70 minus 0.15 at 10:00, nothing at 21:00. Over 2000 visits of 1000 pulls: clock-blind U C B, grey, ends at 158; two rows of U C B, gold, 85. A row player already knowing its best machine would lose under 1 crumb per 1000 pulls, so nearly all is learning’s cost.

contextual:8.t: Finer rows?. Why not one row per hour? Such rows are exactly right about their hour, but learning is the real cost, and each of twelve sees only one pull in twelve, from scratch. Twelve rows end at 125 regret after 1000 pulls: worse than two. More rows, less data in each. Real contexts, like a visitor’s age, place and history, would need millions of rows.

contextual:9.t: Share what you learn: a line. Instead of rows, give each machine a straight line: chance equals start plus slope times lateness, lateness running from 0 at 10:00 to 1 at 21:00. Every pull of D, at any hour, helps place D’s line. Here are D’s 45 results from one visit’s first 100 pulls, placed at their hour: top for a crumb, bottom for nothing. The line is the best fit.

contextual:10.t: Lin U C B: a line plus a bonus. To explore, add a bonus, like U C B. The shaded band shows each line’s doubt: narrow where a machine’s pulls pile up near that hour, wide where they are few, like U C B’s bonus shrinking with n. Score: line plus half the band. This is Lin U C B (Li, Chu, Langford and Schapire, 2010). Lines start flat at 0, so untried machines get tried only for their wide bands.

contextual:11.t: Lines win. Lin U C B, in purple, ends at 24 after 1000 pulls, far below two rows (85) and twelve rows (125). Be fair to the rows, though: here the true chances really are straight lines, so the line model fits perfectly. When the real pattern is curved, a line can be wrong for some hours however much data it gets; then richer models, even neural networks, are used.

contextual:12.t: Your turn. Drag the hour: Lin U C B’s lines after 1000 pulls of one visit, with its scores and pick. A and B were pulled only 3 times each and dropped nothing, so their lines sit at 0; only wide bands keep them in the running. Try 15:00. B is truly best (50%), but Lin U C B picks D (45%), missing by about 6 percentage points.

contextual:13.t: The fine print. A bandit sees only the pulled arm’s result. With rows, if Pip never pulled A in the evening, it has no evening data on A. A line can guess from morning pulls, but only if a line is the right shape. The same gap bites later: old records show only the old strategy’s choices, so testing a new strategy on them fairly takes care.

contextual:14.t: Where it is used. In 2010, Lin U C B chose which news stories to show on the Yahoo! front page. In the authors’ tests, it earned about 12.5 percent more clicks than a bandit that ignored the context. Contextual bandits now help choose ads, recommendations and notification times, and are studied for personalised treatments in medicine. The context is whatever you know about the user and the moment.

contextual:15.t: Recap. A contextual bandit looks at the context before choosing, because the best arm can depend on the situation. Few contexts: keep a row of tallies for each and run a bandit per row. Many contexts: learn a model that shares data, like Lin U C B’s line plus bonus. Either way, the pull does not change the next context.

dt:0.t: Decision Transformer. What if R L were just predicting the next word?

dt:1.t: A box of old diaries. Pip finds a box of 40 diaries. Each records one walk by the Wanderer, the mouse from earlier reels who moves at random, bumping into walls. Pip may not walk itself; it can only learn from these pages, as in the offline R L reel. In this box, 2 walks reached the cheese, 8 met the cat, and the other 30 were stopped after 30 moves.

dt:2.t: Rules for this reel. Same maze, dry floor, new scoring: each move costs 0.05; the cheese pays plus 1, the cat minus 1, either ends the walk. Rewards are summed, undiscounted: a Decision Transformer works with plain totals, so the total still wanted drops by each reward. So shorter is better. The best walk takes 7 moves: 1 minus 7 times 0.05 equals 0.65. The box’s best diary scores only minus 0.10.

dt:3.t: Return-to-go. The key number is the return-to-go: the total still to come. Here is the box’s best diary: 22 moves, 7 of them bumps into walls or rocks. At the start it is minus 0.10, the whole total. Each paid move cost is no longer to come, so it creeps up by 0.05. On the last move the cheese arrives, leaving 0.

dt:4.t: A walk as a sentence. Write each diary step as three tokens: the return-to-go, the cell, the move. The return-to-go enters as a plain number; each token becomes numbers the network reads. A walk becomes a sentence. Cells run 1 to 20, as in the loop reel; the start is 16. A transformer, the network behind chatbots, predicts the next move token, as a chatbot predicts the next word.

dt:5.t: Training is plain prediction. Training needs no values or Bellman updates: the model just predicts the logged move from what came before. Simple and stable: no values feeding on their own guesses, which inflated numbers in the offline R L reel. Ours is a stand-in lookup: in this cell, copy the most common move of diary steps whose return-to-go is closest to the total still wanted, up on ties. A real network also reads recent steps and generalises.

dt:6.t: Ask for 0.65. Now ask for the best total, 0.65. In cell 16 the closest return-to-go is 0.40, from a diary back in cell 16 late in its walk, so Pip copies up. After each move Pip subtracts its reward from the total still wanted, and looks again. Pip reaches the cheese in 7 moves: 0.65, beating every diary in the box, whose best scored minus 0.10.

dt:7.t: Pieces of different walks. How can it beat every diary? At each cell it copies a step from whichever diary fits the total still wanted, and those steps came from 2 different diaries, the box’s only 2 that reached the cheese. Pieces of different walks make a better one: stitching. The Decision Transformer paper saw this too: trained only on random walks, asking a high return gave short paths.

dt:8.t: Ask for less. The number is a dial. Ask for 0, and Pip reaches the cheese the long way, in 20 moves: 0.00. Ask for minus 1.5, and it wanders until it is stopped after 30 moves: minus 1.50. Nobody wants a bad walk, but it shows the model really listens to the total it is given.

dt:9.t: Asked versus got. Requests run from minus 1.5 to 1 in 0.05 steps. Across: the total asked. Up: the total got; on the dashed diagonal they match. Below minus 0.5 Pip always wanders until stopped, minus 1.50. No diary made a quick trip to the cat: the quickest of 8 cat walks took 10 moves. From minus 0.5 to 0.65 the dots sit on the diagonal. Above, they stay flat: asking 1 still gives 0.65. No better walk exists to copy.

dt:10.t: Only what is in the box. Another box, where no diary ever reached the cheese. Ask for 0.65 and Pip wanders until stopped: minus 1.50. No total, however high, can produce cheese steps never written down. A copier is limited by its data’s pieces. Value learning on that box reaches no cheese either: it heads for the cat in 5 moves, minus 1.25, the least bad ending it has seen.

dt:11.t: When pieces do not join. A third box holds every piece of the 7-move route. Asked for 0.65, Pip still takes 9 moves: 0.55. In cell 11 the closest return-to-go came from a diary going right, the long way. Value learning, here a table over logged moves only, so nothing is invented, finds 0.65: a move’s value is its reward plus the best value where it lands, so good endings flow back through shared cells. The lookup joins pieces only when the countdown lines up.

dt:12.t: A hundred boxes. Now 100 boxes per size: 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80 diaries. Across: diaries per box. Up: boxes of 100 giving the 7-move walk. Grey: a single diary already was it. Blue: the lookup asked for 0.65. Green: value learning. Both join pieces far beyond any single diary. The lookup is less reliable: with 40 diaries, 78 boxes against 85.

dt:13.t: Your turn. Drag the total to ask for, and Pip plays it from the start, in the first box. Tap the maze to switch to the third box, where the pieces do not line up. Watch where it lands below 0.65, and what happens when you ask for more than the maze allows.

dt:14.t: Where it came from. Lili Chen and colleagues introduced the Decision Transformer in 2021, alongside the similar Trajectory Transformer. On offline Atari and robot benchmarks, it matched that era’s offline R L methods. Later studies found stitching unreliable, as here, and that in worlds with chance it copies merely lucky moves: on a wet floor, a lucky slide carries a high return-to-go, so a high request copies it. Its appeal: training is plain, stable prediction.

dt:15.t: Recap. A Decision Transformer treats R L as sequence prediction: write each logged step as return-to-go, state and action, and learn to predict the action. At play time, ask for a high return and subtract rewards as they arrive. It can join pieces of walks, but less reliably than value learning, and it cannot use pieces the data never had.

grpo:0.t: R L for L L M Reasoning (G R P O). Let the model try, let a checker grade it, repeat.

grpo:1.t: Bot’s homework. Bot, the answer machine from the R L H F reel, now helps Pip with sums like 4 plus 7 times 3. These can be checked by a program: compute the true value, compare the final number. Right scores 1, wrong 0. No people comparing answers, no learned reward model to fool: just a cheap, exact check, a verifiable reward. A checker can still have loopholes; more later.

grpo:2.t: Four ways to answer. A real language model writes its working word by word. Bot is a stand-in: it picks one of four ways of answering, each with a chance, learned by copying examples. Guess a number. Work left to right, which goes wrong whenever times follows plus. Do times first, with an occasional slip. Or do times first and then check, which catches most slips.

grpo:3.t: How good is each way?. Only the simulation knows this. On 400 test sums, half like 3 plus 5, half like 3 plus 5 times 2: guessing gets 0.18 right, left to right 0.50, times first 0.89, times first and check 0.97. Bot starts with chances 0.30, 0.40, 0.20 and 0.10, in the same order: 0.53 right overall. Bot never sees this table, only the checker’s 1s and 0s.

grpo:4.t: A group of eight. Take one question, 7 plus 8 times 7. Bot answers it 8 times, a group, each time picking its way of answering by chance. The checker marks each one. 2 of the 8 are right. The small names show which way Bot used: both right answers did times first; a third times-first answer slipped to 64.

grpo:5.t: Grade on the curve. The group’s average score, 0.25, is the yardstick, as in the baselines reel. An answer’s advantage is score minus average: plus 0.75 if right, minus 0.25 if wrong. G R P O, Group Relative Policy Optimization, also divides by the 8 scores’ spread, the standard deviation, here 0.43, giving plus 1.73 and minus 0.58. That puts every question on one scale, though a lone right answer in 8 would get plus 2.65. Equal scores mean zero spread, and advantages set to 0.

grpo:6.t: No critic needed. P P O usually trains a critic, a second network that predicts the expected score, to serve as the yardstick. For a language model the critic is about as big as the model itself. G R P O uses the group’s average instead. The price is several answers per question; the gain is one less big network to train and store.

grpo:7.t: One update. As in the policy gradient reel, a chance is e to a preference, rescaled. Each answer adds advantage times (1 minus chance) to its way’s preference and takes advantage times chance from the others, averaged over the group. Times first rises from 0.20 to 0.30, left to right falls from 0.40 to 0.33. A K L leash, beta (beta) 0.04, pulls toward the original Bot, as in R L H F. Real G R P O also clips like P P O; with one pass per batch the clip never acts.

grpo:8.t: A training run. Each update: 8 questions, half easy on average, 8 answers each: 64 answers. Chart: test accuracy per update; bars: Bot’s chances. After 40 updates accuracy rises from 0.53 to 0.95. Guessing and left to right fade to 0.01 and 0.02; times first and check grows to 0.87. Even times first drops to 0.11: its slips lose to checked answers in the same groups.

grpo:9.t: Silent groups. If all 8 answers are right, or all wrong, every advantage is 0: the group teaches nothing. In updates 1 to 10, 11 percent of easy-sum groups were silent, 2 percent of hard. By updates 31 to 40, as Bot improves, that rises to 51 and 49 percent. Easy and hard are now equally silent: left to right, the one way failing only on hard sums, has nearly vanished. Useful questions: those Bot gets right only sometimes.

grpo:10.t: Your turn. Drag the group size. Updates still use 64 answers, so bigger groups mean fewer questions. The curve: the chance a group is not silent, for a question Bot gets right with chance p. The card averages 20 runs after 40 updates, so group 8 shows 0.93, not one run’s 0.95. Tiny groups are often silent. Group 16 does best here, 0.95: a steadier yardstick outweighs fewer questions.

grpo:11.t: It sharpens, it does not invent. Suppose Bot never checks: that chance starts at 0, its share spread over the other three ways. No group ever contains a check, so nothing can reward it. The same training reaches 0.87, against 0.95 with checking. G R P O raises ways Bot already sometimes uses. And a checker is only as honest as its rules: one accepting any answer containing the right number could be gamed.

grpo:12.t: Where it is used. G R P O was introduced in DeepSeekMath (Shao and colleagues, 2024) to train a model on maths problems. DeepSeek R 1 (2025) used it with rule-based rewards: is the final answer right, is the format followed. During R1’s training its answers grew longer and more often contained checking and rethinking, habits the starting model already showed now and then. Many labs now train reasoning models in a similar way.

grpo:13.t: Recap. When answers can be checked by a program, the checker gives the reward. For each question, sample a group of answers and score them. Each answer’s advantage is its score against the group’s average, scaled by the spread: no critic needed. A K L leash keeps the model near where it started, and groups that are all right or all wrong teach nothing.

saferl:0.t: Safe  and  Constrained R L. Win the game, but never cross the line.

saferl:1.t: A room with a glass floor. A new room for Pip: 6 cells across, 4 up, no rocks, no cat. Start bottom left, cheese bottom right: plus 1 on the step onto it, which ends the walk; every other step pays 0; gamma (gamma) equals 0.9. In the middle of the floor are four glass panels. Stepping on them changes nothing in Pip’s reward. That is exactly the problem.

saferl:2.t: A second number: cost. We care about the glass: every step onto a panel risks breaking it. So we count a second signal, the cost: 1 per step onto glass, 0 otherwise. Cost stays separate from reward: reward says how well Pip did, cost how much harm it risked. Ideally harm stays low even while Pip learns; we will see how far this method gets.

saferl:3.t: Two routes. The shortcut runs along the bottom: 5 steps, 2 of them on glass. The detour goes up and around: 9 steps, no glass. Counted from the start with the 0.9 discount, the shortcut’s cheese is worth 0.9 to the 4th, 0.66. The detour’s is 0.9 to the 8th, 0.43. Reward alone prefers the shortcut.

saferl:4.t: Pip ignores the glass. First Pip trains for 300 walks with Q-learning on reward alone, as in earlier reels, one move in five random. It learns the shortcut. Over walks 201 to 300 it stepped on glass 3.0 times per walk on average: the 2 of the shortcut, plus random moves that land on glass.

saferl:5.t: Why not a fixed penalty?. We could subtract a fixed penalty w per glass step, counted plainly, undiscounted. The shortcut is then worth 0.66 minus 2 times w, the detour 0.43. Below w equals 0.11 the shortcut always wins, two glass steps every walk, random moves aside; above it the detour always wins, none. Only w exactly at the tie could mix routes, a knife-edge found only with all these numbers.

saferl:6.t: Say what you want. Constrained R L states the goal directly: maximise reward, with the usual 0.9 discount, subject to the average cost per walk staying under a chosen budget. Ours: at most 1 glass step per walk, on average. The shortcut costs at least 2, the detour almost nothing, so meeting the budget best means taking the shortcut only some of the time. Pip must find that balance.

saferl:7.t: A price on glass. The trick: a price lambda (lambda) per glass step: Pip maximises reward minus lambda times cost. After each walk, lambda rises by 0.01 times the overspend, glass steps minus budget, never below 0. Overspend and the price rises; underspend and it falls. In maths, lambda is a Lagrange multiplier, turning a limit into a price. The 0.01 is a knob: larger reacts faster but swings more; smaller overspends longer.

saferl:8.t: Two notebooks. Pip keeps two numbers per move: reward to come, discounted by 0.9, and glass steps to come, counted plainly like the budget. After each move, both are nudged, as in Q-learning, toward this step’s result plus the next number, scaled by 0.9 for reward, not for glass. “Next” means the move Pip would pick by its score: reward minus lambda times glass. So the glass number reflects how Pip really plans to act, and a new price changes its choices at once.

saferl:9.t: Reading the chart. The chart starts at walk 301, when the price is switched on. Across: walks, up to 1000. Gold, on top: the price lambda. Rose, below: glass steps per walk, averaged over the last 25 walks. The dashed line is the budget, 1. Watch the two lines push against each other.

saferl:10.t: The price at work. At first Pip overspends and the price climbs, peaking at 0.53 on walk 345. The detour then wins and glass drops below budget, so the price drifts down until the shortcut sometimes wins again. Over the last 300 walks the price averages 0.12. Pip takes the bottom on 105 of them, about 2.3 glass steps each, and around on the rest, 0.3 each from random moves: 1 per walk, right on budget.

saferl:11.t: The tipping point. At the cell where the routes split, “right” promises 0.73 reward and 2 glass; “up” 0.48 and 0. The scores tie at a price of 0.13. From the start it was 0.11: reward shrinks with distance, glass does not, so the tie depends on where you stand. The price settles near there, 0.12 on average. Just below, Pip takes the shortcut; just above, the detour: small swings mix the routes.

saferl:12.t: Glass broken while learning. The budget holds on average, once the price settles. Before that, Pip stepped on glass a lot: 754 times in the first 300 walks, 712 more in the next 700. Even on the detour, random moves hit glass 0.3 times per walk. If one break is a disaster, averages are not enough. Safe exploration adds a shield, a hand-written rule blocking known-dangerous moves while Pip learns, or a safe starting habit.

saferl:13.t: Your turn. Pick a budget, in glass steps per walk. The run repeats: 300 free walks, then 700 with the price. Whenever routes must be mixed, the price settles near the tipping point; what changes is how often Pip takes the shortcut. A budget below even the detour’s cost cannot be met, and the price keeps climbing. A loose budget leaves the price near 0.

saferl:14.t: In the real world. Eitan Altman’s 1999 book set out constrained MDPs. In 2017, Joshua Achiam and colleagues proposed Constrained Policy Optimisation for deep R L, and in 2019 OpenAI released Safety Gym, simulated robots that must reach goals while avoiding hazards, where price-based methods like P P O-Lagrangian are standard baselines. The same idea suits robots with limits on force or energy. Real deployments add many more safeguards.

saferl:15.t: Limits to know. The constraint is about the average: single walks can still go over, and learning itself can break the limit, as we saw. Someone must choose the budget. And cost is written by people, just like reward. A badly specified cost can be gamed too, as the reward hacking reel showed.

saferl:16.t: Recap. Keep harm in its own signal, the cost, separate from reward. Constrained R L maximises reward while the average cost stays under a budget. A Lagrange multiplier is a price on cost that rises while you overspend and falls while you underspend; it settles at the tipping point between options.

her:0.t: Goal-Conditioned R L  and  H E R. Missed the target? Pretend you were aiming there all along.

her:1.t: Go to the flag. Cheese and cat are gone. Each walk a flag, the goal, is planted at a random spot for Pip to reach, starting at a random spot at least 0.3 away. Same moves and wobble. Landing within 0.04 of the flag pays plus 1 and ends the walk; other moves pay 0. Walks stop after 30 moves; that is not an ending, so the last target still adds 0.9 times a guess. gamma stays 0.9.

her:2.t: The goal is an input. A new flag every walk means no fixed set of Q-values works: “up” is good for a flag above Pip, bad for one below. So the goal becomes an input. Six inputs: Pip’s spot, the flag’s, and the gap between them, across and up. Handing over the gap, which it could compute, eases this small network’s job. 16 hidden units, four Q-values out: one goal-conditioned network for every goal.

her:3.t: Almost never there. At first Pip’s network knows nothing, so its moves are aimless, and the flag’s circle is tiny, only 0.04 from centre to edge: aimless walks almost never land in it. Here are a training run’s first walks. In the first 100 walks Pip reached the flag 12 times in this run; over four runs, 4.8 on average. Rewards this rare are called sparse.

her:4.t: A memory full of zeros. Look inside Pip’s replay memory after 2000 moves: 2000 cards, only 9 with a reward of plus 1. Every other target is 0 plus 0.9 times a guess, and guesses start near 0. So nearly every lesson copies one guess from another, with no real reward behind it. The 9 successes are drowned out; almost nothing tells the network which way leads to a flag.

her:5.t: Training on zeros. Four training runs, 10000 moves each. Every 500 moves, Pip is tested on 30 fixed start-and-flag pairs, following its largest Q-value. The chart counts the flags it reaches, out of 30. After 10000 moves the four runs reach 21, 2, 6, 0 flags. One run broke through late; the other three stayed low.

her:6.t: A miss, in hindsight. Here is one failed walk from training. The flag was at (0.51, 0.19); after 30 moves Pip was stopped at (0.18, 0.17), well outside the flag’s circle. Now ask a question in hindsight: what if the flag had been where Pip ended? Then the very same walk would have been a success. Nothing about the moves changes; only the goal written on the cards.

her:7.t: Store it twice. This is Hindsight Experience Replay, or H E R (Marcin Andrychowicz and colleagues, OpenAI, 2017). Each failed walk’s cards are stored twice: with the real goal and reward 0, and with the goal moved to where the walk ended. In the copy, each move landing within 0.04 of the new goal pays plus 1 and ends it: always the last move, plus any earlier one that close (here, none). The rest pay 0 but bootstrap from the plus 1, as in T D.

her:8.t: Why that is not cheating. The copied cards tell the truth: from those spots, those moves really did lead to that place. So Pip truly learns to reach it. Early walks often end against the fence, so many hindsight goals sit there, gold below. That still helps: the network reads the gap to the goal, so practice on any goal teaches the skill the real flags need, shrinking the gap.

her:9.t: A memory with successes. With H E R, after 2000 moves: 3620 cards. Only failed walks are copied: 54 walks times 30 moves equals 1620 copies. 313 cards carry plus 1 (without H E R: 9). 285 are copies, about 5 per copied walk, because Pip often lingered near its end spot: 253 from walks pinned against the fence. Real successes stay rare at first, but plenty of lessons now end in plus 1, teaching the network to steer toward a goal.

her:10.t: The race. Now the race: four runs with H E R, teal, and the same four without, orange, same seeds, same number of updates. Each minibatch draws 32 cards at random from the whole memory, real cards and copies alike. Thin lines: single runs; thick: averages. After 10000 moves, with H E R the runs reach 28, 23, 27, 25 of 30 flags, 25.8 on average. Without it, 7.3.

her:11.t: Any flag. Here is the H E R network of run 1 after training, sent to six test flags in turn. It never trained on these exact pairs; it reads the gap and steers. It reaches 5 of these 6. Near a flag it sometimes overshoots: one move covers 0.15, while the flag’s circle reaches only 0.04 from its centre, so the last step must land just right.

her:12.t: Your turn. Tap the meadow to plant a flag. Pip starts bottom left and follows the H E R network’s largest Q-value, no random moves. Try flags far away, near the edges, and close by. The network was never told about your flag; it only reads where it is.

her:13.t: Where it’s used. Andrychowicz and colleagues used H E R with D D P G, the D D P G reel’s off-policy learner for continuous moves, on a simulated robot arm: pushing a block, sliding a puck, picking and placing an object, with reward only on success. Without H E R, plain D D P G failed these tasks; with it, the arm learned all three. A pick-and-place policy trained in simulation also worked on a real arm. Feeding the goal in as input goes back to Tom Schaul and colleagues, 2015.

her:14.t: Limits. H E R needs goals that are reachable places, so wherever a walk ends can be written down as a goal. For a goal like “win the game”, an accidental ending is rarely useful. It also needs an off-policy learner like D Q N or D D P G, since the copies were made chasing another goal. Here each copy uses the walk’s final spot; the paper did even better with its “future” strategy, relabelling each card with spots the same walk reached later.

her:15.t: Recap. A goal-conditioned network gets the goal as input, so one network serves every goal. With a reward only at the goal, early walks almost never succeed, and the memory fills with zeros. Hindsight Experience Replay stores each failed walk again as a success for the spot it reached. The moves really got there, so the lessons are true, and they teach the network to steer.

rnd:0.t: R N D  and  Go-Explore. How agents finally cracked the hardest exploration game.

rnd:1.t: Back in the meadow. Remember the meadow from the function approximation reel? Pip’s position there is two numbers, x and y. Each move goes 0.15 in its direction, plus a little random wobble. Because of the wobble, Pip practically never stands on exactly the same spot twice. Keep that in mind: it is about to break the counting trick from the curiosity reel.

rnd:2.t: A long meadow. Pip’s new meadow is 4 long and 1 wide, with Pip starting at the left. The cheese circle sits at the far right end: plus 1 on the move that lands inside it, and the walk ends. No cat. Each walk is cut off after 40 moves, back to the start. Even walking straight right, the cheese takes at least 25 moves.

rnd:3.t: Random wandering. First, a Pip that picks every move at random, for 30 walks. Each walk is drawn as its own trail of dots. The farthest it ever gets is x equals 1.16, not even halfway. It never reaches the cheese. Random steps cancel out, as they did in the maze.

rnd:4.t: Nothing to count. Those walks landed on 1200 spots. Only 13 were exact repeats, all in the two left corners, where the fence squeezes Pip. So a count bonus would pay the first-visit 0.1 almost everywhere, even a hair away from a spot Pip has crossed many times. Counting only works when places repeat. Here, "near" never counts as "the same".

rnd:5.t: What we want instead. We want a sense of familiarity that spreads to nearby spots: if Pip has been around here a lot, here should feel boring, even if this exact spot is new. Networks do exactly that kind of spreading. In the function approximation reel, a nudge at one spot also moved the guesses at nearby spots.

rnd:6.t: A random network. Burda and colleagues’ 2018 trick: take a small network, fill its knobs with random numbers, and never train it. Feed it a spot: out come 4 meaningless numbers. Call it the fixed random network, not the D Q N reels’ target network, which copies the Q-network. The map shows its first number across the meadow, gold positive, rose negative: meaningless, but smooth and fixed.

rnd:7.t: The copier. A second network, the copier, tries to give the same 4 numbers. But it only gets lessons at spots Pip actually visits: after each move, one small gradient step that shrinks its copying error at that spot. The copying error is the average squared difference between the copier’s 4 numbers and the fixed random network’s 4 numbers.

rnd:8.t: Error marks the new. The copier gets lessons at the random walker’s 1200 spots, three times over. Before: error 0.08 on the left, 0.07 at x equals 3. After: 0.003 on the left, where Pip walked, and 0.047 at x equals 3, where it never went. Both maps share a colour scale; orange marks big error. So copying error works as a novelty bonus: Random Network Distillation, or R N D.

rnd:9.t: Familiar by accident. Before any lessons, a pale band runs along the copier’s middle, where Pip has never been: error 0.042 at x equals 2, against 0.243 near the top fence. By chance, the untrained copier already roughly matches the random network there. Spreading cuts both ways: lessons on the left also cut the error at x equals 3, from 0.07 to 0.047. Such accidents mislead Pip a little, until lessons fix them.

rnd:10.t: Why a random network?. Any fixed pattern would do; random knobs are just easiest. It never changes and looks only at what Pip sees now, so it can be learned: bars: a fresh copier’s error at x equals 2, falling. Next-view prediction must guess the future, which for a noisy TV is unguessable; R N D never predicts the future. But static that is new each time is still new input: less fooled, not immune.

rnd:11.t: Pip peeks. Pip knows roughly where each move leads, but not where the cheese is. Before each move it checks the copying error at the four landing spots and takes the biggest, except 1 move in 10 at random. Then the copier learns the new spot once. This toy Pip only explores, ignoring the cheese. Real R N D adds the bonus to the game reward and trains a policy on the sum.

rnd:12.t: The R N D explorer. Same start, fresh copier. The map shows the copier’s error at each walk’s start: as places grow familiar, the orange retreats, and Pip’s peeks lead it into fresher grass. In walk 1 it gets to x equals 2.06, and first lands in the cheese in walk 14. The bonus knows nothing about cheese: Pip finds it only by going where it has not been.

rnd:13.t: A chart of reach. To compare fairly, we run 20 different seeds of 30 walks each. Across: the walk number. Up: the farthest x reached so far, averaged over the 20 runs. The dashed line is the near edge of the cheese circle. A line that climbs means Pip keeps pushing into new ground.

rnd:14.t: Novelty pushes outward. Averages over 20 runs, not the run we watched. Gold, the random walker, creeps to 1.58 after 30 walks. Teal, the R N D explorer: 1.8 in walk 1, 3.85 by walk 30, at the far end. The bonus ignores the cheese, so hitting the circle, radius 0.12, is partly luck: R N D did in 11 of 20 runs, the random walker in 0. A learning agent would then use that plus 1.

rnd:15.t: Montezuma’s Revenge. The famous hard case is the 1984 Atari game Montezuma’s Revenge. An explorer climbs a pyramid of rooms, 24 on the first level, with keys, doors, ladders and deadly falls. Points are rare, each needing a long chain of exact moves. In 2015 the D Q N agent, master of many Atari games, scored 0 here. In 2018 R N D became the first method to beat the average human score without demonstrations.

rnd:16.t: Forgetting the frontier. Even with a bonus, every walk starts over. The R N D explorer reached x equals 2.06 in walk 1, but walk 2, from scratch, got only to 1.71. Our meadow has no fatal moves, so R N D copes; where a few wrong moves end the try, a promising place may never be reached again. Ecoffet and colleagues turned this around with Go-Explore, shown in 2019, published 2021: first return, then explore.

rnd:17.t: How Go-Explore works. Pip lumps spots into coarse cells, squares 0.25 wide, and keeps an archive: one saved spot per cell, the one reached in fewest moves. Counting again: coarse cells make places repeat, at the price of choosing the cell size by hand, which R N D avoids. Each round: pick a cell, favouring rarely landed ones, restore its saved spot like loading a saved game, then take 40 random moves.

rnd:18.t: Go-Explore in the meadow. Round by round, the archive of shaded cells grows outward. This run hits the cheese in round 31, with 60 cells saved. Over 20 runs it found the cheese within 60 rounds in 20, a median of 29 rounds. Its moves are random: remembering and returning do the work. A round has one walk’s moves but never pays for the trip back, and a real robot usually cannot restore a saved spot.

rnd:19.t: Your turn. Tap the meadow to give the copier 30 lessons around that spot. Watch the orange, its copying error, fade there and a little around it. Tap a few spots in a row to paint a familiar trail. Tap below the meadow to start over with an untaught copier.

rnd:20.t: Where it worked. R N D, from OpenAI in 2018, first beat average human play on Montezuma’s Revenge without demonstrations. Go-Explore, from Uber AI Labs, scored far higher there and did well on Pitfall, another very sparse game. Go-Explore explored by restoring saved game states, then trained a network policy by imitating its own best routes, so it could follow them even when the game behaves a little randomly.

rnd:21.t: Recap. When places never repeat, counting fails. R N D measures novelty as the error of a copier chasing a fixed random network: small where you have been, large elsewhere, and it spreads to nearby spots. Go-Explore keeps an archive of reached places, returns to one, and explores from there. Reward novelty, and remember the frontier.

curriculum:0.t: Curriculum Learning. Nobody learns calculus before counting. Neither should agents.

curriculum:1.t: A long way to the cheese. A bigger maze: 8 cells wide, 6 high, two walls of rocks, no cat. Cheese top right, Pip bottom left, shortest route 12 steps. plus 1 for the step onto the cheese, which ends the walk; gamma (gamma) 0.9. A walk without cheese after 30 steps is stopped and pays nothing. That is not a real ending: the last update still uses the landing number.

curriculum:2.t: How Pip learns. Pip uses Q-learning, as in its reel: a number per move per cell, nudged after each step toward the reward plus 0.9 times the best number where Pip landed. It mostly takes the biggest; one move in five is random. All numbers start at 0, so until Pip first reaches the cheese, every nudge is 0 toward 0: it learns nothing and just wanders.

curriculum:3.t: Wandering in the dark. Walk 1, from the real start. With every number 0, each move is a random pick among four. After 30 steps Pip has not found the cheese: stopped, reward 0, and nothing learned. It goes on like that. In its first 50 walks, Pip never reached the cheese; the first time was walk 57.

curriculum:4.t: Rare rewards, slow learning. The strip shows Pip’s first 300 walks, one bar each: teal if it reached the cheese, pale if stopped. Gold shading shows each cell’s best number. Each success pushes the good news only about one move further back, so the next is still mostly luck. Pip reached the cheese 22 times in 300 walks; only from walk 288 did its best numbers lead home.

curriculum:5.t: Start easy. A curriculum is a list of lessons, from easy to hard. Lesson 1: Pip starts only 3 steps from the cheese, for 20 walks. Lesson 2: 6 steps away, 20 walks. Lesson 3: 9 away, 20 walks. Then the real start, 12 away. Only the starting cell changes. The maze, the rules and the way Pip learns stay exactly the same.

curriculum:6.t: Lesson 1. Curriculum walk 1 starts 3 steps from the cheese, same seed as before. Even at random the cheese is close: Pip finds it in 9 steps, and the last move gets the first non-zero number. In lesson 1, 19 of 20 walks reached the cheese. The gold shading shows a trail of good numbers growing back from the cheese.

curriculum:7.t: Each lesson builds on the last. Lesson 2 starts 6 steps away. Pip still wanders, but only has to stumble into the gold trail; then the big numbers lead it home. 20 of 20 walks succeeded, then 13 of 20 in lesson 3. Then the real start: in its next 40 walks Pip reached the cheese 36 times. From walk 65, its best numbers led home from the real start.

curriculum:8.t: The same strip, with lessons. The same kind of strip, for the curriculum run. The black ticks mark the ends of lessons 1, 2 and 3; after that, every walk starts at the real start. Teal from the very beginning: the reward is no longer rare. Without the curriculum, the same seed gave 22 cheese walks in 300; with it, 287.

curriculum:9.t: Fifty runs, same seeds. One seed could be luck, so we repeat with seeds 1 to 50, testing after every walk: from the real start, following its biggest numbers, does Pip reach the cheese? Lines count passing runs; lesson walks count too. After 100 walks: 0 of 50 without, 50 with the curriculum; after 200, 4 against 50. Grey, another easy fix, starts each walk in a random cell: 19, then 47.

curriculum:10.t: Why it works. Learning needs rewards. On the hard task, rewards were so rare that most walks taught nothing. Easy lessons pay off almost every time, and what Pip learns there is exactly what it needs later: the end of the route. Compare reward shaping: shaping changes the rewards to give hints. A curriculum keeps the rewards and changes the tasks.

curriculum:11.t: Order matters. Bad pacing is slower. Too big a jump: 60 walks 3 steps away, then straight to the real start. After 100 walks 35 runs pass, against 50; all 50 pass from walk 146, against 69. Too slow: 120 walks on lesson 1. No run can pass before meeting the real start, so the fair measure is when all 50 pass: walk 172. The extra walks went on a skill Pip already had.

curriculum:12.t: Your turn. Drag the number of walks per lesson: the three lessons, 3, 6 and 9 steps away, each get that many walks before the real start. 0 means no curriculum. All 50 runs are redone; the rose line is always no curriculum. Too few walks per lesson and the trail is not ready; too many and walks are wasted.

curriculum:13.t: Automatic curricula. Hand-written lessons take knowledge and trial and error. Instead, a teacher program can pick the next lesson, like start cells where Pip now succeeds about half the time: not hopeless, not boring. Pip’s recent walks from each start tell it, without extra tests. Self-play, from the multi-agent reel, is a curriculum too: the opponent gets harder exactly as fast as the learner improves.

curriculum:14.t: Where it is used. In 2009 Yoshua Bengio and colleagues named machine curriculum learning, inspired by how people are taught. In 2017 Carlos Florensa and colleagues trained simulated robots by starting them near the goal and moving the start farther away, as here. OpenAI’s 2019 Rubik’s cube hand widened its randomised simulation as it improved: automatic domain randomisation, an automatic curriculum.

curriculum:15.t: Recap. When rewards are rare, an agent must stumble on success before any learning starts. A curriculum starts with easy versions of the task and makes them harder step by step. Easy lessons pay often and build skills the hard task needs. Order and pace matter: too big a jump or too slow both waste practice. A teacher can choose the lessons automatically.

metarl:0.t: Meta-R L: Learning to Learn. Train on many tasks so a new one takes minutes, not months.

metarl:1.t: A family of mazes. A new game: one room, five cups along the top, the cheese under one. Pip can’t see under a cup; it finds out only by stepping onto that cell. The cheese pays plus 1 and ends the walk; walks stop after 30 steps; gamma (gamma) 0.9. Each new maze, the cheese moves to a random cup and stays for that maze’s 10 walks.

metarl:2.t: Starting from scratch. Plain Q-learning, as in its reel, treats every maze as brand new: numbers start at 0, one move in five random, alpha (alpha) 0.2. Across: walks 1 to 10 on a new maze; up: steps taken, averaged over 300 new mazes; 30 means stopped. From scratch: 27.0 steps on walk 1, still 20.6 on walk 10. The shortest walk averages 5.2.

metarl:3.t: Learning to learn. But these mazes are alike: the cheese is always under a top-row cup. A learner that has seen many could know that, and search smartly. Meta-R L trains on many related tasks so a new one takes few tries. Two loops: an inner one adapting to one maze within its 10 walks, and an outer one, across thousands of mazes, improving how the inner loop adapts.

metarl:4.t: The task is hidden. Which cup hides the cheese is part of the state, and Pip can’t see it, just like the corridor cells in the fog reel. So this is a P O M D P, and the same fixes apply. With memory, Pip can carry what it found from one walk to the next. That is exactly what an adapting learner needs.

metarl:5.t: Memory across walks. So give Pip a memory that survives between walks of one maze: which cups were empty, and where the cheese was. It is wiped when a new maze begins. Pip’s policy now reads its cell plus memory: 925 situations, 3,700 numbers. A table copes here; a real R L squared agent’s memory is far bigger, so it uses a network. Pip is never told where the cheese is; it must find out, and remember.

metarl:6.t: Training on many mazes. The outer loop is ordinary Q-learning on cell plus memory, across mazes; the inner loop is memory filling up within a maze. It runs 3,000 mazes of 10 walks, one move in five random, alpha 0.2: 218,432 steps of experience. Every maze rewards the cheese. But to collect it fast in a new maze, the habit that pays is: search the cups, then remember. The numbers come to encode that.

metarl:7.t: A new maze. A new maze, cheese under cup 5. Walk 1: Pip heads for the cups and looks under them, finding the cheese in 10 steps; memory now holds the spot. Its order, nearest cup, then left, then right, is among the best, 6.8 steps on average without random moves; cup 5 is its worst case. Walk 2: straight there, 6 steps, the shortest. No random moves in these walks.

metarl:8.t: Where the learning lives. On new mazes Pip’s numbers are frozen, yet it adapts: the fast learning lives in its memory. The slow outer loop learned a fast inner learner. This is R L squared, written R L squared, from Duan and colleagues and from Wang and colleagues, both 2016. There a recurrent network also had to learn what to remember; our toy hands Pip ready-made memory slots.

metarl:9.t: Another idea: a good start. A second family, mammal (Finn, Abbeel and Levine, 2017), keeps ordinary learning as the inner loop and learns starting numbers from which a few steps fit any maze in the family. Our toy uses Reptile, mammal’s simpler cousin: copy the start, run Q-learning on one maze for 3 walks, move the start a tenth of the way toward the result; repeat for 3,000 mazes. Each pull is toward one maze’s answer; over thousands, the start settles on what all mazes share.

metarl:10.t: What the start knows. The learned start: in each cell, the move with the biggest starting number. From any cell the arrows reach the top row, sweep right along the cups, and come back from cup 5. It can’t know which cup, since that changes every maze; only where cups are. Without memory, it is one fixed set of numbers; on a new maze, ordinary Q-learning takes over.

metarl:11.t: Three learners, new mazes. Same 300 new mazes, all three still one move in five random. From scratch: 27.0 steps on walk 1. Learned start: 10.8, then 8.7 by walk 3 as Q-learning adapts. Memory: 9.0 on walk 1, then about 6.6 per walk. Random moves keep both above the shortest, 5.2. The start stalls higher: each visit moves a number a fifth of the way, so overriding its pull to every cup takes many walks.

metarl:12.t: The catch. Meta-learning helps only on tasks like its training ones. New family: the cheese on the left wall, in one of three cells, 3 to 5 steps from the start. By walk 10: scratch 10.5 steps, learned start 13.7, memory 24.5. Our memory has slots only for cups, so it can’t record this cheese; a real R L squared network might do better or worse. And the 218,432 training steps pay back only after about 1,200 new cup mazes.

metarl:13.t: Your turn. Slide to change how many mazes the memory learner trained on, from none to 3,000. The chart shows its steps per walk on the same new mazes, with the from-scratch line for comparison. How much outer-loop experience does it take before Pip has learned how to learn?

metarl:14.t: Where it matters. Meta-R L is studied for robots that must cope with a new load, a new surface or a damaged leg after a few tries, and for systems that must adapt quickly to a new user or opponent. Most results so far are in simulation, and on task families that are close together, like Pip’s cups.

metarl:15.t: Recap. Meta-R L trains on many related tasks so that a new one takes a few tries. The hidden task makes it a P O M D P. R L squared learns a fast learner that lives in memory: it searched the cups once, then remembered. mammal learns a good starting point for ordinary learning. Both help only on tasks like those they trained on.
